Of these, 813 (57%) newly acquired spectra from VLT/Xshooter or Palomar/Doublespec offer enhanced resolution (R>2500) and broad wavelength coverage (3200-10000 A). Our revised catalog includes newly identified AGN counterparts for the entire dataset and discusses key aspects for population studies, with 44 AGN redshifts discovered and 780 black hole mass and accretion rate estimates obtained. BASS DR2 achieves complete spectroscopic coverage for the entire AGN sample, boasting 99.8% redshift measurements and 96% completion of black hole mass estimates for unbeamed AGN outside the galactic plane. The AGN sample within this release represents a comprehensive catalog of the brightest hard X-ray selected AGN, spanning multiple orders of magnitude in Eddington ratio, black hole mass, and AGN bolometric luminosity.

Distortions to galaxy power spectrum and bispectrum signals arise from peculiar velocities and relativistic effects caused by a perturbed spacetime background. Furthermore, studies of Fourier-space correlation functions of tracers typically assume the plane-parallel approximation, where line-of-sight vectors are parallel. This work demonstrates the use of a simple perturbative approach to efficiently evaluate beyond plane-parallel (wide-angle) corrections to the power spectrum and bispectrum. It also introduces a straightforward method for finding the evolution of linear matter density fluctuations in a relativistic framework. By comparing wide-angle contributions to multipoles of the galaxy power spectrum with relativistic corrections, we estimate their possible contamination on local fNL measurements to be minor. We also compute wide-angle corrections in the presence of nonlinear terms at one-loop order. Notably, wide-angle effects generate imaginary, odd-parity multipoles of the galaxy bispectrum, often larger than previously known relativistic ones. We provide an estimator for measuring the leading order bispectrum dipole from data and calculate corrections to multipoles of real plane-parallel bispectrum multipoles, estimating the apparent local fNL induced to be of order unity.

This paper derives lower and upper limits for the blow-up durations in a system of stochastic partial differential equations influenced by two-dimensional fractional Brownian motion. By employing explicit solutions to related equations and a formula attributed to Yor, under certain conditions, we derive lower and upper limits for the blow-up time of the solution. Furthermore, we establish a time estimate for solutions that blow up within a finite time by adjusting specific parameters. Moreover, we calculate a lower bound for the likelihood of blow-up solutions using the techniques of Malliavin calculus.

In high-risk situations, it's essential for Deep Learning models to provide predictions with a measurable degree of certainty. The Conformal Prediction framework offers a flexible solution that ensures an optimal level of error, but its computational inefficiencies hinder its application to big data sets. We propose a new conformal loss function that streamlines the traditional CP process into a single step, allowing the model to directly link input data to the expected CP output distribution. By penalizing deviations from the expected CP output, our approach significantly reduces training times by up to 86% compared to the Aggregated Conformal Prediction method. In terms of performance, our novel loss function has been shown to be competitive with ACP in binary and multi-class classification tasks using the MNIST dataset.

The axion is a leading candidate for explaining the composition of our universe's dark matter. Researchers demonstrate that with current technology, the same experimental setup can be used to search for axions within the mass range of $500$ to $5000~\mu$eV within a year. By placing a magnetic rod inside a high-precision optical cavity, the interaction time is prolonged, enhancing the Faraday effect and yielding a significant signal. This is achieved through the rotation of the probe light's polarization plane. Different axion masses are isolated via a dc magnetic field, while detection occurs by counting optical photons using a high-efficiency photon counter in a quiet environment. Furthermore, a proposed optical interferometric method would provide valuable information on the properties of the targeted axions.

In a 2+1 spacetime setting, we translate the nonlocal BMS charges for a massless free Klein-Gordon scalar field into expressions involving the Green functions of polyharmonic operators. By examining the properties of these Green functions, we are able to investigate the asymptotic behavior of the field configurations necessary for the existence of the charges, and demonstrate that they yield a realization of the 2+1 BMS algebra within the canonical phase space. Furthermore, we explore the transformations in configuration space and find that the algebra only closes upon including skew-symmetric combinations of the field's equations of motion. This formulation using Green functions enables a potential extension of the formalism to higher dimensions and other systems.

In two-dimensional Rashba materials with a gate, electron pairs with specific properties arise from the combination of the effects produced by the Coulomb fields and the unique structure of the energy bands. This phenomenon is studied within the framework of the four-band Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang model and is driven by the charges on the gate. As a result, electron pairs are formed across the entire energy gap, with their binding energy being highly dependent on the applied gate voltage. Notably, despite the disruption of spin quantization by the spin-orbit interaction, these electron pairs possess a magnetic moment primarily generated by the orbital motion of the electrons, which can be controlled by adjusting the gate voltage.

An investigation is conducted into the relationship between the confinement scale $\Lambda_c$ in a gauge theory and the Hubble scale $H$ in a background quasi de Sitter space, particularly focusing on the Festina Lente criteria as dictated by the swampland principles. The study utilizes a holographic theory within the Karch-Randall setup, revealing that an unstable de Sitter extremum arises from a purely gravitational description. The Festina Lente requirements impose restrictions on the parameters of the perturbative gravitational dual, ruling out an arbitrarily small hierarchy for other parameters. The introduction of a scalar sector enables the theory to admit metastable de Sitter minima, with the Festina Lente requirements further constraining the parameters. However, in some scenarios where Festina Lente exerts a constraint, the de Sitter minimum approaches instability, thereby invalidating its applicability. The study also examines the consequences of the finite lifetime of the de Sitter extrema and its relation to other swampland conjectures, concluding that no contradictions arise. These findings bolster the consistency and practicality of the Karch-Randall setup, shed light on the implications of Festina Lente for holographic theories, and forge connections between Festina Lente and other swampland conjectures.

Recent advancements in domain generalization (DG) methods have been made, primarily using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). However, vision transformers (ViTs), which are gaining prominence, have been overlooked in terms of DG performance, despite surpassing CNNs on various benchmarks. Consequently, the practical application of ViTs is uncertain due to their limited ability to handle out-of-distribution scenarios. One major issue hindering the effectiveness of ViTs is overfitting to specific source domains. We introduce a novel DG approach for ViTs, referred to as self-distillation for ViTs, which aims to alleviate overfitting by simplifying the learning process and generating informative intermediate signals for the transformer blocks. This proposed method is lightweight and can be easily integrated into various ViT architectures. Our experiments demonstrate significant performance improvements in five challenging datasets, surpassing recent state-of-the-art DG techniques. Furthermore, we make our code and pre-trained models publicly available on GitHub.

This research establishes a framework for Anderson acceleration in combination with Newton's method for solving nonlinear systems, focusing on scenarios where the Jacobian matrix becomes singular at the solution. The standard Newton algorithm is known to exhibit linear convergence near the solution, but our analysis demonstrates how incorporating Anderson acceleration significantly enhances convergence without requiring additional a priori information and with minimal added computational expense. We present a thorough analysis of the Newton-Anderson algorithm in this context, introduce a safeguarding approach supported by theoretical underpinnings, and validate the convergence results using the Chandrasekhar H-equation and standard benchmark examples.

This paper delves into the realm of cybersecurity defense by integrating an innovative simulator with optimization techniques for informed decision-making. A primary focus is placed on a relatively new methodology - dynamic causal Bayesian optimization (DCBO). Our proposal suggests that DCBO can function as a proactive agent within a simulated network, armed with a network map and a causal model of how an attacker spreads malware. To evaluate the effectiveness of DCBO in making optimal adjustments to network nodes, thereby minimizing the costs associated with intrusions, we develop a comprehensive cybersecurity simulation system. Using this system, we gather empirical data for DCBO and present numerical findings that serve as a stepping stone for future research in this area.

To evaluate lepton flavour universality, we define the semi-inclusive ratio, 
$R_\Sigma$, for $\mu/e$ universality in $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions at 
$e^+e^-$ $B$-meson factories. Combining various decay channels in $R_\Sigma$ enhances sensitivity to potential LFU violations caused by short distance effects, and retains a straightforward theoretical explanation even if it deviates from the Standard Model prediction of $R_\Sigma^{\rm SM}=1$.

The primary aim of this research is to examine the constancy of a specific topological invariant known as non-barotropic generalized cross helicity within the context of non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics. Previous studies have predominantly focused on ideal barotropic and non-barotropic magnetohydrodynamics, leaving the non-ideal scenario largely unexplored due to its inherent mathematical intricacies. This study delves into the effects of dissipative processes such as thermal conduction, finite electrical conductivity, and viscosity on the cross helicity conservation. Through an analytical approach, we derive mathematical expressions for the time derivative of cross helicity, and the results reveal that generalized cross helicity is not conserved in non-ideal MHD conditions. Our findings also specify which dissipative processes impact helicity conservation and which do not, and identify the configurations where this topological constant remains preserved despite these dissipative processes.

We examine the fractional Burgers equation, $ \Delta^{\alpha/2} u + b\cdot \nabla (u|u|^{(\alpha-1)/\beta})$, on $d$-dimensional space, for $d \geq 2$, with $1 < \alpha < 2$ and $\beta > 1$. We demonstrate the existence of solutions for a broad class of initial conditions that include functions lacking $L^p$ norms for any $1 \leq p \leq \infty$. Furthermore, we apply these general results to the specific initial condition $u_0(x) = M|x|^{-\beta}$, $1 < \beta < d$, and prove the existence of a self-similar solution, as well as derive its properties, including smoothness, two-sided estimates, asymptotic behavior, and gradient bounds.

Our study is the first cosmological examination of $eROSITA$ clusters, which were discovered in the $eROSITA$ Final Equatorial Depth Survey. We used a joint analysis of X-ray and optical data to identify $455$ clusters across the redshift range of $0.1<z<1.2$. Out of these, $177$ clusters had sufficient data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam survey, allowing us to make uniform mass measurements using weak-lensing techniques. We used minimal assumptions to establish empirical relationships between the cluster mass and various observables, and to model the completeness of our X-ray selection. We also used the richness distribution of our clusters to directly measure their X-ray completeness and use those findings as informative priors. Our analysis framework was validated using mock data, and a blinded analysis of our real data further validated our approach through consistency tests. Following our unblinded analysis, we obtained cosmological constraints for $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$, $\sigma_{8}$, and $S_{8}$ in a flat $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, and for the equation of state parameter $w$ in a flat $w$CDM cosmology. Our findings were in agreement with previous results from the $Planck$ mission, the Dark Energy Survey, and the SPT-SZ survey, with differences of less than one standard deviation.

Through high-resolution numerical simulations of three distinct turbulent magnetohydrodynamic flows, we investigated the statistical characteristics of the energy transfer rate towards small scales. Our analysis of the energy cascade in both kinetic and magnetic energy revealed unique properties of each flux component, which varied depending on the flow's magnetic field strength and structure. We found that the probability distribution of the local energy flux exhibited extreme events, similar to those in hydrodynamic flows, and that its correlation with magnetic field gradients was stronger but more dispersed than in hydrodynamic flows. Additionally, the local energy flux was influenced by the local amplitude of the magnetic field. These findings have significant implications for developing subgrid scale models.

Autonomous vehicles and mobile robots often utilize multi-beam LiDAR sensors to collect series of 3D range scans ("frames"). Due to restricted angular resolution and occlusions, each frame provides incomplete and sparse data, hindering downstream applications such as object identification and 3D reconstruction. However, as the sensor moves, frames from multiple viewpoints are captured, offering complementary information and a more comprehensive understanding of the environment when combined. Yet, dynamic objects in the scene present a challenge, as merely reversing the scanner's motion is insufficient to accurately register their points. This paper delves into the accumulation of multiple 3D scan frames as an intermediate representation of the sequence and develops a novel method that leverages inherent patterns in urban environments, including their geometric layout and rigid object arrangements. In comparison to current state-of-the-art scene flow estimators, our approach aims to accurately register all 3D points within a common reference frame, effectively accumulating points on moving objects. The proposed method significantly reduces registration errors across several benchmark datasets and enhances the accuracy of high-level tasks such as 3D reconstruction.

The BAT AGN Spectroscopic Survey (BASS) aims to compile a comprehensive database of properties for local active galactic nuclei (AGN), focusing on supermassive black holes (SMBHs) with low redshift values (z < 0.3), including their luminosity, mass, and other defining characteristics. In this context, we discuss the second data release of BASS, which represents the most extensive spectroscopic survey to date in terms of spectral range, resolution, and sensitivity, encompassing over 1,400 optical and near-infrared spectra for the brightest 858 AGN in the observable sky, spanning a wide range of obscuration levels. This comprehensive dataset provides precise measurements, including redshifts and black hole masses for nearly all AGN, with nearly complete sets of essential data points and accurate assessments for a vast majority of cases. By offering a detailed examination of nearby powerful AGN, spanning a broad spectrum of luminosity, mass, Eddington ratio, and obscuration, BASS DR2 facilitates a deeper understanding of SMBH growth, its relationship to host galaxy evolution and feedback, and other fundamental questions surrounding SMBH physics.

One of the primary objectives of the JWST is to investigate the early universe's first galaxies. A comprehensive photometric analysis of extremely distant galaxies in the JWST's first deep field, which lies near the massive galaxy cluster SMACS0723, has led to the discovery of several galaxy candidates at early stages in the universe's history. Specifically, we found two potential galaxies existing around 250 million years after the Big Bang, or at redshifts $z\sim 16$, and identified other candidates at redshifts $z\sim 12$ and 6 at redshifts between 9 and 11. By incorporating color data from seven filters on the NIRCam and NIRISS instruments, we expanded our search to galaxies as distant as those at redshifts $z\sim 21$. Utilizing the \texttt{EAZY} and \texttt{BEAGLE} tools, we validated our photometric redshift estimates. While the intrinsic brightness of our high-redshift galaxies matches that of typical galaxies at redshifts greater than 10, they generally exhibit smaller sizes and are consistent with disk-like morphologies. The galaxies at the highest redshifts display exceptionally blue UV light, young ages ranging from 10 to 100 million years, and stellar masses equivalent to $\log(M_{\star}/\mathrm{M}_{\odot})=8.8$, indicating a rapid growth of their star masses. The results of our research clearly demonstrate the JWST's capability to identify reliable galaxy candidates at very high redshifts and offer insights into the early stages of galaxy formation.

Finding the wormhole solution involves solving Einstein's field equations under the condition of violating the null energy condition, which allows for its discovery in the context of the $\kappa(R,T)$ gravity framework. Two approaches are used to represent wormhole solutions: Firstly, a shape function is derived from a redshift function and linear equation of state, resulting in a wormhole model that accommodates realistic matter. Secondly, four combinations of two redshift functions and two shape functions are considered, leading to the analysis of the resulting solutions, some of which demonstrate the possibility of wormhole existence with minimal amounts of exotic matter.

Lattices governed by non-Hermitian Hamiltonians exhibit a distinctive form of energy gap and sensitivity to boundary conditions due to the skin effect. The conventional relationship between bulk and boundary states is disrupted in such systems. To address this, we establish the bulk-boundary correspondence for a fundamental class of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians lacking symmetries and characterized by one complex band. We obtain this class of Hamiltonians through the mean-field dynamics of driven-dissipative cavity arrays where non-reciprocal hopping amplitudes and gain and loss are explicitly modelled via interaction with engineered and non-engineered reservoirs. By removing the ambiguity in defining the topological invariant, we demonstrate that spectra differing in a complex energy shift are distinct; the origin of the complex plane provides a unified reference for evaluating the invariant. Consequently, topologically non-trivial Hamiltonians represent a subset of those with a point gap, and the skin effect does not stem from topological properties. We apply the singular value decomposition to these non-Hermitian Hamiltonians to express the bulk-boundary correspondence in a simplified form: the integer topological invariant defined in the bulk corresponds to an equivalent number of singular vectors localized at the system edge under open boundary conditions, with the sign of the invariant determining the edge location. Topological properties manifest as directional amplification of coherent inputs with exponential gain in system size. Our findings resolve a long-standing problem in non-Hermitian topological phases and open new avenues for topological photonics research.

Our study shows that magnetic impurities near the surface of FeSe$_{1-x}$Te$_x$ lead to the formation of stable energy-neutral states. We discovered that the magnetic field produced by the impurities causes the formation of spin-triplet inter-atomic pairs rather than the common spin-singlet intra-atomic pairs found in the pure material. This type of pairing preserves the symmetry of time reversal and has topological properties, resulting in the emergence of stable energy-neutral modes at the boundary between areas with different types of pairing. Moreover, these modes exist in pairs that remain unchanged regardless of the orientation of the magnetic field or the distance between the impurities. We believe our theoretical findings are in line with the results of recent experiments on FeSe$_{1-x}$Te$_x$.

We are releasing the second near-infrared dataset of the BAT AGN Spectroscopic Survey, which comprises observations of 168 active galactic nuclei from a broader Swift survey. The study shows that 45% of Seyfert 2 and 60% of Seyfert 1 galaxies exhibit specific high-ionization features. A comparison of near-infrared and X-ray emissions found a stronger relationship between the Si vi line and X-ray emissions than between the O iii line and X-ray emissions. No correlation was detected between the ionization potential and the X-ray photon index. The study also observed a trend of increased line blueshift with higher ionization potential in several lines, indicating a radial structure. The measurements of black hole mass using the Hα line were found to be underestimated due to dust obstruction, whereas the measurements based on the Paα and Paβ lines were in line with the established relation. The combined dataset of near-infrared observations now consists of 266 active galactic nuclei, representing the largest set of such observations assembled to date.

Our study focuses on the faint radio source population found in early data from the COSMOS field using the MeerKAT International GHz Tiered Extragalactic Exploration (MIGHTEE) telescope, with a specific emphasis on active galactic nuclei (AGN) emitting radio waves. From an extensive dataset, we identified 88% of 5223 radio sources in the COSMOS field as AGN or star-forming galaxies. By analyzing a subset of radio-loud AGN with redshifts up to 6 and moderate radio luminosities, we classified them as high-excitation and low-excitation radio galaxies and discovered no substantial differences in their host galaxy properties. Contrary to previous research, we found that both high-excitation and low-excitation radio galaxies exhibit similar Eddington-scaled accretion rates, suggesting that a previously unknown population of slowly accreting AGN may share characteristics with high-excitation radio galaxies. Furthermore, we determined that a black hole mass exceeding 10 to the 7 point 8 solar masses is necessary for launching a jet with mechanical power exceeding the radiative luminosity of the AGN, and both a high black hole mass and its spin might be required to maintain a dominant radio jet.

The total entropy from identified objects in the universe falls drastically short of the maximum possible entropy, which is indicated by the holographic limit. This disparity leads us to propose the existence of dark matter, comprised of extremely large, ancient black holes, alongside the dark matter already confirmed within galaxies and galaxy clusters.

Cardiovascular diseases pose a significant threat to global health, and their prevalence continues to rise, emphasizing the importance of early and precise diagnosis in achieving effective treatment and prevention outcomes. The electrocardiogram (ECG) is the primary diagnostic tool for identifying a wide range of cardiovascular disorders. Standard 12-lead ECGs are widely used in clinical settings and research, but employing a reduced number of leads can enhance the accessibility and feasibility of ECG monitoring through portable or wearable devices. This research develops a cutting-edge deep learning model that accurately detects multiple cardiovascular anomalies using only three ECG leads.

A new interpolation method is developed to estimate magnetic fields from scattered, unstructured data. It reconstructs the global magnetic field by combining orthogonal functions and calculates the coefficients by minimizing the difference between the true field and the reconstructed field on a set of training data. A constraint is applied to ensure that the method produces a divergence-free field, allowing for nearly zero divergence error. Experimental results demonstrate that the method's error decreases exponentially, outperforming local spline methods, and reduces computational complexity significantly. Unlike existing local methods, which use computationally expensive search algorithms, the new method efficiently evaluates magnetic fields while maintaining a small divergence error, even in complex magnetic configurations with islands and stochastic effects. This method is applied to calculate Poincaré sections from magnetohydrodynamic simulations in toroidal geometry, yielding more accurate results than current local methods.

A novel noise cancellation approach is introduced to accurately calculate clean measurements from multi-qubit systems that have been affected by noise. The protocol is universally applicable and adaptable to any noise model, regardless of the number of qubits or correlations present. Specifically, for a general observable influenced by Pauli noise, our technique yields a significant speed increase and consistently scales the Pauli basis components. Furthermore, we demonstrate how deconvolution can be achieved simultaneously with the estimation of noise parameters, thus avoiding computationally intensive methods like process tomography. Various examples and simulations are provided.

In the context of intelligent self-driving vehicles and ADAS systems, understanding behavioral and semantic relationships is crucial. Unlike other research focusing on trajectory, position, and bounding boxes, relationship data offers a concise, human-interpretable description of object behavior, allowing for the description of past and future states. As a result, it forms a foundational approach for tasks such as risk assessment, environmental understanding, and decision-making. This paper introduces RSG-Net (Road Scene Graph Net), a graph convolutional network designed to forecast potential semantic relationships from object suggestions and generate a graph-structured output, known as the "Road Scene Graph." Experimental outcomes show that the network, trained on the Road Scene Graph dataset, effectively predicts potential semantic relationships between objects surrounding the ego-vehicle.

This paper presents an extension of Proth's theorem for numbers in the form $Kp^n+1$. A corresponding primality test is developed, using one modular exponentiation similar to Fermat's test but without requiring GCD calculations. Furthermore, two additional tests are introduced to enhance the probability of confirming the primality of $Kp^n+1$ numbers. As corollaries, we establish three families of integers $N$, where primality can be verified solely by demonstrating that $a^{N-1} \equiv 1 \pmod N$. The concept of Safe Primes is also generalized as $a$-Safe Primes. The distribution of these numbers is examined, and a conjecture regarding their related $a$-SophieGermainPrimes appears to hold true for large primes.
We establish that all off-diagonal entries of the Moore-Penrose inverse of a tree's distance Laplacian matrix are negative.

We theoretically confirm the possibility of creating entangled photon pairs with a specific threshold in a system that uses a single three-level atom, two random light sources, and two specific coherent lights in a bimodal cavity setup. We found that the entanglement of these photons occurs only at low levels of the random light sources and is solely due to the specific coherent lights. Our findings show that using random lights with no coherent lights results in a strong reduction in the cavity's field fluctuations, along with inter-mode correlations, but no entanglement is observed. On the other hand, using only coherent lights produces entangled photon pairs but is unable to amplify them beyond a certain limit. However, our research reveals that adding small amounts of random light to the coherent lights significantly amplifies the entangled photon pairs. We analyzed our results in terms of an interplay between coherent and random processes, as well as in relation to dressed states of the cavity. The temporal correlations between the cavity's modes exhibit oscillations in the strong-coupling regime. Our theoretical approach for generating entangled and non-classical photons can have interesting applications in quantum metrology and quantum information science.

A mathematical model describes a strongly connected system that enters a non-Fermi liquid state at high temperatures. As a specific interaction is strengthened, the system's ground state transitions from an insulating phase to a superconducting phase through a quantum phase transition, where both states arise from the same underlying interaction mechanism. In the insulating state, resistance behaves according to activation principles with an activation energy that diminishes as the system reaches the quantum phase transition, resulting in an extended quantum critical regime with a resistance temperature dependence governed by algebraic principles. As the system's temperature increases within the superconducting phase, it undergoes a finite temperature transition to a Bose metal phase, thereby separating it from the non-Fermi liquid metal.

The Scintillating Bubble Chamber Collaboration is developing advanced liquid-noble bubble chambers for detecting low-mass dark matter and neutrino interactions. The team has successfully commissioned the SBC-LAr10 device, a 10-kg liquid argon bubble chamber at Fermilab, to test its ability to detect nuclear recoils with minimal background noise at extremely low energies. This setup will allow the researchers to refine the detector's sensitivity to dark matter and neutrino interactions. In parallel, a radiopure detector is being built for a dark matter search at SNOLAB, with the aim of achieving a sensitivity of $10^{-43}$ cm$^2$ at a 1 GeV$/c^2$ particle mass. The technique holds promise for future dark matter searches and neutrino interactions, with the potential to detect solar neutrino interactions in the near future and study neutrino interactions at nuclear reactors with high statistics.

This paper examines the challenge of creating a confidence sequence for bounded random processes. By expanding on a gambling approach introduced by Hendriks and others, this paper revisits and enhances the concept of Cover's universal portfolio in generating confidence sequences and establishes novel properties. This is achieved by adopting a two-horse race perspective on the gambling approach. A new algorithm is proposed, utilizing a mixture of lower bounds, which closely emulates the performance of Cover's universal portfolio with a low time complexity per round. A higher-order generalization of a previously developed lower bound may also be of separate interest.

Multi-agent problems that require coordination and involve partial observability are common in real-world scenarios. This paper focuses on a specific category of coordination challenges where humans can identify actions that clearly indicate abnormal circumstances, taken with the purpose of making other agents realize the unusual situation. We introduce a new concept called self-explaining deviations (SEDs) and provide a formal definition. To generate such SEDs, we propose the improvement maximizing self-explaining deviations (IMPROVISED) algorithm. Our evaluation of IMPROVISED is conducted in both a controlled environment and the widely recognized Hanabi benchmark, where it successfully produces finesse plays, exemplifying exceptional human-level theory of mind.

The use of electron quasiparticles has greatly simplified the description of many-body physics in solids, achieving remarkable results. Despite this, the application of Landau's Fermi-liquid theory to high-temperature superconducting cuprates remains a subject of debate. An alternative framework has been developed, known as electron fractionalization, to explain systems displaying fractional quantum Hall effects and Mott insulating behavior, although its relevance to cuprate pseudogap and superconducting phases remains uncertain. In this work, we demonstrate that excitonic excitations in optimally doped Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+\delta}$, occurring at energies far exceeding the superconducting-gap scale, are unexpectedly amplified as superconductivity develops. Our findings confirm the participation of these high-energy excitons in superconductivity. As a result, the observed enhancement in the spectral weight of excitons imposes a significant constraint on theories aiming to describe pseudogap and superconducting mechanisms. Furthermore, a two-component fermion model, incorporating electron fractionalization in the pseudogap state, is able to account for these changes, offering a new pathway for understanding the electronic structure of superconducting cuprates.

In this paper, we rigorously develop a broad class of complex self-similar 
solutions for the generalized surface quasi-geostrophic equation, marking 
the first successful derivation of its kind. Our solutions are non-symmetrical, 
locally integrable and can have multiple values, and interestingly, they 
share certain features with a previously computationally suggested finite time 
singularity scenario proposed by Scott and Dritschel in the SQG patch context.

The Little Glaisher theorem for positive integers $k, l, n$ establishes a fundamental relationship between the number of partitions of $n$ under specific constraints, specifically that the count of partitions meeting these constraints is equivalent whether parts are restricted by $k$ or $l$. Although this connection has been verified through generating functions, its underlying reasoning remains unclear. Our paper provides an explanation of this phenomenon via an arithmetic-based method and also explores potential applications of weighted words to a special case involving the number two.

Four previously unknown fast radio bursts have been identified in an exhaustive search through the Parkes 70-cm pulsar survey data archive. Utilizing the HEIMDALL and FETCH algorithms, a range of dispersion measures between 0 and 5000 pc cm$^{-3}$ were investigated. Each of these newly discovered FRBs exhibited remarkably wider pulse widths than the vast majority of previously cataloged FRBs. These broad pulses cannot be attributed to interstellar scattering or dispersive effects within channels. One of these FRBs possessed a remarkably high dispersion measure of 3338 pc cm$^{3}$, a value unparalleled in FRB history. Moreover, these findings demonstrate that pulsar survey archives remain a viable source for discovering previously overlooked FRBs. Our research further indicates that extending search durations beyond $\sim 100$ ms may unveil a significantly larger population of FRBs with broad pulses.

This paper introduces an innovative guidance algorithm based on model predictive control that optimizes the performance and robustness of a launch vehicle's upper stage, ensuring it meets the critical splash-down constraint. The algorithm effectively mitigates the uncertainty of engine performance and burn time, reducing the possible footprint of impact points. To minimize the risk of impact near inhabited areas, the proposed strategy includes a neutral axis maneuver that reduces the sensitivity of impact points to engine uncertainty. Unlike conventional approaches, the model predictive control algorithm can autonomously determine the neutral axis direction by efficiently solving a series of optimal control problems, thus enabling high update frequencies and rapid convergence to the optimal solution. The robustness and performance of the proposed algorithm are demonstrated through comprehensive Monte Carlo simulations.

This study analyzed the outcomes of a surgical procedure known as anterior temporal lobe resection (ATLR), used to treat severe epilepsy that has not responded to medication. ATLR involves the removal of a large amount of brain tissue. To understand how this surgery impacts brain structure, researchers examined 101 individuals with epilepsy before and after surgery using MRI scans. They developed a new method to analyze the brain's surface and found significant changes in various measures of brain morphology after surgery, including alterations in cortical thickness and other structural characteristics. These changes were most pronounced near the site of the surgery, but also occurred in regions of the brain that were connected to the affected area. To account for the effects of aging, the researchers also analyzed data from 924 healthy individuals. They found that the brain's restructuring following ATLR was reflected in changes across a wide area of the cortex. These changes may be caused by physical damage, degeneration, or the brain's ability to adapt and compensate for the loss of tissue. An additional analysis of the data revealed further effects beyond those observed using traditional measures.

We've investigated the potential for longitudinal, pinching instabilities in cosmic strings under various conditions. Using the thin string approximation and developing an enhanced analysis that accounts for small-scale fluctuations, we've predicted when these instabilities occur. Our simulations verified our predictions and showed that these instabilities often occur over a broader range in strings with magnetic properties than previously thought, and even in strings with electric properties. However, our findings confirm that certain strings, particularly those near the chiral limit and large vortons, are resistant to these instabilities.

In standard imaging scenarios, several essential components are required, including a light source, object interaction, and spatial resolution detection. However, these fundamental elements can hinder imaging of fragile biological samples or other sensitive specimens due to the lack of photons and potential damage. To overcome these challenges, we've developed and successfully implemented a novel quantum imaging approach that eliminates the need for these three requirements. This was achieved by integrating a Michelson interferometer with an induced coherence-based nonlinear interferometer, combined with single-pixel imaging, resulting in the first-ever demonstration of interaction-free, single-pixel quantum imaging of an object without using any undetected photons. Our breakthrough has pushed the limits of quantum imaging by removing the need for object-photon interaction and significantly reducing detection requirements. This pioneering work opens the door to new applications, including non-invasive single-pixel imaging of delicate specimens at visible wavelengths detectable by silicon-based technology.
This paper explores the subdifferential set of an operator and its connection to the subdifferential of its value at points where the operator reaches its maximum magnitude.

This tribute article is filled with fond and heartfelt memories of our cherished Prof. A.P. Balachandran. The main body delves into our newly developed quantum mechanics framework applied to (1+1)D noncommutative space-time, utilizing Hilbert-Schmidt operators. As a key example, we show how a system of a time-dependent forced harmonic oscillator within the Moyal space-time can exhibit a geometric phase.

Two pioneering technologies, Semantic Communication (SemCom) and Edge Computing, address the pressing needs of the Metaverse for vast data communication, efficient bandwidth, and swift data processing. However, Edge Computing resources are typically supplied by computing service providers, making it crucial to devise effective incentive mechanisms for the provision of limited resources. A Deep Learning-based auction, recently proposed as a mechanism, aims to optimize revenue while upholding key economic properties. In this research, we develop a design for the Deep Learning-based auction to allocate computing resources in the context of SemCom-enabled Metaverse. Initially, we provide a concise overview of the Metaverse's fundamentals and challenges. Next, we discuss the basics of SemCom and Edge Computing. Subsequently, we examine existing incentive mechanisms for trading Edge Computing resources. Finally, we present our design for the Deep Learning-based auction to allocate Edge resources in the Metaverse. The simulation results confirm that the auction enhances revenue while closely meeting individual rationality and incentive compatibility requirements.

Science evaluates the validity of competing theories or models by assessing how closely their predictions align with observed data. Consequently, the method used to measure alignment plays a critical role in shaping the knowledge gained. In the fields of machine learning and scientific modeling, similarity metrics serve as objective functions. For instance, mean squared error is an optimal measure of similarity when errors are normally distributed and follow specific patterns, but in many situations, this is not the case. In such instances, researchers must determine the most suitable objective function to guide their analysis. We will explore how information theory can inform this decision and illustrate this approach with a straightforward example from hydrology.

The bulk photovoltaic effect, despite being considered a weak effect, generates photovoltages exceeding the band gap due to its ability to produce photocurrent from an asymmetric material. We demonstrate the possibility of achieving high photoresponse by exploiting the BPE in BaTiO$_3$ films through tuning their fundamental ferroelectric properties via strain and epitaxial growth on various substrates. We discovered that the photoresponse does not increase linearly with ferroelectric polarization and obtained an unusually high BPE coefficient, exceeding previously reported values. The conventional descriptions of BPE in bulk materials cannot account for our findings, leading to the proposal of a novel mechanism that links polarization and responsivity in ferroelectric thin films. This work suggests that ferroelectric photovoltaics in standard planar film geometries can be optimized by combining bulk structure modification, enhanced light absorption, and improved electrode-absorber interfaces.

Fake news detection is no longer solely an academic pursuit due to its significant societal implications. Recent research primarily focused on text-based methods but has now moved to incorporate additional contextual information such as news article dissemination patterns and user behavior on social media. We suggest constructing social context graphs around news articles and reformulating the task as a graph classification challenge. Through experimentation with various information types and graph neural networks, our approach has demonstrated high effectiveness and robust results on a standard benchmark dataset.

Treating stance detection as a specific type of textual entailment recognition has potential benefits, including access to a broader range of training data and a more generalizable learning framework. This paper provides an initial empirical study of this approach, utilizing a challenging test scenario where existing stance detection datasets are lacking. By leveraging relevant insights from the social sciences, we aim to enhance the model's performance, and discuss potential avenues for future research.

The widespread adoption of home-based solar panels has led to frequent power surges, causing correlated reverse power flows. To protect electronics, solar inverters currently mitigate damage by temporarily halting energy production in response to power surges. This practice, however, unfairly affects households located far from the power source, resulting in an uneven allocation of the energy's value. To optimize curtailment and ensure fairness, accurate feeder data is necessary, which is often lacking. This study examines the effectiveness of reinforcement learning in developing a fair strategy for curtailing solar panel production by interacting with the power system. The evaluation of six fairness metrics reveals that all definitions facilitate efficient learning when compared to an optimal solution. The results suggest that reinforcement learning is a viable method for balancing the need for safe and equitable solar panel coordination.

The study of relativistic hydrodynamics has shown significant promise in explaining the behavior of matter produced in heavy-ion collision experiments, particularly in the context of hadron spin polarization. Despite current models offering some insights, there remains a lack of comprehensive understanding in the field, particularly in the realm of differential measurements. This indicates that a more nuanced approach is needed, one in which the spin is treated as an independent entity, not solely dependent on flow circulation. By considering the spin as a macroscopic property, its dynamics should conform to hydrodynamic laws. This thesis proposes a novel framework of relativistic hydrodynamics, incorporating spin dynamics from kinetic theory to model the behavior of matter produced in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. By assuming small polarization effects, we derive conservation laws for key quantities and investigate the properties of the spin polarization tensor. Our analysis reveals that only the transverse spin components propagate, similar to electromagnetic waves. We then examine the spacetime evolution of spin polarization under various symmetries, and find that our predictions for mean spin polarization per particle align with some experimental findings and model calculations, offering promising insights into the field.

Future wireless communication systems may utilize cell-free massive MIMO technology, offering enhanced coverage and spectral efficiency. In this study, we examine the potential of integrating cell-free massive MIMO with federated edge learning. By taking advantage of wireless channel properties, over-the-air computation is used to simultaneously send local updates, reducing communication overhead in federated learning over wireless networks. Accounting for channel correlation and imperfect channel information at the central server, we propose an implementation of OTA-FL on cell-free massive MIMO systems. Analytical and experimental analysis confirm the advantages of this approach for OTA-FL.

Attosecond pulse generation has utilized gating techniques, which restrict high harmonics to a single laser cycle, thereby limiting achievable pulse energy. To overcome this limitation, a new method, pumping ionizing gating (PIG), has been developed. PIG differs from traditional techniques by incorporating a long pulse that is reflected by an expanding plasma grating, thereby continuously feeding energy into the driving pulse. This process creates a narrow, dynamic "gating" mechanism that enables energy transfer from the long pulse to the generated attosecond pulses. A computational simulation demonstrated the effectiveness of this regime across a broad range of plasma densities and grating modulation depths. Results showed that a high-intensity, 330-as laser pulse can be produced using a relatively long pump pulse with a peak intensity significantly exceeding the pump, and a modest conversion efficiency.

Least-squares Magnetic Resonance (MR) reconstructions using an iterative method often rely on the Conjugate Gradient algorithm despite its known numerical problems. However, recent research has shown that LSMR (Least Squares Method for Regression) algorithm offers better numerical stability, making it a preferable choice when utilizing Toeplitz embedding is not feasible for accelerating Conjugate Gradient method.

Recent years have seen a surge of research activity arising from the convergence of non-Hermitian principles and topological concepts. This fruitful interplay has given rise to numerous novel non-Hermitian topological phenomena. In this review, we delve into the fundamental aspects governing non-Hermitian phases, focusing on topological properties. By examining exemplary models, including the Hatano-Helson, non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger, and non-Hermitian Chern insulator, we elucidate key features of non-Hermitian topological systems. Specifically, we explore exceptional points, complex energy gaps, and non-Hermitian symmetry classification, discussing the non-Hermitian skin effect and the generalized Brillouin zone, which enable the restoration of the bulk-boundary correspondence. Concrete examples are used to investigate the impact of disorder and to analyze the Hall transport properties of non-Hermitian topological systems. Additionally, we survey recent experimental advancements and outline promising research avenues for future investigations.

For a closed subspace within a given range space, certain conditions allow us to determine when a subspace of compact operators valued in this range space constitutes a proximinal subset of compact operators into the range space.

This paper provides three separate, independently derived proofs from its authors to prove a key assertion: for an Anosov flow on a 3-dimensional oriented manifold, having a Birkhoff section with positive values is identical to the flow's properties of being positively twisted and fully traceable.

SAP's Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system is a highly utilized platform supporting numerous organizational processes, such as Order-to-Cash (O2C) and Procure-to-Pay (P2P). However, its vast scope and vast amounts of contained data make it difficult to identify and document specific processes within a particular SAP instance, leading to the need for a list of related database tables. Ultimately, extracting an event log for process mining purposes from SAP ERP is a significant task. This demo paper presents the tool Interactive SAP Explorer, which overcomes the challenge of process identification and selection by translating the complex relational structure of SAP ERP into a labeled property graph. This approach enables users to formulate intricate queries and visualize the relational structure in a more advanced and meaningful way.

The proliferation of hateful memes on social media has detrimental effects not only for platforms but also for society as a whole.  Identifying such memes is difficult due to their ever-changing nature; hateful content can arise by incorporating malicious undertones into existing cultural ideas or symbols. This paper introduces a novel framework that employs OpenAI's multimodal contrastive learning models, notably CLIP, to identify the targets of hateful content and investigate the evolution of memes. Our analysis reveals that CLIP-generated embeddings exhibit inherent semantic regularities that describe relationships within the same or different modalities. We utilize this property to examine how hateful memes are created by combining visual elements from multiple images or integrating textual information with an image containing hateful content. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in analyzing the evolution of hateful memes by focusing on antisemitic content, specifically the Happy Merchant meme. Through our framework's application to a dataset extracted from 4chan, we identified 3.3K variants of the Happy Merchant meme, some of which were linked to specific countries, individuals, or organizations. Our framework is envisioned to assist human moderators in flagging new variants of hateful memes, thus enabling moderators to manually verify and mitigate the spread of hateful content online.

Our simulations examined the effect of adding small quantities of solute to a solvent, modeled with a two-scale potential that mimics water's unique properties. We varied the strength of the attractive interactions between the solute and solvent, and found that when the solute has a strong affinity for the solvent, it acts as a structure-forming agent, increasing the solvent's maximum density temperature with addition. Conversely, when the solute has a weak affinity for the solvent, it acts as a structure-disrupting agent, decreasing the solvent's maximum density temperature.

Recent breakthroughs in patch-based models such as Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Mixers have led to significant advancements in various visual recognition tasks, gradually replacing classic convolutional networks. However, the initial models treated patches equally without considering spatial information. Recent research indicates that incorporating inductive bias such as spatial awareness can improve patch representations. Nevertheless, previous works have predominantly focused on patch locations rather than the overall structure of images. In response, our proposed model OAMixer incorporates object information into patch mixing layers, adapting to the object labels obtained via unsupervised or weakly-supervised methods, eliminating the need for human annotation. OAMixer computes a learnable reweighting mask that prioritizes patch interactions based on object similarity, thereby enhancing object-centric representations in various models, including ViTs, MLP-Mixers, and ConvMixers. Moreover, our results demonstrate that OAMixer boosts classification accuracy and background robustness, while also improving performance in large-scale classification, self-supervised learning, and multi-object recognition tasks, solidifying its generic applicability.
This talk revisits the challenge of creating a developable surface segment enclosed by two curves that can be expressed using rational or NURBS (Non-Uniform Rational B-spline) functions.

To accurately determine the minimal surfaces with the same boundary from the boundary geometry, we suggest a fast and accurate numerical approach. Our numerical strategy relies on the fundamental solutions method. We conduct a convergence analysis for the Dirichlet energy and examine the $L^\infty$-error in mean curvature. Crucially, each approximate solution in our scheme is a continuous, smooth surface, which contrasts with previous methods that necessitated mesh discretization.

In the Maker-Breaker game on a graph G, the goal is to either select a dominating set as Dominator or a closed neighborhood of a vertex as Staller. We investigate scenarios where Staller emerges victorious. When Dominator and Staller initiate the game, the minimum number of moves needed for Staller to win is represented by γ SMB (G) and γ SMB'(G), respectively. For every positive integer k, the properties of trees T with γ SMB'(T) = k are identified. Utilizing hypergraphs, a general upper bound for γ SMB'is established. We consider subdivided stars, obtained from stars by subdividing their edges multiple times. For subdivided stars, the minimum number of moves for Staller to win, γ SMB'(S), is determined for most cases except when the number of subdivisions is four or more and all subdivisions have an even number of edges. In the simplest scenario with at least two odd subdivisions, the minimum number of moves for Staller to win is the ceiling of the base-2 logarithm of the sum of the smallest two odd subdivisions. Furthermore, we derive exact formulas for the minimum number of moves for Dominator and Staller to win on caterpillars.

The evolution of social dilemmas is significantly influenced by environmental changes in various ecosystems and societies. Environmental changes can be categorized into global fluctuations and local feedbacks, which have traditionally been examined separately. However, the effects of these changes when combined are still poorly understood. We have developed a theoretical framework that considers group strategies alongside their dynamic environments, incorporating a non-linear element in public goods games and describing local feedbacks through eco-evolutionary games. Our research demonstrates that the interplay between game-environment dynamics differs depending on whether the global environment is static or dynamic. Notably, our findings indicate the emergence of recurring cycles of cooperation among groups and local environments, creating complex patterns in phase space, influenced by the relative speeds of global and local environmental changes compared to strategic shifts. The insights gained from this study shed light on how diverse evolutionary outcomes arise from non-linear interactions between strategies and changing environments.

Researchers have found that even smooth, fractal surfaces can scatter acoustic waves when they have minimal surface area. To address such scattering problems, they developed a boundary element method where each basis function is supported within a fractal set and integration is performed with respect to a non-integer Hausdorff measure, rather than the traditional surface measure. By applying recent theories on function spaces in fractals, they established the convergence of a Galerkin formulation for acoustic scattering in higher dimensions, given a compact fractal scatterer within a predefined dimension range. Furthermore, they derived convergence rates for specific fractals and superconvergence for specific functional classes. Additionally, they proposed and analyzed a numerical method, including routines and a fully discrete convergence analysis, to implement the new method on fractal surfaces, and provided supporting numerical evidence for their results, including examples of Cantor sets and Cantor dusts.

Deep learning models often falter when data comes from a distribution different from the one used for training, posing a significant problem in critical applications such as medical imaging. Out-of-distribution detection can help identify such data samples, thereby increasing the reliability of the model. Recent studies have developed deep learning-based OOD detection methods, yielding promising results for 2D medical images. However, most of these approaches are computationally impractical for 3D images and struggle to accurately identify synthetic OOD samples. This limited performance may indicate that deep learning models have difficulty embedding large volumetric images efficiently. We argue that the intensity histogram of the original medical scan provides a sufficient embedding for OOD detection. Therefore, we propose a histogram-based method that relies on non-deep learning techniques, achieving near-perfect results in this domain. Our proposal is backed by two lines of evidence: we achieved perfect AUROC scores in various setups using publicly available datasets, and we ranked second in the Medical Out-of-Distribution challenge without any fine-tuning or leveraging task-specific knowledge. After carefully considering the limitations, we conclude that our histogram-based method effectively solves the sample-level OOD detection problem for 3D medical images in the current context.

We created and studied an acoustic metasurface composed of a series of sound-hard cavities, 
configured into a 1D array and featuring a unique, complex internal structure created 
by 3D printing. This internal structure is achieved by strategically embedding connecting 
cavities beneath the surface, allowing for the manipulation of localized acoustic surface 
waves. By introducing these additional power-flow channels, we observed and experimentally 
verified the presence of negatively dispersing 'backwards' waves within the first Brillouin zone. 
This discovery offers a potential pathway to improve acoustic sensing capabilities using 
acoustic metasurfaces.

A new determination of the $C\!P$-even fraction $F_+$ in the $D^0$ decay to $K^+K^-\pi^+\pi^-$ is provided using $2.93$ fb$^{-1}$ of $e^+e^-\to\psi(3770)$ data from the BESIII detector. By analyzing the relative rates of double-tagged charm meson decays in signal and $C\!P$ eigenstate modes, the $F_+$ value is found to be $0.730 \pm 0.037 \pm 0.021$. This is the first model-independent measurement of $F_+$ in $D^0 \to K^+K^-\pi^+\pi^-$ decays.

We focus on the PT-symmetric quantum Rabi model (PTQRM), which is a system of a PT-symmetric qubit interacting with a quantized light field. By employing the adiabatic approximation (AA) and numerical diagonalization, the model can be solved analytically, allowing us to explore various physical properties in the relevant parameter regime. Using the adiabatic approximation and numerical diagonalization, the model is analyzed with regard to its static and dynamic properties, including the emergence of exceptional points (EPs) in the eigenspectrum, which are found to be closely linked to the exactly solvable points of the model's Hermitian counterpart. Notably, the EPs are observed to appear and disappear in relation to the strength of light-matter coupling. Furthermore, the time-dependent behavior of physical observables is discussed under the system's Hamiltonian, and the results can be easily generalized to other light-matter interaction models, offering valuable insights into the study of non-Hermitian quantum systems.

The advent of gravitational wave astronomy is expected to allow for the detection of the astrophysical gravitational wave background from merging binary black holes and potentially reveal the presence of gravitational waves from the universe's early days. Specifically, the low-frequency end of the gravitational wave spectrum may offer a clear opportunity to accurately measure fundamental cosmological parameters, such as the universe's equation of state or the presence of free-streaming particles at early epochs. We investigate whether uncertainty in the astrophysical gravitational wave foregrounds, which coexist with a primordial background, pose a threat to this research programme. We outline the assumptions necessary to consider the astrophysical foregrounds as known in shape but uncertain in magnitude, enabling a simple and efficient method to calculate sensitivity to a primordial signal by subtracting similar foreground components. Our analysis reveals that foreground uncertainty only marginally reduces signal sensitivity, primarily at frequencies where the signal is close to the foregrounds, underscoring the need to accurately model the contributions of eccentric or intermediate-mass black hole binaries to the GW background to achieve precise cosmological measurements with primordial GW backgrounds.

We utilize computational simulations to examine how active particles change and evolve over time in systems where they move continuously. The findings are compared to those from a different system where the particles don't move, called the 2D Ising case. By quickly changing these systems from a uniform state to a state where they don't mix and to a state where they are at a critical point, we study how they change and evolve far from a state of equilibrium. We measure the characteristics of these systems and their scales, as well as the aging process that occurs when they don't mix. The patterns and dynamics we see match the predictions from the Ising model, which also holds true for other active lattice models where the particles change and evolve quickly.

This paper presents the 5th iteration of the Predicting Video Memorability Task within MediaEval2022. To foster more in-depth analysis, the task has undergone significant revisions to refine its complexity. Building on last year's setup, two datasets are provided to facilitate generalization, with this year's edition replacing the TRECVid2019 dataset with the VideoMem dataset due to data quality concerns and focusing on short-term memorability forecasting. A new EEG-based prediction component is integrated into the task. The paper details the core components of the task and its associated subtasks, discussing the datasets, evaluation methods, and submission requirements.

This study tackles two main issues: developing metrics to measure the utilization of trained AI models, and explaining how the data used to train AI models are represented in these models, based on the measurements obtained. The motivation behind this research stems from the lack of transparency in AI models, particularly in high-risk applications such as self-driving cars that use AI for classifying traffic signs. To address the problems, this study provides theoretical foundations for measuring AI model utilization and identifies patterns in class representations of traffic signs at different levels of AI model computation, from entire models to individual computation units. Utilization is defined as the number and distribution of unique output possibilities within the space of all potential outcomes. This work extracts utilization metrics from both legitimate and poisoned AI models, where the poisoned models were trained on manipulated traffic sign images containing triggers that change the correct classification. The analysis compares class representations of both legitimate and poisoned AI models, leading to conclusions with implications for detecting and preventing trojan attacks.

This study examines how defects of different geometries impact the buckling behavior of spherical shells subjected to external pressure. We compare two distinct types of Gaussian defects, inward dimples and outward bumps, using validated finite-element simulations. Notably, the simulations reveal that spherical shells containing outward bumps are significantly more susceptible to buckling than those with inward dimples. Additionally, the simulations show that the relationship between the buckling behavior and defect size is different between the two types of defects, resulting in distinct post-buckling behavior.

In few-shot learning scenarios where a validation set is scarce, a common issue in the field is being overlooked. To address this, researchers have turned to combining pre-trained neural networks with classifiers that rely on distances, such as nearest class mean. This work proposes a Gaussian model of the feature distribution to predict generalization error in new classification tasks with limited data. We find that precise distance estimates between class-conditional densities are crucial for accurate generalization performance, so we develop an unbiased estimator for these distances and apply it in our numerical analysis. The results show that our approach outperforms existing methods, including leave-one-out cross-validation, in few-shot learning settings.

Recent experiments have successfully created a many-body system using dense laser-driven atomic gases, where in the long-term, a boundary time-crystal forms due to a balance between coherent stimulation and collective absorption. This state allows researchers to observe the system's out-of-equilibrium behavior by analyzing the output light field. We found that the photon count and homodyne current signals can be used to recognize and analyze the system's critical behavior at its time-crystal phase transition. As the system approaches the transition point, the emitted signal's dynamics exhibit slow variations accompanied by sudden significant fluctuations. These fluctuations' average time intervals demonstrate a size-dependent power-law relationship, and their unusual behavior can be explained using a simple nonlinear phase model. Moreover, we discovered that the time-integrated homodyne current can be a useful indicator of the system's dynamic order. This perspective views the time-crystal as a state where distinct oscillation patterns coexist.

The Antarctic ice sheet's decadal mass loss causes significant elastic uplift across the ANET GNSS network, at a rate of up to 20 mm/yr. For the first time, researchers are investigating whether the network's elastic deformation data can be used to determine the regions responsible for ice mass changes. To do this, they used a Load Sensitivity Kernel to model elastic deformation at each GNSS site. The results show that most ANET sites are influenced by mass changes occurring more than 200 km away. However, by comparing the deformation at neighboring sites, it is possible to pinpoint near-field mass changes. The researchers also developed a new approach, using weighted LSKs from multiple GNSS sites, to isolate the effects of mass changes within specific regions. This method was applied to 7 GNSS sites in the Amundsen Sea, demonstrating the network's potential to constrain ice mass changes, particularly in regions with high GNSS site density. The ANET configuration has been shown to effectively utilize elastic deformation data to determine ice mass changes in Antarctica.

We focus on the domain of satisfiable formulas within satisfiability modulo theories, particularly on the automatic creation of numerous satisfying assignments for such formulas. Although satisfiability modulo theories has had a long and successful history in model checking and formal verification, the generation of multiple satisfying assignments remains relatively under-explored. Existing work primarily deals with generating satisfying assignments for Boolean formulas and quantifier-free first-order formulas involving bit-vectors, arrays, and uninterpreted functions. Our new approach addresses this by providing a solution for theories involving integer arithmetic and integer arithmetic combined with arrays and uninterpreted functions. This is achieved by transforming the general sampling problem into a simpler instance of sampling from a set of independent intervals, which can be solved efficiently. This transformation is accomplished by expanding a single initial model, or seed, using top-down constraint propagation based on the original first-order formula.

This study presents the first measurement of the alignment of the spin of D*+ vector mesons and their charge conjugates, produced through the hadronization of charm and beauty quarks, in proton-proton collisions at the LHC. The experiment, conducted by the ALICE collaboration, measured the alignment at midrapidity as a function of transverse momentum in collisions at 13 TeV. The study focused on the diagonal spin density matrix element of D*+ mesons produced directly (prompt) or through the decay of beauty mesons (non-prompt) and found evidence of alignment for the latter. The results indicate that the alignment for non-prompt D*+ mesons is not random, with a measured value of the spin density element of 0.455, in contrast to a random alignment value of 1/3. The findings suggest that the alignment observed in non-prompt D*+ mesons could be a result of the conservation of helicity during their production, rather than a global alignment due to the initial angular momentum and magnetic field in heavy-ion collisions.

We derive general equations for the oblique-correction parameters $S$, $T$, $U$, $V$, $W$, and $X$ within an extended version of the Standard Model, allowing for an arbitrary number of singlet, doublet, and triplet quarks with specific electric charges that interact with the standard quarks having matching charge values.

A fixed target experiment at CERN's Super Proton Synchrotron called NA61/SHINE has specific objectives. The primary objectives of this experiment are to identify and analyze the critical point of matter under strong interactions and investigate the properties at the point of deconfinement. The researchers study the properties of hadron production in nucleus-nucleus, proton-proton and proton-nucleus interactions. The focus lies in the variation of collision energy and the sizes of colliding nuclei. This presentation includes the latest findings on identified charged kaon production in intermediate size collisions, as well as new measurements of strange mesons and baryons in proton-proton interactions.

As the world's push towards decarbonization gains momentum, integrating renewable energy into power grids is becoming increasingly complex. For Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), this shift creates both opportunities and challenges in the energy market. One lucrative option is energy arbitrage, which benefits from rising price fluctuations caused by the imbalance between renewable power generation and electricity demand. Additionally, Frequency Control Ancillary Services (FCAS) can provide substantial returns for BESS due to their ability to respond rapidly. Consequently, it's essential for BESS to strategically allocate their capacity across multiple markets to optimize their total revenue in an uncertain market environment. This paper frames the BESS bidding problem as a Markov Decision Process, enabling it to participate in both the spot market and FCAS market to maximize profits. To address this complex problem, a model-free reinforcement learning algorithm called Proximal Policy Optimization is employed to develop an optimal bidding strategy under a continuous bidding scale. By training and validating the proposed model with real-world data from the Australian National Electricity Market, our research shows that a joint bidding strategy across both markets yields significantly higher profits compared to individual markets.

To overcome the challenge of limited data in Named Entity Recognition (NER), the technique of Distantly-Supervised NER (DS-NER) generates training samples automatically. Unfortunately, this process may introduce noisy labels that degrade the performance of the learned models and hinder real-world applications. In response, researchers have been utilizing self-training teacher-student frameworks that refine the training labels over time and improve the models' generalization capabilities. However, the effectiveness of these frameworks is often undermined by their simplistic designs, which involve insufficient student learning and infrequent updates to the teacher model. In this study, we attempt to address these shortcomings by proposing two novel techniques: adaptive teacher learning, which trains two teacher-student networks simultaneously to improve student learning, and a fine-grained student ensemble that updates each model fragment using a weighted average of the corresponding teacher and student components, resulting in more accurate predictions. Our experiments on four DS-NER datasets show that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

A groundbreaking technology, spatial transcriptomics, is poised to revolutionize the field of tissue-based RNA expression research. Traditional array-based methods generate multi-cell data that must be processed through deconvolution to obtain single cell insights, but recent advancements in subcellular RNA expression analysis necessitate a novel approach. Our method, TopACT, combines single-cell RNA sequencing with spatial transcriptomics using topology to automatically identify cell types, without relying on prior cell boundary knowledge. By integrating TopACT with persistent homology, we found that in a model of lupus nephritis, immune cells form a ring-like structure surrounding kidney glomeruli, a finding confirmed through immunofluorescence imaging. This topological data analysis framework seamlessly integrates multiple scales of biological complexity, from gene expression within cells to tissue organization.

We prove optimal Lipschitz continuity for very weak solutions of the elliptic PDE $-\mathrm{div}(A(x) \nabla u) = Q \;
\mathcal{H}^{n-1} \llcorner \Gamma$ within a smooth domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, where $\Gamma$ is a smooth hypersurface, $Q$ is a function defined on $\Gamma$, and $A$ is a uniformly elliptic matrix. This PDE involves a special combination of two harmonic functions across an interface $\Gamma$ and is crucial in various free boundary problems, which will be discussed.

One of the fundamental principles in quantum theory, the Born rule, describes
how the likelihood of a particular outcome $a$ in a quantum state $|\psi\rangle$
can be calculated as $P(a)=|\langle a|\psi\rangle|^{2}$. Although it accurately
predicts experimental results, there has been a long-standing challenge in
proving the Born rule directly. In this work, we propose a method to directly
measure a superposition wavefunction using the concept of weak values,
enabling the verification of the Born rule. We also outline the details of a
plausible experiment that could make this possible.

Matrix factorization leverages the understanding that meaningful patterns in high-dimensional data are often embedded within lower-dimensional structures, which can be more easily interpreted, particularly when they are sparse.  Incorporating sparsity also offers the benefit of regularization, helping to prevent over-fitting.  A computationally efficient approach for matrix factorization is developed, using Bayesian shrinkage priors and modeling row and column relationships through sparse factor patterns.  This approach accommodates external information by allowing for inherent structures to emerge without imposition.  A numerical strategy combining the proposed approach with sequential estimation of low-rank contributions, informed by data-driven stopping criteria, is introduced, drawing inspiration from boosting algorithms.  The practical effectiveness of this method is showcased through a simulation study and an analysis of soccer heatmap data obtained from advanced tracking systems.

This paper details the performance evaluation of a High Angle Time Projection Chambers prototype, which is a key component for the T2K experiment's ND280 upgrade. The prototype features 32 advanced Encapsulated Resistive Anode Micromegas, allowing for precise detection of ionization electrons across multiple pads. The TPC prototype was equipped with a newly developed ERAM module and tested using the DESY Test Beam to assess its spatial and dE/dx resolution capabilities. The results indicate exceptional spatial resolution, exceeding 800 micrometers, and dE/dx resolution, under 10%, for all relevant angles and drift distances. A novel simulation of the detector response accurately replicated these findings, thereby validating the prototype's performance and meeting the T2K experiment's requirements for the HA-TPCs.

In a preceding study, arXiv:2210.16738, we established a set of flavor mass correlations that the beta-deformed A_{n-1} quiver matrix model reverts to in the massive scaling limit with maximal symmetry, and we noted the presence of an Argyres-Douglas critical hypersurface. In this letter, we determine the precise requirements on moduli parameters that cause the Seiberg-Witten curve to degenerate maximally, all while adhering to the previously identified flavor mass correlations. These requirements define the A-D hypersurface.

We have analyzed the holographic QCD and electroweak models with first-order phase transitions and found that the gravitational wave power spectra can be used to determine the strength of the phase transition.
