We propose a new approach for grounded situation recognition that leverages an interactive relationship between activity classification and entity estimation. This method is achieved through Collaborative Glance-Gaze TransFormer (CoFormer), comprising two interconnected modules. The Glance transformer module predicts the primary activity with support from the Gaze transformer module, which examines entities and their connections. Conversely, the Gaze transformer module determines the entities grounded in the image by concentrating only on the entities pertinent to the activity predicted by the Glance transformer module. CoFormer outperforms current state-of-the-art performance on the SWiG dataset in all evaluation metrics. The training code and model weights are publicly accessible on https://github.com/jhcho99/CoFormer.

Inverse wave propagation problems can be reformulated into computationally more manageable forms known as source extension methods. At the heart of these methods lies a core challenge: solving a linear inverse problem for a source by minimizing data discrepancies in the least squares sense, while incorporating physical constraints through a quadratic penalty function. Utilizing a time reversal approach from photoacoustic imaging can yield an approximate solution, thereby accelerating convergence in Krylov space iterations to solve this subproblem. This preconditioning technique has been effectively demonstrated in an acoustic 2D example, where sources were confined to a surface with a soft point support constraint.

For cross-domain image segmentation at test time, we developed a straightforward adaptation method. Our approach modifies a pre-trained model at test time by recalibrating the instance-specific BatchNorm statistics. The key elements of our method are two-fold. First, we substitute a fixed BatchNorm recalibration rule with a learnable component. Secondly, we employ aggressive data augmentation to mimic various domain shifts, allowing the model to learn the recalibration rule. In contrast to existing methods, our approach doesn't need access to target domain data during training or expensive test-time model retraining. Using standard training methods, our approach significantly outperforms several state-of-the-art techniques in domain generalization and one-shot unsupervised domain adaptation. When combined with domain generalization methods, our approach achieves even better results, setting a new state-of-the-art benchmark.

The orbital angular momentum of light is viewed as a valuable asset in quantum technology, particularly in applications like quantum communication and sensing. Unfortunately, the OAM state of light is vulnerable to adverse experimental conditions, including distance traveled and phase distortions, limiting its practical use. In this article, an advanced deep learning network is employed to distinguish various OAM modes of light under different conditions of propagation distance with phase distortions. Our developed deep learning network can accurately identify the topological charge of vortex beams and their respective propagation distances with nearly 97% accuracy, offering significant implications for OAM-based communication and sensing protocols.

Minor mergers between galaxies within clusters are a common occurrence. These events have the potential to create sloshing cold fronts in a cluster's core, but their durability when faced with additional mergers is unclear. Our investigation examines the impact of a second minor merger on sloshing cold fronts formed by a preceding off-axis merger. We conducted 13 simulations of triple cluster mergers, altering the approaching direction and distance of the third cluster. We found that clear cold fronts existed in all simulations, except for a short period following the first core passage. Subsequent head-on minor mergers significantly reduced the number of cold fronts, while those occurring off-axis had a moderate impact. Specifically, cold fronts beyond 500,000 light-years proved resilient. Our results indicate that cold fronts can be easily created during a minor merger and persist, even after additional mergers occur. Consequently, they are likely ubiquitous, but reconstructing a cluster's merger history from its observed cold fronts is more complicated than initially thought.

To create a reliable reduced-order model of the compressible Euler equations, it's necessary to choose the right inner product spaces. Typically, vector-valued L2({\Omega}) spaces are used but this approach can lead to inconsistent models with poor robustness. In this research, we investigate an alternative approach by examining dimensionally-consistent inner product spaces, particularly those that incorporate non-dimensional and physics-based entropy principles, to improve the accuracy and robustness of POD and Galerkin/least-squares ROMs. Our analysis involves three well-known test cases: the Sod shock tube, Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, and homogeneous isotropic turbulence.

Dimensionality-reducing techniques like reduced order models can significantly lower computational costs but might still involve terms related to the full model's dimension. To overcome this, sampling-based methods known as hyper-reduction techniques have been developed, enabling approximation of these terms with much smaller dimensions. This work presents a points selection algorithm, originally designed for uncertainty quantification, as a hyper-reduction method, referred to as S-OPT due to its goal of maximizing a quantity S. S-OPT outperforms an over-sampled Discrete Empirical Interpolation algorithm, delivering more accurate full order solution predictions at a given index number.

We've proposed that boson stars, an exotic hypothetical object, can be identified through distinctive signals detected by gravitational wave observatories. Our research found that boson stars adhere to a single, universal relationship, encompassing key characteristics such as moment of inertia, angular momentum, and quadrupole moment. This newly established connection is distinct from the one associated with neutron stars, offering a means to differentiate boson stars from other celestial entities. This breakthrough not only aids in distinguishing boson stars but also provides an opportunity to study the behavior of strong gravity within general relativity and understand the matter composition within compact stars.

Recent breakthroughs in coreference resolution are built upon individual mention pair-wise decisions, whereas our proposed approach takes a novel document-level perspective and makes global decisions instead. This method constructs a graph to model coreference links within a text, where tokens serve as nodes and the connections between them signify their relationships. Our model first predicts the entire graph in a non-autoregressive manner, followed by an iterative refinement process informed by previous predictions, enabling global interdependencies between each decision. Consequently, our experiments yielded significant improvements over competing models, providing empirical evidence that leveraging document-level information can enhance coreference resolution capabilities.

The second public dataset release from the DECam Local Volume Exploration survey, DELVE DR2, combines newly collected data from DECam observations with existing archival data from multiple DECam projects. This dataset comprises over 160,000 exposures that cover over 21,000 square degrees of high Galactic latitude sky through four distinct optical/near-infrared filters. DELVE DR2 includes detailed photometric measurements for nearly 2.5 billion sources with high sensitivity, covering over 17,000 square degrees in all four filters and over 21,000 square degrees in multiple filters. Compared to its predecessor, DELVE DR2 expands coverage to over four times the previous area and contains approximately five times the number of astronomical objects, all of which are accessible through the NOIRLab Astro Data Lab platform.

Current galaxy simulations are capable of resolving individual giant molecular clouds, precursors to dense star clusters. However, the fate of young massive clusters (YMCs) and their potential to evolve into observed globular clusters (GCs) is influenced by a complex interaction of internal dynamics and external galactic factors. We've developed the first star-by-star models of massive star clusters formed in a simulation of a Milky Way-like galaxy, accurately accounting for their initial conditions and the galaxy's gravitational effects. By simulating 895 randomly selected YMCs, we found that a Milky Way-like galaxy would have approximately 148 globular clusters, primarily formed during an early period of rapid star formation. Our simulated GCs are younger, less massive, and more compact than their real counterparts due to their assembly history and host galaxy's age-metallicity relationship. This reveals that a galaxy's specific evolutionary path influences the masses and sizes of its GCs. These findings stress the importance of incorporating realistic stellar physics and galaxy evolution into numerical models to accurately understand the properties of galactic globular cluster systems.

The digital era has witnessed a resurgence in the application of dark mode design in everyday tools and software, and it is also being considered for incorporation into astronomical journals. A modified template is presented, and the advantages of this design feature are highlighted, such as energy conservation and reduced eye strain on OLED devices. Furthermore, dark mode is found to enhance navigation through figures, harmonize with accessible color schemes, and minimize visual fatigue during observations. An analysis of recent conference design trends suggests that a significant proportion of the community would appreciate the introduction of dark mode in journals, potentially exceeding 42%. However, there are limitations associated with this design feature, including increased ink consumption in print media and reduced legibility in low-light settings. Nonetheless, these drawbacks can be addressed by providing both dark and traditional layouts, and the overall effect may ultimately contribute to improved astronomical practices among users.

Discovering accurate parameterizations for constitutive models using full-field experimental data, particularly for materials undergoing significant deformation, has long been an unresolved issue. To address this, we introduce a new deep-learning approach grounded in physics that uses displacement data from various sources and force-displacement relationships to determine constitutive model parameters. Unlike many recent studies, our framework relies on the weak form of the governing equations to ensure physical constraints on neural network predictions, resulting in efficient computation, adaptability to complex domains, and straightforward data integration without interpolation. We apply this approach to three fundamental hyperelastic materials models - the Neo-Hookean, Gent, and Blatz-Ko - to represent various material behaviors, and demonstrate how physics-informed machine learning can revolutionize the use of full-field experimental data in calibrating constitutive models under finite deformations.

We introduce dGSLM, the pioneering "textless" model that can produce authentic audio clips of conversations. It leverages breakthroughs in spoken unit discovery and combines them with a unique dual-tower transformer framework that utilizes cross-attention to analyze over 2000 hours of raw conversational audio data (Fisher dataset) without text or labels. The model successfully generates synchronized audio of conversations, laughter, and other subtle cues in two channels, and outperforms text-based models by creating more natural-sounding and smooth turn-taking interactions.

Our research focuses on Data Assimilation issues resolved through Partial Differential Equation (PDE) based methods, utilizing variational approaches and the Kalman filter algorithm. We introduced a Domain Decomposition framework, known as DD-DA, which splits the physical space and time domain, combining Schwarz' methods and parallel time approaches. To effectively parallelize DD-DA algorithms, it is essential to distribute the computational load evenly across subdomains, taking into account the distribution of data entities and minimizing communication during calculations. To address the challenges posed by non-uniform and sparse data distributions in DD-DA problems, we have developed a dynamic and adaptive load balancing algorithm, dubbed DyDD, which adjusts the boundaries of DD subdomains to balance workload based on data location. To validate DyDD, we employed the constrained least square model as the reference problem in the discretize-then-optimize approach, testing it in various scenarios.

Floquet time crystals with discrete periods can develop a unique property known as the spontaneous breaking of a specific temporal symmetry. This occurs when the system exhibits critical behavior, manifesting as periodic oscillations whose periods are a multiple greater than two times that of the driving force's period. A new, unambiguous parameter has been introduced to detect crystalline phases regardless of their periods and can also be used for chaos diagnosis. By using this new paradigm, a detailed analysis of the phase diagram of a kicked Ising model with long-range interactions was possible, revealing a complex landscape with intricate, fractal boundaries. A comprehensive theoretical model has been developed to explain the emergence of discrete Floquet time crystals based on the drive's strength, period, and its underlying $\mathbf{Z}_p$ symmetry in wave patterns.

A precise calculation of the Cabbibo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix element $|V_{cb}|$ using inclusive data relies heavily on a precise understanding of the semileptonic $b \to c$ decay rate.  This particular observable exhibits poor convergence properties when using the on-shell or $\overline{\text{MS}}$ schemes for the heavy quark masses, prompting the utilization of the kinetic mass scheme in recent studies.  To ensure accurate results, it's essential to have a high-precision understanding of the relationships between these different schemes.  This proceedings outlines our latest calculations, which achieve an unprecedented precision of $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s^3)$ in both key components, thereby enhancing the determination of $|V_{cb}|$ through inclusive methods.

Astronomical observations of faint targets can be processed more effectively by using electron multiplying CCDs in photon counting mode, where the amplified signal is refined through a thresholding technique that separates photo-electrons from noise.

To further enhance accuracy, researchers have developed photometric corrections, enabling the extraction of precise photo-electron signals. The Nancy Grace Roman Telescope's coronagraph instrument will utilize a mathematical model for the signal-to-noise ratio, based on calibrated noise parameters, to optimize observation planning. 

This paper presents derived formulas for the signal-to-noise ratio in photon counting before and after the application of these photometric corrections.

This research focuses on a discrete-time Stackelberg mean field game, consisting of multiple leaders, a limited number of prominent followers, and a virtually unlimited number of minor followers. Leaders possess private type information that evolves as independent, controlled Markov processes, which they utilize to determine dynamic policies. Two categories of followers exist: prominent and minor, each with distinct, private type information. These followers respond optimally to the Stackelberg leaders' strategies as well as one another's. Recognizing the followers would engage in a mean field game, based on the leaders' chosen policies, each Stackelberg leader selects a policy that maximizes her own reward, leading to a Stackelberg mean field equilibrium with multiple leaders (SMFE-ML). In this work, we derive a master equation to compute SMFE-ML outcomes. This concept is further extended to a scenario with an infinite number of leaders.

The importance of an open-source software (OSS) vulnerability management process is growing as the number of identified OSS vulnerabilities continues to increase. To prevent exploitation of these vulnerabilities, monitoring fix-commits is a crucial aspect of this process. However, manual detection of these commits can be time-consuming due to the high volume of commits to review. To address this challenge, various machine learning-based techniques have been developed to automatically detect fix-commits, but many of these solutions either lack the use of deep learning or only utilize limited information sources. This paper presents a novel tool called VulCurator, which employs deep learning on a more comprehensive set of information sources, including commit messages, code changes, and issue reports, to accurately classify fix-commits. Experimental results demonstrate that VulCurator significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions by up to 16.1% in terms of F1-score. The VulCurator tool is publicly available for access and includes a supporting demo video.

Using a newly developed flavoured jet algorithm, specifically the flavoured anti-$k_{\text{T}}$ method, we have studied $Wb\bar{b}$ production at the Large Hadron Collider operating at 8 TeV energy. We have calculated the total cross section and differential distributions at the next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) of QCD. We have investigated the influence of the flavoured anti-$k_{\text{T}}$ algorithm's adjustable parameters and compared the results with the standard flavour-$k_{\text{T}}$ method. We have found that our NNLO QCD corrected predictions match well with the CMS data, indicating a substantial improvement with the incorporation of the NNLO corrections.

Relativistic magnetic reconnections occur frequently across various astrophysical settings, where the plasma faces substantial cooling due to the emission of synchrotron radiation. We are examining the impact of strong synchrotron cooling on these magnetic reconnections in highly magnetized environments with magnetic field compactness comparable to one. As a result of synchrotron radiation, electron and positron pair production becomes inevitable, regulating the ambient magnetization surrounding the current sheet. We analyze this regulatory process theoretically and identify a self-regulated equilibrium for a specified level of magnetic field compactness and initial magnetization. This discovery enables us to estimate the self-regulated upstream magnetization in cases with uncertain plasma density, which can be beneficial for various astrophysical studies. We demonstrate this by applying the findings to the reconnection processes near the M87 supermassive black hole and outside the Crab pulsar's light cylinder.

We studied the internal dynamics of the young star-forming area NGC 346 within the Small Magellanic Cloud by examining a decade's worth of F555W and F814W observations taken by the Hubble Space Telescope ACS. We analyzed proper motions of two distinct epochs, which allowed us to investigate the movement patterns of various populations. Observations reveal a complex pattern of movement among the young stars in NGC 346, which is consistent across different parts of the cluster. The upper-main sequence and pre-main sequence stars within the cluster display similar movement patterns, while the outer regions show signs of outflows and inflows. In the cluster's central area, there's evidence of a combination of rotation and inflow. The rotation speed peaks at approximately 3 km/s, whereas the inflow speed peaks at around 1 km/s. Additionally, the proper motion field changes noticeably at points where sub-clusters and massive young stellar objects are located, indicating that turbulence plays a significant role in driving star formation. The comparable dynamics observed in metal-poor NGC 346 and the Milky Way's star-forming regions suggest that variations in metal content and dust density between the Small Magellanic Cloud and our galaxy do not have a substantial impact on the process of star cluster formation and growth. Our results align with various proposed models for the assembly and growth of star clusters.

Code element names exhibit inconsistent usage among developers due to personal preferences, leading to variable names that may convey different meanings or identical meanings using distinct terminology. Establishing precise name comparisons is hindered by this variability, necessitating an approach that considers not only exact matches, but also accounts for word variations, such as typos and reorderings, as well as semantic equivalencies between synonyms. A library of name comparison functions has been developed to address this challenge, offering a range of methods for calculating name similarity that may align with specific research objectives while approximating human perception of similarity at the expense of lexical precision.

In this paper, a general formula was established for the $n$th term of the $k$-generalized Fibonacci-like sequence, which generalizes the classic Fibonacci sequence and allows for $k$ initial terms. The derivation of this formula was facilitated by identifying patterns within previously obtained expressions for the Fibonacci-like, Tribonacci-like, and Tetrabonacci-like sequences. The $k$-generalized Fibonacci-like sequence formula was pivotal in the proof of the main result presented in this paper.

Graph AI has made significant strides in modeling intricate systems, from biological networks to physical systems of interacting particles. Yet, its increasing application to heterogeneous data necessitates the development of multimodal methods that can effectively combine various assumptions and prediction strategies. This proves to be a daunting task due to the varying nature of data modalities and the lack of explicit graph input in many cases. In response to these challenges, researchers combine multiple data modalities and exploit cross-modal relationships to improve their models. This article conducts a comprehensive analysis of 145 studies in graph AI and identifies a growing trend towards integrating diverse datasets using sophisticated multimodal approaches. Based on this analysis, we propose a framework for multimodal graph AI that enables researchers to examine existing techniques and inform the design of future innovations.

Nonlinear conservation laws present significant challenges in adjoint-based optimization due to concerns over the direct and adjoint solution existence, uniqueness, and the well-posedness of the problem when applying sensitivity analysis and gradient-based optimization. This work will examine the convergence of the adjoint equations to exact solutions for the inviscid Burgers' equation, using various numerical schemes and investigating factors including non-differentiable Riemann solvers, complete vs incomplete differentiation, and time advancement inconsistencies.

When a small, rounded particle settles in still liquid, it experiences a rotational force caused by its movement, which causes it to orient itself with its largest side facing downwards. We demonstrate that an active particle also experiences this force as it sinks in stationary fluid. For an active spherical particle that moves on its own, this torque is given by $\boldsymbol{T}^\prime = -{\tfrac{9}{8}} m_f (\boldsymbol{v}_s^{(0)} \wedge \boldsymbol{v}_g^{(0)})$ where $\boldsymbol{v}_s^{(0)}$ is the velocity at which the particle propels itself forward, $\boldsymbol{v}_g^{(0)}$ is the rate at which the particle settles due to gravity according to Stokes' approximation, and $m_f$ is the fluid mass equivalent. This torque causes the direction of movement against the gravitational force: moving upwards is a stable state, while moving downwards is unstable.

This study investigates the stability of cosmic strings endowed with bosonic superconductivity, focusing on the effects of curvature on the stability of charge-carrying particles. The research examines decay rates for diverse model parameters, curved string configurations, and decay processes. Additionally, the work applies cosmological principles to assess the stability of superconducting strings within cosmic networks and vortons, evaluating their evolution in the universe. The findings indicate that in various scenarios, the stability of zero mode vortons is compromised, such as when there is a mass hierarchy between charge-carrying particles and string tension, or when these particles interact significantly with light particles, such as those in the Standard Model.

Using circularly polarized and longitudinal light emanating from a waveguide, the Hofstadter butterfly in single-twist trilayer graphene has been studied. Our research revealed two distinct chiral limits for single-twist trilayer graphene in equilibrium and a more pronounced Hofstadter butterfly. We found that circularly polarized light creates a significant gap in the Hofstadter butterfly's energy spectrum and Landau levels with a notable asymmetry around zero energy. Notably, circularly polarized light causes the central band to shift downwards for right-handed light and upwards for left-handed light. Furthermore, our study found that longitudinally polarized light originating from a waveguide breaks the chiral symmetry of the Hofstadter butterfly energy spectrum at low driving strengths, but restores it at high driving strengths, contrasting the observations made for twisted bilayer graphene.

Compounds exhibiting noncentrosymmetric crystal structures have garnered significant interest as potential candidates for unconventional superconductivity, offering a diverse platform to explore this phenomenon. The discovery of superconductivity below 7.3 Kelvin in NbIr$_2$B$_2$ has added another material to this class, distinguished by its exceptionally high upper critical field that surpasses the Pauli limit. Our muon spin rotation experiments investigated the temperature and field dependence of the effective magnetic penetration depth in this compound, revealing evidence of fully gapped s-wave superconductivity. The high upper critical field observed in NbIr$_2$B$_2$ is also supported by high-field transport measurements. The compound's ratio of critical temperature to magnetic penetration depth squared is comparable to that of unconventional superconductors. Our zero-field muon spin rotation data showed no notable change in the muon spin relaxation rate above or below the critical temperature, indicating preserved time-reversal symmetry in the superconducting state. The findings presented here are expected to motivate theoretical investigations into the origin of superconductivity with preserved time-reversal symmetry in this distinctive noncentrosymmetric system.

In the context of distributed storage, computing, and homomorphic secret sharing, we investigate efficient schemes that calculate the linear combination of coded symbols with minimal communication. Our focus is on designing schemes that compute the weighted sum of $\ell$ coded symbols in a codeword $\pmb{c}\in\mathbb{F}^n$ using $d$ available components, with $d$ subject to certain conditions. Given a field extension $\mathbb{F}$ of $\mathbb{B}$ of degree $t$ and a codeword $\pmb{c}$ in a Reed-Solomon code of dimension $k$, we develop an explicit scheme to achieve this task by downloading a specific number of sub-symbols from $d$ nodes. This scheme outperforms existing solutions in several scenarios and offers an improved evaluation bandwidth for Reed-Solomon codes by characterizing a lower bound.

Recent interest in high-entropy alloys has been fueled by their superior mechanical properties and vast design possibilities, but understanding their underlying mechanisms is complicated by the complexity of their chemical composition. To overcome this hurdle, theoretical models need precise information about atomic interactions, while macro-scale models must be able to efficiently analyze a vast number of alloy candidates. Machine learning offers a solution to these challenges by providing a means to represent highly intricate relationships. This review showcases the potential of machine learning to address these obstacles and highlights its current and future applications in alloy design. It starts by introducing the fundamentals of machine learning algorithms and their relevant applications, followed by an overview of state-of-the-art models that simulate atomic interactions, thermodynamic properties, and mechanical behavior. The review then delves into macro-scale properties, including lattice structures, phase formation, and mechanical characteristics, utilizing examples of machine-learned phase-formation rules and order parameters to illustrate the workflow. Finally, it discusses remaining challenges and proposes research directions, including uncertainty quantification and machine learning-assisted inverse materials design.

The root-mean-square velocity of warm dark matter particles scales inversely with the universe's expansion factor. This velocity dispersion causes a cut-off in the power spectrum of density fluctuations due to dark matter's free-streaming effect. Given values for the velocity dispersion at the present time, $v_{h\textrm{rms}}(1)$, and the free-streaming comoving cut-off wavenumber at the time of matter-radiation equality, $k_\textrm{fs}(t_\textrm{eq})$, have been estimated from observations of galaxy stellar masses and ultra-violet luminosities, resulting in values that are consistent with reionization. Alternatively, the velocity dispersion cut-off implies $v_{h\textrm{rms}}(1) < 0.54 \textrm{ km/s}$ and $k_\textrm{fs}(t_\textrm{eq}) > 1.5 \textrm{ Mpc}^{-1}$. These results agree with earlier measurements based on spiral galaxy rotation curves and the formation of the first galaxies. The temperature-to-mass ratio of warm dark matter is found to be consistent with a specific scenario involving scalar dark matter particles that decouple from the standard model sector early on, but disfavors scenarios involving spin 1/2 or spin 1 dark matter. An extended standard model featuring scalar dark matter is also discussed, along with potential discrepancies with existing limits on dark matter particle mass.

We develop the fluctuation algebra for fermions in a state with minimal correlations, and then analyze its evolution over time under minimal correlated dynamics. Furthermore, we identify a form of Bose-Einstein condensate and investigate its stability when interactions are present.

Countless scientific computations rely on linear algebra expressions that are computed through sequences of calls to pre-existing libraries such as BLAS and LAPACK. Each sequence represents a specific computing strategy or algorithm, often with multiple alternatives existing for a single linear algebra expression. While these algorithms are mathematically equivalent, they can differ significantly in terms of performance due to differences in operations. Various languages and tools, such as Julia and Linnea, make algorithmic choices based on the number of Floating Point Operations (FLOPs), but this metric is not always reliable for distinguishing between algorithms with nearly identical execution times. It is also possible for the algorithm with the lowest FLOP count to be outperformed by others. In order to assess the reliability of FLOPs as a performance discriminant, we develop a method that ranks algorithms according to their performance and iteratively measures them until the rankings converge. This methodology classifies instances where FLOPs are a valid discriminant as ones where all algorithms with the lowest FLOPs are assigned the top rank, otherwise they are considered anomalies for further investigation.

This research presents a comprehensive analysis and computational verification of how the rate of backscattering in HgTe and (Hg,Mn)Te quantum wells is influenced by various interactions in the quantum spin Hall state, including s-p and sp-d exchange interactions, Kondo coupling, and Luttinger liquid effects. It examines the impact of these factors, as well as precessional dephasing and bound magnetic polarons, on the measured electrical conductivity and its temperature dependence, finding alignment with experimental data.

The contextual bandit problem has far-reaching applications across diverse fields and is supported by theoretical frameworks. Most prior research on this subject typically relies on the assumption that noise is independent of context, whereas our study considers a more realistic scenario where noise functions as a latent confounding variable influencing both contexts and rewards. This more realistic confounded setting has broader applicability but comes with challenges such as biased reward function estimation and increased regret due to unresolved confounding. To address these issues, we employ dual instrumental variable regression, which can accurately identify the true reward function. We demonstrate that this method achieves a near-optimal convergence rate within two commonly used reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, thereby allowing for the development of efficient and regret-optimal algorithms for confounded bandit problems. Numerical results confirm the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms in the confounded bandit context.

We previously demonstrated that every minimal symplectic filling of any oriented lens space can be derived from the minimal resolution of its associated cyclic quotient singularity through a series of symplectic rational blowdowns. In this context, we introduce a significantly simplified visual representation of our rational blowdown algorithm based on the triangulations of a convex polygon. As a result, we establish a structured graph to organize the symplectic deformation equivalence classes of all minimal symplectic fillings of any given lens space, with the minimal resolution serving as the graph's root and each directed edge corresponding to a symplectic rational blowdown along a specific linear plumbing graph. Furthermore, we establish an upper limit on the depth of rational blowdowns required for each minimal symplectic filling.

The challenge of efficiently generating trajectories in complex dynamic environments persists in the unmanned surface vehicle (USV) field. A novel cooperative trajectory planning algorithm is proposed for USV-UAV systems, allowing the USV to safely and smoothly navigate multi-obstacle maps. The UAV acts as a sensor, transmitting real-time global maps and obstacle data through a lightweight semantic segmentation network and 3D projection transformation. An initial obstacle avoidance trajectory is generated using a graph-based search method. Given the unique kinematic constraints of the under-actuated USV, a numerical optimization method incorporating hull dynamics is applied to improve trajectory trackability for motion control. A motion control method using NMPC is also proposed, prioritizing the lowest energy consumption during execution. Experimental outcomes validate the effectiveness of the integrated system, producing locally optimal trajectories for USV with high tracking accuracy.

Autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) play a pivotal role in marine exploration and conservation. To guarantee their mission success, two fundamental technologies, trajectory planning and motion tracking, must be employed. A new trajectory generation and tracking method is introduced, grounded in optimization principles, to optimize USV performance. The method utilizes a differential flatness-based dynamic model, enabling trajectory generation via dynamic RRT* in a linear system framework that aligns with optimal boundary conditions. To optimize efficiency, local adjustments are made to the trajectory, taking into account dynamic constraints that ensure adherence to the under-actuated hull's kinematic properties. Furthermore, motion tracking is reinforced with model predictive control, leveraging a sequential quadratic programming problem. Experimental outcomes confirm that the planned trajectory aligns better with ASV kinematics, and the tracking accuracy is preserved at a higher level.

Across the globe, currency facilitates numerous business transactions. In many developing countries, notably those in Africa, physical cash is the preferred medium of exchange in daily transactions. In Ethiopia, one of the countries with a high rate of blindness (1.6%) and low vision (3.7%), a substantial 4 million people are visually impaired, with approximately 1.7 million in complete blindness. The visually impaired face significant challenges when engaging in physical currency exchanges at locations like bus stations and shopping centers. This study aims to alleviate these issues by leveraging AI and machine learning technologies. An Android and iOS compatible mobile app was developed, featuring a voice-enabled component that accurately identifies and announces the scanned currency in Amharic, Ethiopia's primary language. The app was designed to be user-friendly, with the primary objective of easing the difficulties faced by visually impaired individuals in Ethiopia.

Researchers investigating the role of vortices in planetary formation have been trying to understand when they remain stable and can accumulate dust, and when they break up. To answer this question, they ran high-resolution simulations of vortices filled with dust in protoplanetary discs. Their findings indicate that a vortex's stability is influenced by its size relative to the disc's scale height and the type of dust present. Small vortices are stable for an extended period, while larger ones collapse over time due to a drag instability caused by the dust, with larger dust particles leading to a quicker instability. This suggests that dust in the disc affects the lifespan of vortices formed through certain instabilities, allowing for considerable enrichment of the vortex cores, even if the vortices are short-lived.

Lately, in chemistry and materials science, researchers have been highly interested in machine learning potentials for atomic simulations. This led to the development of various new approaches aiming to apply electronic structure calculations' accuracy to complex systems containing numerous atoms. Despite the recent advancements, it is still challenging to determine the reliability of these machine learning potentials in accurately reproducing the intricate characteristics of the potential-energy surface in large systems. Furthermore, it is not often that systems of moderate size, suitable for systematic quality control, are studied. This work uses precise harmonic and anharmonic vibrational frequencies to test the validity of high-dimensional neural network potentials. For the formic acid dimer, a widely used model system with available precise data, we show that using state-of-the-art calculations yields high-quality frequencies in excellent agreement with coupled cluster theory and experimental data.

Medical imaging data for studying human anatomy and related health issues is often hindered by access restrictions due to governance, privacy concerns, ownership issues, and high costs. This limits our understanding of the human body. One solution is developing a model capable of learning and generating realistic, synthetic images of the human body based on specific characteristics like age, sex, and disease status. Generative models using neural networks have successfully produced synthetic 2D images of scenes, but generating high-resolution, 3D volumetric imaging data with correct anatomy remains a challenge. This research presents a scalable model capable of producing anatomically accurate, high-resolution, and realistic human brain images that can support downstream analysis. By generating unlimited data, this model enables large-scale studies of human anatomy without compromising patient privacy, while also advancing research in areas such as anomaly detection, learning from limited data, modality synthesis, and fair AI.

Remote hacking incidents involving laptop computers have become increasingly prevalent. These malicious attacks frequently utilize malware to gain unauthorized access to laptop users' webcams and microphones, thereby enabling surveillance. Although commercially available webcam privacy covers provide some defense against webcam-based attacks, there is a pressing need for a solution to counter microphone-related threats despite recent efforts. In a pioneering move to counter these attacks on laptop microphones, we have developed TickTock, a novel mic status detection system that relies on externally monitoring the electromagnetic emanations produced by laptop circuitry. These emanations are emitted from the mic clock signals transmitted through laptop connectors and cables only when the microphone is recording. To demonstrate the feasibility of our system, we have implemented a proof-of-concept and tested it on thirty diverse laptops executing different applications. The results indicate that TickTock can accurately identify the mic status in 27 of these laptops with a high success rate, thereby providing a robust defense against remote hacking incidents.

We generalize Krasnoselskii's fixed point theorem to functions that do not involve self-reference. Our method provides a novel and straightforward proof of Hillam's result, dispensing with the requirement that the image of the associated mapping be compact or bounded. Consequently, we expand upon Hillam's result by applying it to self-mappings on the set of real numbers. Furthermore, we offer an alternative proof of the global convergence of the Newton-Raphson method.

Research has demonstrated that iron chalcogenides are natural topological superconductors, with potential applications in quantum computing due to their distinctive electronic properties. The surface states of FeTe$_{0.5}$Se$_{0.5}$, characterized by topologically non-trivial properties, were previously predicted through calculations and later confirmed by precise experiments involving photoemission and scanning tunneling. Yet, thus far, conclusive electrical transport evidence supporting the presence of topological surface states remains absent. Through electrical transport experiments, we discovered evidence of a topological transition marked by a non-linear Hall effect and simultaneous linear magnetoresistance near the superconducting transition temperature. Additionally, we observed a reversal in the Hall coefficient and a softening of the ${A}_{1g}$ phonon mode at approximately 40 K, signifying a nematic transition. The synchronized phonon softening with nematicity suggests an enhanced fluctuation state resulting from interactions between phonons and spins. Our findings definitively establish the presence of topological surface states in FeTe$_{0.5}$Se$_{0.5}$ and provide insights into the mechanism driving superconductivity in iron chalcogenides.

In the linear regime, we explore the potential of two-dimensional subwavelength quantum emitter arrays as high-performance optical devices, manipulating light with precision for normally incident beams. By exploiting the dipole exchanges between emitters, the array's transmission, resonant frequency, and bandwidth can be precisely controlled. The behavior of fully polarized light, including linear and circular polarizers as well as phase shifters, can be engineered and characterized through Jones matrix representations. Our comprehensive analysis, combined with numerical simulations, pinpoints the most effective configurations for these operations and highlights the importance of adjusting the array's geometry and carefully optimizing the external magnetic fields' amplitude and direction.

Understanding SARS-CoV-2's evolution and transmission dynamics presents a significant scientific hurdle.
By merging artificial intelligence, patient-derived viral genomes, extensive mutational data, biophysics, and advanced data analysis, researchers discovered that the virus's evolution is largely influenced by natural selection based on its ability to infect hosts.
In 2020, AI-powered predictions identified crucial mutation sites L452 and N501 on the spike protein's receptor-binding domain, which eventually emerged in dominant variants including Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, Kappa, Theta, Lambda, Mu, and Omicron.
Subsequent studies uncovered a new driving force behind natural selection: the development of antibodies resistant to the virus.
AI-based forecasting correctly predicted Omicron's infectiousness, vaccine breakthroughs, and antibody resistance, validating these predictions with subsequent experiments.
AI models also accurately forecasted the replacement of BA.1 with BA.2 in March and predicted the rise of Omicron BA.4 and BA.5 as dominant variants by late May, which was later confirmed in June.
Furthermore, AI-driven topological models have successfully predicted how specific mutations affect the efficacy of monoclonal antibodies used to combat the virus.

Classical mechanics relies on position and momentum, which must be expressed in specific coordinates to accurately translate to quantum operators. To ensure a valid quantization, it is essential to select unique variables and a method that guarantees a precise conversion. Failure to do so may result in misinterpretation of quantizations, leading to flawed physics. This discussion will cover the favored variables and operators for both particle and field systems, as well as gravity.

One of the key areas of focus in detecting continuous gravitational waves from rapidly rotating neutron stars involves non-axisymmetrical deformations of their crust. A crucial factor in evaluating the strength of these gravitational wave sources is the maximum possible ellipticity that crust deformations, or "mountain" formations, can accommodate. Utilizing a force model that primarily acts in the transverse direction and drawing on a formalism established by Gittins et al in 2021, we calculate a maximum ellipticity of 7.4$\times$10$^{-6}$. This outcome surpasses the original estimates of Gittins et al in 2021 but aligns with earlier predictions made by Ushomirsky et al in 2000, indicating that rotating neutron stars could be significant emitters of continuous gravitational waves.

Deep learning model developers must now balance performance with the need to safeguard sensitive information in their training data. The primary method for ensuring model privacy involves differential privacy, which has proven effective in countering attacks but comes with the drawback of reduced model accuracy. This research compares DP-SGD's performance against conventional optimization techniques with regularisation. It examines the trade-off between model utility and training efficiency as well as its susceptibility to membership inference and model inversion attacks. The study highlights the limitations of differential privacy and shows through empirical evidence that dropout and l2-regularisation often provide superior privacy protection.

We have developed an innovative, compact, and low-power optomechanical inertial sensor designed for low-frequency acceleration measurements. This advanced sensor boasts a 4.7Hz resonant frequency, a 476,000 quality factor, and a 2.6 gram test mass, while its projected noise floor of 5E-11 m s^-2 per root-Hz at 1Hz enables exceptional performance. Owing to its minimal size, weight, and environmental susceptibility, this technology is poised to revolutionize geodesy missions in the future. Our experimental study involves a live demonstration of detecting low-frequency ground seismic noise in real-time, directly comparing it to a commercial seismometer, and developing data analysis algorithms to identify and mitigate several noise sources.

The purpose of this brief note is to demonstrate that for two sequences of positive real numbers $\{ a_{n}\}$ and $\{ b_{n}\}$ where $a_{n}$ converges to positive infinity and $b_n$ follows the asymptotic relationship $b_n\approx k\cdot a_{n}$, with $k$ being a positive constant, the limit as n approaches infinity of $\left(1+\frac{1}{a_{n}}\right)^{b_{n}}$ equals $e^k$.

Object detection models in critical applications like automated driving and robotics require reliable performance under dynamic conditions. To assess this, evaluating their robustness against unexpected hardware malfunctions is crucial. Standard metrics that assess detection accuracy at the object level fail to account for image-level vulnerability to silent data corruption. This oversight can result in over- or underestimation of potential hazards. To address this, we present IVMOD, an image-level vulnerability metric for object detection, which takes into consideration the combined impact of false positives, false negatives, and severity analysis. Our evaluation of several object detection models reveals that single bit flips or stuck-at-1 faults can have severe consequences, resulting in numerous false positives, missed true positives, and persistent ghost detections that can be misinterpreted as actual objects, compromising the overall safety and performance of critical workloads.

The application of Deep Learning has the potential to significantly enhance the classification accuracy in Hyperspectral Imaging. However, training models on the limited hyperspectral datasets presents a complex task. Key difficulties arise from the high-dimensional nature of the recorded data and the compatibility issues between cameras from different manufacturers. Our proposed solution involves incorporating a tailored model bias and adaptively defining the channel dimension, utilizing a 2D convolutional approach specifically designed to address these HSI challenges. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through evaluations on two distinct hyperspectral applications: inline inspection and remote sensing. Besides outperforming existing models, our modification also provides additional interpretability and enables the data-driven learning of necessary camera filters. These camera filters can, in turn, be used to design an optimal camera configuration.

Recent research indicates that any observed capacity, such as potential, can theoretically be produced via quantum mechanics by utilizing a specific wavefunction. Our study investigates a tangible instance, specifically the gravitational force experienced by an object at varying scales, from planetary to cosmic, and identifies the corresponding wavefunction responsible for generating its quantum effect. Essentially, our findings demonstrate that the gravitational interaction observed at all scales can be attributed to an underlying quantum mechanism encoded in a wavefunction. We explore the consequences of this outcome.

Hadronic vacuum polarization effects on atomic energy level transitions are estimated semi-empirically for hydrogen-like ions and muonic hydrogen. A parametric hadronic polarization function is inferred from e+e- annihilation cross-sections and used to obtain an effective relativistic Uehling potential. Energy corrections from hadronic vacuum polarization are calculated for low-lying states using Dirac-Coulomb wave functions, as well as bound wave functions that consider the nuclear size's finite nature. Closed-formulas are derived for the extended nucleus's hadronic Uehling potential and the point-like nucleus's relativistic energy shift. These findings are compared with corresponding non-relativistic analytical formulas.

The researchers used 5.7 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected at 13 TeV from proton-proton collisions with the LHCb detector to determine the time-integrated charge-parity asymmetry of $D^0$ decays to $K^-K^+$, which were initially produced from $D^{*+}\to D^0\pi^+$ decays and had their charm meson flavor identified via the pion's charge. The calculated asymmetry was $\left[6.8 \pm 5.4 \text{ (stat)} \pm 1.6 \text{ (syst)} \right]\times 10^{-4}$. Using this result along with the difference in charge-parity asymmetry between $D^0\to K^- K^+$ and $D^0\to\pi^-\pi^+$, the direct charge-parity asymmetries were determined as $a_{K^-K^+}^{d} = (\phantom{2}7.7 \pm 5.7) \times 10^{-4}$ and $a_{\pi^-\pi^+}^{d} = (23.2 \pm 6.1) \times 10^{-4}$, which showed evidence of direct $C\!P$ violation in specific $D^0$ decays, a phenomenon that was previously unseen.

Our results demonstrate that determining the validity of first-order logical statements about words that do not overlap in pairs, or more broadly, the ${\alpha}$-free words with a specific ratio between 2 and 7/3, can be done algorithmically. This achievement enables the verification of many earlier findings related to this word class through a more efficient automated approach.

The partially populated network variant D3(K;M) of the Swapped Dragonfly, which consists of KMM routers with M routers per group and K global ports per router, is studied in this paper, with K and M restricted. This specific topology is denoted as D3(K;M) [1] and has n=KMM routers. The performance of four network operations - matrix product, all-to-all exchange, broadcast, and ascend-descend - is analyzed on D3(K,M), showing significant time improvements compared to a Boolean hypercube and a fully populated Dragonfly. The findings on D3(K,M) are particularly useful due to its emulation capabilities of every Swapped Dragonfly with K and/or M restricted to a lower value. The time complexities are compared to those of the Boolean hypercube and the fully populated Dragonfly, with the results on D3(K,M) applicable in real-world scenarios. Keywords include the Swapped Interconnection Network, Matrix Product, All-to-all exchange, Boolean Hypercube, Ascend-descend algorithm, Broadcast, and Edge-disjoint spanning tree.

We study a specific type of random walk on finite networks where particles enter randomly and exit at the network's boundaries. Despite the non-reversible dynamics and uncertainty about the network's equilibrium state, we are able to precisely determine the time it takes for the network to settle and establish that a key characteristic of this process is equivalent to a certain condition. We also derive precise estimates of the time frame during which the network settles and illustrate our findings with explicit examples of finite network substructures of certain infinite graphs and large finite graphs that have a single point of exit, resolving a previously proposed conjecture. Our proof involves a detailed analysis of a recent concept related to the stationary state and a specific process involving particles moving randomly.

The supersymmetry breaking mechanism typically forecasts the presence of sgoldstinos, which can act as wave-like dark matter. As a result of their widespread interaction with electromagnetic fields, the light scalar sgoldstino dark matter may cause fluctuations in the fine-structure constant. By utilizing highly accurate atomic clock data, it has been possible to determine that the supersymmetry breaking scale $\sqrt{F}$ can be tested up to the grand unified theory scale within the sgoldstino mass range of $10^{-22}$ eV $<m_\phi <$ $4\times10^{-7}$ eV.

A novel approach to deriving the action for vacuum decay has been formulated using the tunneling potential. This method builds upon a previous derivation, which involved ensuring the action's variation resulted in the correct equations of motion and a consistent action value obtained from the Euclidean bounce. An alternative derivation of the tunneling action using canonical transformations is now presented, addressing both single-field, multi-field, and gravitational cases. Additionally, the potential for applying this new method to calculating the prefactor in the tunneling rate is considered.

At the AWAKE CERN experiment, advancements were made to the electron bunch's stability and brightness during proton-driven plasma wakefield injection using machine learning (ML) automation techniques. The combination of numerical optimisers and various reinforcement learning agents was explored and implemented. To eliminate bias, reinforcement learning agents were trained with unsupervised state encodings using auto-encoders. Additionally, a synthetic model of the beamline was developed using a variational auto-encoder to aid in hyper-parameter selection and generate surrogate data from equipment settings. This study presents novel ML and reinforcement learning methods for automating low energy line setups, similar to the one used in AWAKE. The results from applying different ML approaches, including automated feature extraction from images using computer vision, are shared. The potential for operational implementation and broader applications is also discussed.

Revenue in freemium games primarily stems from in-app purchases and advertising exposure. A player's prolonged engagement significantly increases the likelihood of generating revenue. To maximize revenue potential, identifying and preventing player dropout (churn) is crucial. To address this, researchers aim to enhance churn prediction accuracy by merging sequence-based and aggregated data using diverse neural network models. Experimental analysis reveals that integrating both data types yields superior prediction accuracy over models relying on individual data types.

The knowledge of an instrument's point spread function is crucial for astronomical research, and our work presents a novel PSF Reconstruction algorithm specifically designed for the LBT LUCI instrument. Leveraging the SOUL SCAO module, our method focuses solely on real-time wavefront sensor data and limited asynchronous calibration. It bypasses calculations of the Optical Transfer Function and corresponding filters, instead generating a sequence of wavefront maps accompanied by their respective instantaneous point spread functions. We have thoroughly tested the "BRUTE" algorithm in both controlled laboratory settings and actual nighttime observations, adapting its performance to varying SOUL configurations, guide star brightness, and atmospheric conditions.

One of the biggest unsolved mysteries in fundamental physics is why the cosmological constant is not significantly larger, given the predictions of quantum field theory. In fact, calculations based on naive assumptions could result in a value up to 10$^{120}$ times larger than the observed value. Resolving this vast discrepancy between theory and observation is a key goal of a comprehensive theory of quantum gravity. In this work, we explore the potential of generalized uncertainty principle models, which are inspired by quantum gravity theories, to address the cosmological constant problem. Specifically, we investigate how these GUP models alter the phase space of quantum field theory and how this impacts the calculation of zero-point energies in momentum space. However, we also highlight several concerns that make it improbable for GUP models, in their current state, to adequately resolve the cosmological constant problem.

The interaction between the dark $U(1)_d$ sector and the visible Standard Model sector is facilitated by the kinetic mixing between the dark photon $Z_d^\mu$ and the Standard Model $U(1)_Y$ gauge field $B_\mu$. After electroweak symmetry breaking, the dark photon acquires mass and mixes with the Standard Model neutral vector boson $Z_\mu$, resulting in a parity-violating coupling. This coupling can be studied in low-energy phenomena and particle collider experiments, including those at high-energy colliders. The Large Hadron-electron Collider, in particular, will allow for detailed analysis of the Lorentz structure of the dark photon's interaction with Standard Model fermions using cross-sections and asymmetries from polarized dark photon decays in leptons. A statistical comparison of multiple variables for both charged and neutral currents is conducted, yielding $90\%$ confidence level contours in the $\epsilon$-$m_{Z_d}$ and $\epsilon$-$g_V$ planes, which impose limits on the mass of the dark photon up to $100$ GeV, its coupling strength $\epsilon$, and the Lorentz structure of its interaction with Standard Model fermions ($g_V$), at a collision energy of approximately $1.3$ TeV.

A groundbreaking paper introduces MBURST, a revolutionary multimodal system for audio-visual speech enhancement, drawing from recent neuroscientific breakthroughs about the prefrontal cortex and other brain regions. MBURST addresses the complex problem of credit assignment through a biologically inspired mechanism called burst propagation, leveraging feedback, multiplexing, connection approximation, and linearized signals to assign plasticity more accurately. This innovative system leverages its capabilities to establish connections between noisy signals and visual stimuli, thereby assigning meaning to speech by amplifying relevant information and suppressing background noise. MBURST demonstrates superior performance in comparison to a baseline multimodal backpropagation-based method, showcasing remarkable energy efficiency through significant reductions in neuron firing rates, up to 70%, thus enabling more sustainable implementations in devices such as hearing aids.

Within the realm of autonomous driving, vehicles inevitably face more extreme weather conditions where public safety remains paramount. As the climate rapidly evolves, winter storms such as heavy snowfalls are projected to become increasingly prevalent and pose significant risks to navigation. Although research has focused on enhancing navigation resiliency in winter conditions, a standardized metric to gauge the reduction in lidar sensor visibility due to precipitation is still lacking. This chapter introduces a new, real-time metric to measure lidar visibility loss, drawing on the principles of meteorological visibility. This proposed metric is tested using the Canadian Adverse Driving Conditions dataset, correlated with the performance of a cutting-edge lidar-based localization algorithm, and examines the benefits of filtering point clouds before the localization process. Interestingly, our findings show that the ICP algorithm is surprisingly resistant to snowfalls but experiences significant accuracy decline in response to sudden weather fluctuations like snow gusts. Furthermore, our research highlights the necessity for better datasets focused on these exceptional events to accurately assess their effects on navigation.

We assume the area of a black hole's event horizon is discretized into distinct units,
$A = l_P^2 \, (4 \ln 2) \, N$, and the related degrees of freedom are a finite, fermionic quantity.
Subsequently, we explore the entropy $S_{BH}$, focusing on black hole self-similarity.
Initially, we discover a 2-to-1 relationship between black hole states and the organized partitions of the integer $N$.
By using this relationship, we develop a composition rule for the constituent parts of the overall configuration space.
This allows us to interpret black hole self-similarity as a consequence of the inherent self-similarity of ordered $N$ partitions within a unified framework.
Lastly, we examine how these findings relate to previously known results on subleading quantum corrections, which necessitate varied statistical weights for different configurations.

The MICADO instrument at ESO's ELT telescope has a critical role in capturing first light images and spectroscopic data at near-infrared wavelengths. To further enhance its capabilities, the PSF Reconstruction Team is developing a pioneering software service for MICADO. This tool utilizes adaptive optics telemetry data to independently reconstruct the point spread function (PSF), regardless of the science data. It supports both Single Conjugate and Multi-Conjugate Adaptive Optics, facilitated by the MORFEO module. With the PSF-R service now past the Final Design Review phase, we report on its current status and discuss recent findings from simulated and real data tests using similar instruments.

We'll employ commutators to express $3\times 3$ matrices as sums of terms that satisfy specific polynomial conditions, and apply this method to bounded linear operators and endomorphisms of infinite rank free modules. Specifically, it is shown that any bounded operator on an infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space can be decomposed into four order $3$ automorphisms, and every simple ring derived from the endomorphism ring of an infinitely dimensional vector space, modulo its maximal ideal, can be represented as the sum of three nilpotent subrings.

For massless particle states, the Wigner little group, also known as the stabilizer group of the four-vector, is derived as the Borel subgroup of the proper orthochronous Lorentz group in four dimensions, with its maximal solvable subgroups being ${\rm sol}_2^\pm$ of order two. In the massless scenario, particle states are split into left-handed and right-handed chiral states governed by these subgroups. Using these subgroups, induced Lorentz transformations are constructed and applied to particle states, with the resulting spin-flip contribution closely related to the nonphysical nature of certain spin operators.

Constructing a call graph without dynamic elements necessitates a delicate balance between accuracy and precision. Current program analysis methods often yield imprecise results when generating call graphs. To address this shortcoming, researchers have introduced a machine learning-based approach to refine call graphs post-processing by applying call graph pruning. By training a machine learning model on structural features using a random forest classifier, researchers can remove predicted false-positive edges from the call graph. Despite the enhancements achieved through machine learning models, they still fall short as they neglect source code semantics, thereby struggling to effectively differentiate between true and false positives. To address this limitation, we propose a novel call graph pruning technique called AutoPruner that combines statistical, semantic, and structural analysis to remove false-positive edges from call graphs. AutoPruner takes a transformer-based approach to analyze semantic relationships between caller and callee functions associated with each edge in the call graph, leveraging a pre-trained code model to represent source code based on semantic descriptions. The model then extracts semantic features from related functions and combines them with structural features to classify each edge using a feed-forward neural network. Our evaluation on a real-world benchmark dataset reveals that AutoPruner surpasses existing baselines by up to 13% in accurately identifying false-positive edges in static call graphs.

This study focuses on examining the structural characteristics of the sandpile group in a specific subset of self-replicating graphs. Specifically, it involves Abelian sandpiles on Sierpinski gasket graphs, where under normal boundary conditions, we derive a description of the identity element and develop a recursive model for the sandpile group. Furthermore, we explore Abelian sandpile Markov chains on these graphs, resulting in enhanced bounds on the rate at which these chains converge to a stationary state.

This study employs local projections in high-dimensional scenarios to derive impulse responses. The desparsified lasso is utilized to estimate the high-dimensional local projections, with the impulse response parameter of interest exempt from the penalization. We achieve the uniform asymptotic normality of the proposed estimator under broad conditions. Additionally, our small sample performance is assessed through simulations, and the proposed method is applied to two prominent macroeconomic research contexts, including monetary policy and government spending.

Real-time object detection on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) poses significant technical challenges due to the limited processing capabilities of edge GPU devices that are commonly used as Internet of Things (IoT) nodes. To overcome this issue, this paper introduces a novel, lightweight deep learning architecture called FasterX, built upon the YOLOX model for edge GPU-based real-time object detection. We first create an optimized, compact PixSF head to enhance detection of small objects and embed it within the depthwise separable convolution (DS Conv) framework. Next, we develop the SlimFPN layer to significantly reduce network parameters while maintaining a delicate balance between accuracy and speed. Furthermore, we integrate an attention mechanism into the Head layer to elevate feature extraction performance. Additionally, we revise the label assignment approach and loss function to mitigate category imbalance and box optimization issues specific to UAV datasets. Finally, auxiliary heads are introduced for online distillation to boost the PixSF head's position embedding and feature extraction capabilities. Our lightweight FasterX models are empirically validated on NVIDIA Jetson NX and Jetson Nano embedded platforms and demonstrate superior trade-offs between accuracy and latency on the VisDrone2021 dataset compared to state-of-the-art models.

High-performance ground-based telescopes, capable of diffraction-limited observations, rely on detailed knowledge of their point spread function (PSF) to unlock their full scientific potential. This requirement becomes even more critical as new AO instruments are developed for 30-meter class telescopes. As a result, researchers are working on creating precise tools to accurately reconstruct the PSF of AO systems, known as PSF reconstruction. Our team is developing a PSF reconstruction service for the MICADO@ELT instrument, focusing on a blind approach that can be applied broadly to various science cases without utilizing science data. Our PSF reconstruction algorithm is now mature enough to test its performance using real data from actual observations, such as the SOUL+LUCI instrument at the LBT. This demonstration marks the first time our algorithm has been applied to real data, showcasing its readiness for further testing and validation. Our algorithm successfully reconstructs the Strehl ratio and full-width at half maximum of the observed PSFs with high accuracy, and we have evaluated its performance through simulated observations of an ideal science case.

In various scientific fields, numerous standalone sparse linear equations are frequently encountered, such as in plasma physics and astrophysics simulations, chemical reactions in combustion processes, and subdomain solutions in domain decomposition solvers. Although one can combine these systems into a single larger equation and use standard solvers, this method fails to capitalize on their independent structure and the theoretical benefits of Krylov solvers are therefore lost. Modern computing accelerators, particularly those with many processing elements, are well-suited for handling each of these systems individually, and this "batch" approach allows for the retention of Krylov solver optimality, substantial reduction in kernel launches, and minimized global communication. This research aims to create portable solvers capable of performing a complete linear system solve on a single processing element within a single kernel launch, utilizing the PETSc numerical library.

The redshift anisotropy in the bispectrum can be quantified using multipole moments, but measuring these moments depends on the statistical variability of the data. A new method for calculating this variability in galaxy surveys has been developed, specifically for surveys like Euclid. This approach involves determining the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), which measures the detectability of each multipole, and the rank correlation, which assesses the correlation between measurement errors for any two multipoles. Based on SNR values, researchers have found that Euclid has the potential to measure bispectrum multipoles up to a certain level (four) across various configurations in Fourier space, with maximum detectability observed in linear triangles. The SNR values also depend on the observational scales and redshifts. Although multipoles with a low level (two or less) can be measured with a high SNR (above five) at larger scales, those with a higher level (above two) can only be measured by observing smaller scales or increasing the size of the data bins. Most multipole pairs have only a weak correlation across various configurations, making it possible to combine the measurements of different multipoles to increase the overall signal-to-noise ratio.

This paper delves into the realm of online Reinforcement Learning (RL) within partially observable dynamic systems, particularly focusing on Predictive State Representations (PSRs). A key model in this context, PSRs captures the essence of more prominent models like Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDP). The PSRs model utilizes future observation predictions to represent states and relies solely on observable quantities. A novel algorithm for PSRs has been developed, capable of learning nearly optimal policies at a sample complexity that scales polynomially with system parameters. Our algorithm seamlessly integrates function approximation to efficiently handle large state and observation spaces. Notably, given a realizable model class, the algorithm exhibits polynomial sample complexity scaling, independent of the state and observation space sizes. Most significantly, this work marks the first instance where polynomial sample complexities are shown to be competitive with the globally optimal policy in PSRs. Furthermore, a general theorem derived in this work can be directly applied to establish sample complexity bounds for specific models, including m-step weakly revealing and decodable tabular POMDPs, low-rank latent transition POMDPs, and linear emission and latent transition POMDPs.

Accelerating matrix multiplication can significantly lower the costs associated with neural network inference. Building upon previous research that employed table-lookups by fitting hash functions to training data, this work offers improvements tailored to the deep learning inference context, where training data and fixed model weight matrices are available. We also introduce a fine-tuning procedure to speed up entire neural networks without compromising accuracy. Our analysis on a basic image classification task reveals enhanced performance over prior work; however, the classification accuracy still remains substantially lower than that of exact matrix multiplication. Although our study yields a less than ideal outcome, it provides a direction for future research on hastening inner product computations using rapid nonlinear hashing techniques.

We perform detailed calculations of Vafa-Witten invariants for 3-dimensional manifolds, drawing a parallel with Floer groups in Donaldson theory. We specifically calculate the Vafa-Witten invariants of 3-dimensional manifolds in several concrete instances, which relate to various geometric modifications (the Gluck twist, knot surgeries, log transformations). Additionally, we outline the expected properties for Vafa-Witten invariants in general 3-dimensional manifolds, encompassing the behavior under modular transformations, connection to Floer homology, the infinite-dimensional nature of these invariants for any 3-manifold, and the non-existence of instantons.

Heavy Higgs bosons expected in certain model extensions of the Standard Model are key targets for high-energy colliders, driving significant research at the Large Hadron Collider to analyze their results. For particularly heavy Higgs states, a fundamental symmetry drastically limits the ways they can break down. When these states are made up solely of Higgs doublets, researchers expect fermions to be the primary decay channels, but some boson modes may produce cleaner signals. However, a more complex picture emerges when singlet states are also present, as this can make boson-to-Higgs decays the dominant mode. To accurately interpret the experimental data, scientists must also consider the impact of various radiative corrections within the model, as examined in this study for the MSSM and NMSSM at full one-loop order. This investigation highlights the effects of a fundamental symmetry and the emergence of significant non-resonant contributions to specific final states.

Our research reveals that discontinuous shear thickening can occur even in
suspensions of low or moderate particle density, comprising smooth particles
that experience minimal friction. This phenomenon is akin to an ignitable and
quenchable transition within inertial suspensions. A kinetic model, validated
without any adjustment, successfully predicts simulation outcomes across a broad
range of particle concentrations.

In meeting global climate objectives and sustainable development goals, small dam reservoirs require consistent geographic data. To bridge the existing data gap, utilizing remote sensing imagery for automated dam reservoir extraction is a promising approach. This process is a refined aspect of water body extraction, involving the identification of water areas and distinguishing dam reservoirs from natural water bodies. A proposed pipeline utilizes a deep neural network to separate water bodies from background land in a segmentation phase and classify each as either a dam reservoir or natural water body. To address contour ambiguities, point-level metric learning is incorporated into the segmentation model, while prior-guided metric learning is used in the classification model to optimize the image embedding space based on reservoir clusters. A new benchmark dataset has been created using earth imagery data and labelled reservoirs in West Africa and India. Experiments conducted on this dataset reveal superior performance of the proposed method compared to state-of-the-art approaches in tasks including water body segmentation, dam reservoir recognition, and joint extraction.

Concentrations of localized residual stress and elastic strain in microelectronic devices, specifically in the sub-$\mu$m scale, significantly impact electronic performance and resistance to thermal and radiation damage. The main difficulty in measuring these concentrations lies in the limited spatial resolution of traditional methods. This study successfully utilizes non-destructive synchrotron X-ray based differential aperture X-ray microscopy (DAXM) for a depth-resolved analysis of stress and strain concentrations within high electron mobility transistors (HEMTs) featuring gallium nitride (GaN) layers. The technique provides sub-$\mu$m spatial resolution for two-dimensional strain field mapping between source and drain in the GaN layer. The results include strain field images from both pristine and irradiated HEMT specimens along with an initial stress analysis estimating the stress distribution within the GaN layer. $\gamma$-irradiation was observed to induce substantial lattice plane contraction along the sample's normal direction, primarily due to radiation-induced damage from transistor components bonded to the GaN layer.

To ensure the safety, effectiveness, and user-friendliness of AI-powered medical devices before clinical use, it's essential to evaluate their performance under real-world data variations.
