Secondly, it provides a straightforward proof of a closed formula for the expected Sackin index of phylogenetic trees, which are labelled with species, under the uniform model.

This study provides a detailed microscopic analysis of four-wave mixing with a dressed system, showcasing the capability of spectral control over quantum entanglements. We start with a model of double Λ configuration for a single pump four-wave mixing, incorporating a dressing field interacting with the excited level to facilitate a six-wave mixing process. The proposed model elucidates how the interaction with the dressing field boosts the amplification and intensity difference squeezing, influenced by the experimental parameters. Notably, this model predicts that the quantum correlations between adjacent sidebands can be precisely controlled through adjustments in the dressing field.

Power grid efficiency can be notably enhanced by price-driven demand response systems. Moreover, it's desirable for such systems to also improve power system operation, particularly by lowering peak electricity consumption. A new Intraday Block Pricing (IBP) plan is introduced to stimulate effective demand response from consumers by pricing their electricity use according to daily time slots. To create the pricing structure, a complex optimization model is developed, focusing on minimizing Peak-to-Average Ratio and simultaneously benefiting both the consumers and utility company. This problem is converted into a more manageable mathematical framework, which is later transformed into a Mixed Integer Linear Program by handling the complexities. A conservative benchmark is established for evaluating the proposed approach's effectiveness. Case studies reveal significant Peak-to-Average Ratio reductions and economic advantages for both the utility and consumers, demonstrating the practicality of the proposed scheme. Additionally, simulation outcomes confirm that the original and relaxed models produce equivalent solutions, highlighting the efficacy of the introduced solution method.

Geschke demonstrated the existence of a 3-saturated, clopen graph in $2^\omega$, yet clopen graphs in $2^\omega$ lack 4-saturated infinite subgraphs, whereas an $F_\sigma$ graph is known to be $\omega_1$-saturated. Interestingly, there is no $\omega$-saturated closed graph in $2^\omega$. This note fills the remaining gaps by showing that for every $n$, a closed, $n$-saturated graph exists on the Cantor space $2^\omega$, with the key contribution being a probabilistic lemma. The construction ultimately involves taking the inverse limit of finite graphs.

For permutation groups acting on a set, an intersecting subset is one where any two elements from the subset map some element in the set to the same value. The intersection density of a transitive permutation group is determined by the maximum size of an intersecting subset relative to the size of a point's stabilizer. A permutation group with a maximal intersecting subset as its largest stabilizer is said to have the Erdos-Ko-Rado property. This study focuses on transitive groups with point stabilizers of prime order, particularly those of order 2 or 3. These groups lack the Erdos-Ko-Rado property and various families of these groups with specific intersection densities are identified.

To determine equilibrium radiation levels and decay times for synchrotron radiation emitted in coupled storage ring lattices, we project standard radiation integral values onto lattice normal modes, accounting for distorted orbits through off-axis radiation integral calculations. This has led to the development of explicit equations for efficient forward calculation, which have been integrated into OPA, a user-friendly lattice design code.

A rare type of galaxy known as CSS J102913+404220 has exhibited unusual optical activity which we have extensively examined across multiple frequencies over a ten-year period since its occurrence. Our data reveals significant increases in mid-infrared radiation roughly two months following the initial optical outburst, with an extremely high energy peak reaching log(L_4.6um)>44 erg/s, surpassing any recorded supernovae event, which may imply the optical activity is caused by a stellar tidal disruption event (TDE). Furthermore, we have discovered late-time brightening in the X-ray spectrum by a factor greater than 30, followed by a swift decrease by a factor of about 4 within two weeks, signifying this is one of the most variable Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) on record. Notably, despite dramatic X-ray fluctuations, we have not observed corresponding fluctuations in the optical, UV and MIR frequencies. This unusual behavior, previously seen in other high-accretion rate AGN, could be caused by varying levels of absorption. In this case, as the TDE progresses, the decrease in the covering factor of the absorber may cause the X-ray brightening, which may have been induced by the TDE. Interestingly, while the UV and optical continuum remain relatively unchanged over time, we have observed an increase in the intensity of the H-alpha broad emission line nearly a decade after the nuclear optical outburst, which has not been seen in any other AGN before. This anomaly can be explained by the replenishment and excitation of gas clouds within the Broad Line Region (BLR) which may result from the interaction between outflowing stellar debris and the BLR. Our results emphasize the significance of the long-term evolution of TDE in shaping the accreting properties of AGN, as predicted by recent simulations.

The way humans recognize images can be influenced by the language used to describe them, known as picture-word interference. This interference depends on how the words are categorized and highlights the close relationship between human language processing and visual processing. Research on artificial models that process both text and images has found similar biases in image classification. By exploring whether these biases can cause interference similar to what humans experience, researchers can gain insight into how well these models understand hierarchical concepts. This study uses methods from cognitive science to analyze biases in artificial models and presents a new test to assess how language affects image classification. The test involves evaluating how the presence of words on images affects image classification across different categories. The results of this study show that language does influence image classification, but in a way that suggests the language representation in the model is separate from the visual representation.

To combat pandemics like COVID-19, essential resources like personal protective gear are crucial to minimize transmission rates and safeguard individuals exposed to infected patients. As outbreaks escalate, demand for these resources surges exponentially, far outpacing local production capacity. Global supply chain disruptions triggered by factory shutdowns and transport restrictions exacerbate resource scarcity. Initially, during the COVID-19 pandemic, a "local first" approach was observed in many areas. Conversely, our research demonstrates that collaborative resource sharing can significantly enhance pandemic preparedness. By establishing a model where communities share resources to ensure access during local outbreaks, we propose that this can prevent resource depletion and reduce overall infection cases. Moreover, the effectiveness of resource sharing is contingent upon sufficient time lag between outbreaks in separate communities. Consequently, a global sharing mechanism must be complemented with measures to slow down inter-community infection transmission. Our study serves as a starting point for designing a robust global supply chain framework that can proactively address future pandemics, rather than relying on chance and uneven resource distribution.

To address the significant cold-start issue in click-through rate prediction, we present the Variational Embedding Learning Framework (VELF), a general approach that resolves data-scarcity induced overfitting in two ways: by developing probabilistic embeddings and incorporating trainable, regularized prior models that leverage rich information from both cold-start users and advertisements. These techniques are organically incorporated into a variational inference framework, enabling an end-to-end training process. Our VELF framework has been extensively tested on standard datasets, demonstrating its efficacy, and further experiments confirm that our adaptable and regularized prior models offer superior generalization capabilities compared to traditional fixed prior models.

One major obstacle in current and future neutrino research using large Liquid Argon detectors is distinguishing genuine neutrino interactions from an overwhelming cosmic-ray background. While conventional methods involve time-consuming and complex algorithms, our approach leverages a cutting-edge 3D convolutional network that analyzes the scintillation light emitted by particles in these detectors. Employing this technique in simulated scenarios from Fermilab's ICARUS detector, we successfully reduced the cosmic background by as much as 76.3% without compromising neutrino interaction detection rates, which remained above 98.9%. Furthermore, to address potential inaccuracies in our simulations, we integrated a domain-adversarial network that adjusts our training samples to mimic real-world data. Our experiments confirm the effectiveness of this approach in minimizing biases and outperforming the original results by a significant margin.

Researchers have lately shown significant interest in constructing LDPC codes using permutation matrices. However, it's crucial to avoid cycles of short lengths in the corresponding Tanner graphs, which can be achieved by obtaining a high girth. This paper offers a framework for constructing such codes. By connecting cycle existence criteria with number-theoretic concepts, specifically Sidon sets, we obtain examples of LDPC codes with specified girth. Furthermore, our framework is expanded to also generate irregular LDPC codes.

We categorize singularities at infinity for cubic polynomials in three variables, expressed as the sum of three homogeneous polynomials, and use this classification to determine the Milnor number jump when transitioning from a special fiber to a generic fiber. Furthermore, we utilize these results to study the global fibrations of cubic polynomials in three-dimensional complex space, exploring the topology of fibers within each equivalence class.

We're examining an alternative to the standard Bayesian mechanism, where participants make decisions based on ex-ante evaluations of their outcomes and constraints. This approach reflects the concerns of modern online advertisers, who aim to maximize their long-term expected utility despite potential changes in their type over time. Our focus is on the incentive compatibility issue in such Bayesian mechanisms, under the assumption that the conditions for these environments are relatively weak. We provide a detailed description of how incentive compatibility can be achieved using the taxation principle and reveal an unexpected finding: that these compatible mechanisms are all variants of auto-bidding systems, which are widely used in the online advertising industry.

Araci et al. initially established a $p$-adic $(\rho,q)$-variant of the Haar distribution. This led to the creation of the $p$-adic $(\rho,q)$-Volkenborn integral. The author of this paper leverages Mahler expansions to develop a Radon-Nikodym theorem in relation to the $p$-adic $(\rho,q)$-distribution over $\Bbb Z_p$.

A network of autonomous entities is considered, whose decision-making processes are governed by a quantum decision framework. Decision-making outcomes result from the combination of utility evaluations, attractiveness assessments, and information availability, ultimately determining probabilities for selecting an alternative. This decision-making process is characterized by its multifaceted nature. Agents interact by exchanging information, which can take the form of direct communication or collectively generated knowledge. The common information field experienced by all agents tends to mitigate sharp fluctuations in probability patterns and may even eradicate them. For entities with short-term memory, probabilities often oscillate rapidly before converging to fixed values, sometimes entering a state of perpetual indecision. However, introducing the information field can dampen or eliminate these oscillations, causing probabilities to settle at stable limits. This phenomenon is referred to as the dynamic disjunction effect.

M. Bhargava and P. Harron demonstrated that for $n=3,4,5$, the distributions of
integer ring shapes within degree $n$ $S_n$-number fields, when ordered by
discriminant, converge uniformly across the spectrum of shapes. In our study, we
replace shapes with grids, which retain more information from the number fields.
The space of grids is a complex structure derived from the space of shapes, where
the grids of integer rings in degree $n$ $S_n$-number fields are shown to be
equally distributed across the grid space.

The Search-Oriented Conversational AI (SCAI) conference is a well-established platform that showcases cutting-edge conversational search research. At the SCAI'21 conference, a virtual event took place, where a conversational question answering shared task was held. Given that participating teams primarily relied on answer generation models, a significant research challenge and gap arose, particularly in assessing the correctness of answers. To supplement automatic evaluation, we conducted two crowdsourcing experiments to gather annotations for answer plausibility and faithfulness. Consequently, the original conversational QA dataset used for evaluation was enriched with alternative correct answers generated by participant systems.

We have successfully incorporated the adaptively compressed exchange (ACE) operator within the linear augmented plane wave (LAPW) framework. The ACE operator achieves a low-rank representation of the Fock exchange, maintaining energy accuracy without compromising precision. Our calculations, utilizing the non-relativistic hybrid functional PBE0, demonstrate the ACE operator's applicability to all-electron total energy calculations. The resulting data for light atoms and molecules closely align with exact multi-resolution-analysis calculations, differing by a few microhartree. Furthermore, our results indicate that employing high-energy local orbitals in conjunction with the ACE operator is crucial for achieving high precision when using Fock exchange. We utilize this implementation to compute PBE0 band gaps in solids and compare them with other all-electron methods.

The Seyfert galaxy NGC 1566, known as a "changing look" Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN), has shown multiple X-ray outbursts, each lasting several years. In 2018, the galaxy experienced a significant increase in X-ray emission, a factor of 24 higher than its minimum historical level. We re-examined data from the XMM-Newton and NuSTAR space telescopes and confirmed a broad emission feature in the galaxy's X-ray spectrum, attributed to the presence of a relativistic iron emission line, during the time of the outburst. This feature correlated with the galaxy's X-ray continuum, providing strong evidence for X-rays originating in a corona above the accretion disk and being reflected by the disk, producing the emission line. Furthermore, the galaxy's narrow iron emission line responded rapidly to changes in the X-ray continuum, allowing us to infer the line-emitting region's size, comparable to the galaxy's optical Broad Line Region. Compared to the similar AGN NGC 2992, NGC 1566's iron emission line varied more in response to X-ray continuum changes, possibly due to differences in the amount of gas or iron abundance. We found a connection between the variability of the broad iron emission line and soft X-ray excess with the galaxy's accretion rate, possibly related to the galaxy's state transition during the "changing look" phenomenon.

In this study, a social learning model is analyzed where agents randomly select a neighbor to share information with at each time step. The model reveals that even with reduced communication, agents ultimately converge to the truth at a similar rate as standard methods that require more communication. Furthermore, the analysis focuses on a specific scenario where agents replace their beliefs with those of their chosen neighbors, yielding log-belief ratio estimates under large deviation conditions.

Approximately two decades ago, Abadi et al. developed the Dependency Core Calculus (DCC) to serve as a versatile framework for analyzing dependencies within typed programming languages. Subsequently, dependency analysis has proven to be highly beneficial in language design, as its outcomes can facilitate users and compilers in enforcing security constraints and removing redundant code, amongst other applications. This work introduces the Dependent Dependency Calculus (DDC), which builds upon this concept, specifically addressing the realm of dependently-typed languages. By employing this calculus, we are able to monitor both runtime and compile-time irrelevance, thus enabling faster type-checking and program execution.

The study of nonlocal dispersion compensation in broadband photon pairs propagated over standard G.652D telecommunications fiber involved precise measurements of their temporal correlation. By adjusting the travel distance of these photon pairs to preserve their timing correlations near the detection device's resolution limit (41.0±0.1ps), near-ideal nonlocal dispersion compensation was achieved. The results suggest that such high levels of compensation are feasible with large increments of fiber (1km), making them compatible with real-world applications. Furthermore, experiments demonstrated the ability to preserve photon timing correlations as low as 51ps±21ps over two separate, long stretches of metropolitan fiber (totaling 20km).

For online food platforms, accurate reviews and personalized recommendations are critical. However, evaluating food and suggesting suitable options is complex due to diverse contexts and interpretations. This study employs various deep learning techniques to address issues in sentiment analysis, automated review categorization, and review retrieval for the food industry. We aim to establish a food review system called NTU Food Hunter at Nanyang Technological University, integrating deep learning strategies to facilitate users' food choices. Initially, we integrate BERT and LSTM models for analyzing the sentiment of food reviews. Subsequently, a POS-based algorithm is developed to automatically identify and extract adjective-noun pairs from reviews for generating tags through part-of-speech tagging and dependency parsing. Furthermore, a RankNet model is trained for re-ranking retrieval outcomes to enhance the precision of the Solr-based search system for food reviews. The experiment results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed deep learning approaches in solving real-world problems.

We examine the sensitivity of nonclassical spin states, including spin-squeezed and Dicke states, that have been split into multiple modes, and can be addressed individually. Using mathematical models, we demonstrate the enhanced precision achievable in multiparameter measurements, as well as the best approaches for achieving the greatest sensitivity with existing atomic systems. Additionally, we investigate the entanglement between these modes by developing a test for genuine multi-part entanglement from the spin-squeezing matrix. Our findings emphasize the benefits of entanglement for distributed sensing, and provide optimal methods for estimating multiple parameters using nonclassical spin ensembles that have been spatially distributed.

We're conducting an in-depth study on the melting and undercooling processes in gold nanoparticles, approximately 100 nm in radius, that are isolated within a vacuum chamber using a quadrupole ion trap. By shining a laser on the particle and measuring its mass, we can gauge its evaporation rate and subsequently its temperature. We're also employing direct optical methods to monitor the distinct optical signatures exhibited by the particle in its liquid and solid states. By repeatedly heating the particle across its melting point and analyzing the impact of particle size on the heating dynamics, we aim to elucidate the effects of undercooling, where the particle remains in a liquid state below its melting temperature, induced through multi-stage laser pulses, and compare our findings with theoretical expectations.

We have translated Emile Mathieu's paper, titled 'On the five-fold transitive function of 24 quantities,' into English to assist with our research project focused on expressing $M_{23}$ in terms of additive functions on a finite field containing 2^11 elements.

Our research is centered on network alignment (NA), the process of determining node correspondences between two networks based on structural and attribute information. Current NA approaches have limitations since they often attempt to identify all node pairs simultaneously, failing to utilize valuable insights gained from intermediate node matches to improve subsequent correspondence detection. To address this challenge, we introduce Grad-Align, a novel NA method that gradually identifies node pairs by leveraging the strong consistency of easily identifiable matches early on in the matching process. Specifically, Grad-Align starts by creating node embeddings for the two networks using graph neural networks along with our custom layer-wise reconstruction loss function, which captures both first-order and higher-order neighborhood structures. Next, node alignment is achieved by computing dual-perception similarity metrics, including multi-layer embedding similarity and Tversky similarity, an asymmetric set similarity measure suitable for networks of varying scales. To further enhance structural consistency, Grad-Align incorporates an edge augmentation module. Comprehensive experiments conducted using real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that Grad-Align consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art NA methods.

The disparity in wealth or resource distribution within a population is a notable phenomenon, with the underlying causes and effective countermeasures being significant areas of research interest. To investigate this issue, we propose a model depicting the interplay between individuals within a network aimed at diminishing capital distribution inequalities. By defining the outcome of basic interactions within the network in such a way that winning leads to reduced disparities, we explore various interpretations of this model and their influence on agent behavior in terms of capital distribution. Using the capital-dependent Parrondo's paradox as a basis, our study provides examples and sheds light on the underlying mechanisms driving inequality formation in society.

Recurrent recommendation systems have effectively modeled the time-dependent behavior of users' actions, yet they are prone to struggling with long-term relationships. As a result, recommendation systems based on recurrent neural networks often focus too heavily on users' short-term preferences, a phenomenon referred to as recency bias. This bias can have a detrimental impact on both long-term user satisfaction and the overall health of the system. In this study, a novel technique called recency dropout is presented, a straightforward yet efficient data augmentation strategy designed to counteract recency bias in recurrent recommendation systems. The efficacy of recency dropout is demonstrated through experiments conducted in a simulated environment, offline tests, and real-world trials on a large-scale commercial recommendation platform.

Minimum flow decomposition is a fundamental problem in computer science with applications in RNA assembly in bioinformatics. Despite being NP-hard, current tools use heuristics or simplified models, often resulting in suboptimal solutions. Integer linear programming formulations are used in RNA assemblers, but are limited by requiring the encoding of exponentially many potential solution paths. There is no scalable exact solver for MFD, making its practical variants unsolvable. We present the first efficient ILP formulation for MFD, enabling an exact solution using a quadratic number of variables. Our approach solves instances in under 13 seconds, outperforming current methods, and can be easily adapted to accommodate various real-world conditions, potentially revolutionizing RNA assembly tools.

The distance measurement between cosmic locations, known as the cosmic distance ladder, poses a challenge in a lumpy universe where observations are made from a single location. The distances to type Ia supernovae in the universe's expansion are linked to nearby local measurements. We have identified how this configuration can be established even in a perturbed universe with minor irregularities on a flat spacetime framework. Our research reveals a substantial, about 11%, alteration to the background universe's distance measurement due to nearby cosmic inhomogeneities near the observer. This modification is primarily driven by a component of the Weyl tensor, indicating distortions in the observer's local spacetime. We demonstrate in detail how this alteration can impact the calibration of type Ia supernovae brightness in the expanding universe, potentially resolving existing discrepancies in supernova brightness and Hubble constant measurements without requiring dark energy at any stage.

This research focuses on a cosmological model with a universe dominated by phantom energy, characterized by an equation of state parameter $w<-1$. The analysis of this scenario's long-term behavior explores the possibility of the Big Rip singularity occurring in the future. Within the framework of general relativity, it is proposed that the Big Rip singularity could be averted due to gravitational particle creation through the Schwinger mechanism, assuming no additional particle-creation processes occur. In this theoretical model, the far-future universe is described by a state of high Hubble rate and energy density, low horizon entropy, and constant values for both, mirroring initial conditions. This analysis suggests that the Big Rip singularity can be avoided and the universe may enter a new phase of inflation, ultimately leading to the creation of multiple new universes.

Quantum sensors that detect rotation are crucial components in navigation systems, 
and scientists are working to improve them beyond the current limits of precision 
using quantum mechanics. Unfortunately, current quantum navigation methods are 
affected by a major issue called decoherence, which makes them less accurate. 
We have proposed a new method that uses two light beams as quantum sensors and 
can work around this problem, even in environments with a lot of noise. Our study 
has shown that it's possible to achieve the highest possible precision, exceeding 
the limits set by classical physics, if each light beam interacts with its 
environment in a special way. This discovery provides a way to improve rotation 
sensing in real-world applications where noise is present.

This paper introduces a novel Boltzmann-Gibbs random field model with localized energy interactions defined by a spatial coupling function. This function uses kernel-based approximations of spatial derivatives from smoothed particle hydrodynamics. A second-degree polynomial based on the Laplace operator is used to represent these interactions. An explicit, kernel-based expression is derived for the spatial coupling function in the case of a squared exponential smoothing kernel, enabling the model to transition from discrete to continuous data without discontinuity. The proposed model is connected to Gaussian Markov random fields and the Matern field with specific parameter values.

This study revisits itinerant ferromagnetism in 2D and 3D electron systems, considering various degrees of spin-orbit separation and significant electron-electron interaction. We have isolated the key scattering events near the Fermi surface, which lead to the destabilization of the ferromagnetic quantum critical point at low temperatures. Unlike prior theoretical investigations, our results indicate that these events cannot be entirely eliminated, even with arbitrary spin-orbit separation. Our self-contained and non-perturbative analysis of electron-electron interaction near the phase transition shows that these events consistently destabilize the ferromagnetic quantum critical point, resulting in a first-order phase transition. These events can be quantitatively assessed through the non-analytic variation of the spin susceptibility in response to a magnetic field, whether at a distance from or close to the phase transition.

In a multi-source system where each source generates updates based on a Poisson process, served by a generally distributed time, we've developed a preemptive policy that prioritizes fresh updates over older ones of the same source. We then derived mathematical expressions for measuring the quality of these updates, and used these to compare three different policies: one that prioritizes fresh updates, one that doesn't prioritize updates, and one that doesn't prioritize updates but still considers the average quality. We found that the policy which doesn't prioritize updates but still considers the average quality performs the best under certain conditions, while the policy which prioritizes fresh updates performs the best under different conditions. Our results highlight the importance of considering higher-level characteristics of the update quality.

Gaussian processes serve as a valuable resource in machine learning and statistics for modeling continuous processes. When a process's value is known at a finite set of points, one can employ Gaussian processes to create an interpolating surface for making predictions and quantifying uncertainty at other locations. However, in situations where data is not limited to a finite set of points, standard Gaussian process techniques are not directly applicable. A prominent example of such situations is boundary value problems, where information about the boundary of a domain is provided, which forms an uncountable collection of points. To address this issue, we develop a Gaussian process model that leverages reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, allowing it to integrate the typical finite case with scenarios having uncountable information. Our approach relies on the equivalence of conditional expectation and orthogonal projections, and we explore its implementation in statistical models, including its numerical aspects and a proof of concept.

The application of deep learning-based segmentation techniques for the liver and its associated lesions has become increasingly relevant in medical practice due to the rising incidence of liver cancer. Although numerous network variants have shown promising results in medical image segmentation, they face significant challenges when accurately segmenting liver lesions. To address this limitation, a novel hybrid network called SWTR-Unet was developed by integrating elements of convolutional and transformer-based architectures. The proposed network, consisting of a pre-trained ResNet, transformer blocks, and a common Unet-style decoder path, was tested on clinical liver MRI scans and the publicly available CT data from the LiTS challenge. Comparative studies involving multiple state-of-the-art networks were also conducted on both datasets to evaluate the performance of SWTR-Unet. The findings showed that SWTR-Unet outperformed other networks, achieving high Dice similarity scores for liver and lesion segmentation on both MRI and CT datasets. The method's performance was comparable to expert manual segmentations, highlighting its potential to reduce clinical time and resource expenditures.

Recent research has exposed the vulnerability of deep neural networks to adversarial attacks, specifically in three-dimensional point clouds. Although prior methods have been developed to target point clouds, their adversarial samples exhibit weak transferability and are easily defendable. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel point cloud attack, AOF, which emphasizes the importance of low-frequency components. By incorporating losses from both the point cloud and its low-frequency representation, AOF produces more robust adversarial samples that demonstrate superior transferability compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our attack produces point clouds with significant deformation rather than solely introducing outliers.

The effects of nuclear structure on the number of produced particles (N_ch) and anisotropic particle movement ($v_2$ and $v_3$) in the isobaric collisions of $^{96}_{44}$Ru + $^{96}_{44}$Ru and $^{96}_{40}$Zr + $^{96}_{40}$Zr at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 7.7, 27, 62.4 and 200 GeV are explored by utilizing the string melting version of the AMPT model. The comparison with recent STAR collaboration experimental data reveals that nuclear structure characteristics have distinct effects on $v_2$ and $v_3$ depending on the collision centrality, with quadrupole deformation influencing the most central collisions, octupole deformation impacting near-central collisions, and the neutron skin effect prevailing in mid-central collisions. Furthermore, the magnitude of these effects intensifies at lower energies.

Revisiting the importance weighted variational inference (IWVI) theory, a method for learning latent variable models, we introduce novel variational bounds called Monte Carlo objectives. These bounds, obtained by replacing intractable integrals with Monte Carlo estimates, primarily through importance sampling, were first shown to tighten the gap between the bound and the likelihood with increasing importance samples. We expand on this insight by establishing nonasymptotic links between Monte Carlo estimates and the tightness of these objectives, challenging the conventional wisdom that lower variance improves the bounds. We provide theoretical support for empirical findings that negative correlation decreases the variational gap and generalise the original monotonicity theorem to accommodate non-uniform weights. This work also draws upon concepts and results from stochastic order theory to discuss the practical implications of our findings.

We investigate the dynamic behavior of simple congestion games with two resources, in which a continuous group of agents follow a variant of the Experience-Weighted Attraction algorithm. The system is governed by three key parameters: a positive choice intensity representing the collective rationality of the population, an exponential memory loss factor ranging between zero and one, and an asymmetry parameter reflecting the disparity in cost functions between the two resources. This framework enables us to demonstrate a diverse range of bifurcation phenomena where behavioral dynamics transition from stable convergence to limit cycles or even chaotic patterns in response to variations in these parameters. We show that increasing the choice intensity can destabilize the system, but as the memory loss factor rises, chaos gives way to predictable two-period cycles. This research, supported by simulations and bifurcation diagrams, highlights the intricate complexity of population dynamics, even in the simplest scenarios.

A recent breakthrough in computer vision tasks was made by a class of neural networks known as capsule networks. Despite initial successes, conventional capsule networks have limitations in handling intricate datasets due to substantial computational and memory demands. To overcome these drawbacks, a novel network architecture, termed Momentum Capsule Network (MoCapsNet), has been developed, drawing inspiration from Momentum ResNets with reversible residual building blocks. By incorporating this design, memory requirements are drastically reduced as network activations can be recalculated during backpropagation. This study presents a framework for integrating invertible residual blocks into capsule networks. Results demonstrate that MoCapsNet surpasses baseline capsule networks on MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, achieving improved accuracy while requiring significantly less memory.

To rigorously discuss continuous functions, one must first establish a framework 
for determining open sets, which can be achieved by defining a topology. A 
topology is defined by three fundamental axioms governing the properties of 
open sets within a space. This paper explores the implications of modifying one 
of these axioms on the continuity of functions.

Determining the most cost-effective route through connected graphs necessitates identifying the minimum total expenditure for traversing the graph's edges. Traditional methods for finding optimal paths in graphs are often limited by predefined costs for all edges, preventing the use of conventional planning approaches when costs need to be dynamically adjusted. However, this limitation can be overcome by mapping path-finding problems to neural networks, where cost values are converted into synaptic weights that can be adapted in real-time through network learning mechanisms. When initialized with a starting activity value, the network's activity propagation will yield solutions identical to those obtained from the Bellman-Ford algorithm, which shares the same computational complexity. Furthermore, the network's adaptive capabilities can be leveraged to refine the optimal paths based on specific task requirements. To illustrate this, the proposed approach was used to train the network to navigate through obstacle-filled environments and follow predetermined sequences of path nodes. As a result, this novel algorithm enables a more intuitive integration of path augmentation and finding, potentially opening up new applications.

The existence of the axion particle remains uncertain, but its field can be leveraged in a local, chiral U(1) gauge theory with both classical and quantum invariance. Analogues of the axion field, which have been introduced, can be combined with their unique properties in a similar framework for nonabelian chiral gauge theories. In this construction, the gauge symmetry is similarly broken, resulting in a massive gauge boson as the axion field is incorporated, rendering it non-physical in this context.

We investigate four-dimensional gauge theories with N=1 supersymmetry, which are S-confining and have a duality to a Wess-Zumino model. Classifications of S-confining theories with simple gauge groups already exist, so we instead verify the associated dualities, particularly when matter fields transform according to rank-1 and/or rank-2 representations. We base our proof on the established S-confining dualities of SU(N) with N+1 flavors and Usp(2N) with 2N+4 fundamentals. To achieve this, we use a systematic approach that involves a series of deconfinements and re-confinements. During each step, we carefully examine the superpotential.

We investigate the local and bipartite entanglement R\'enyi entropies of a free Fermi gas in a multi-dimensional space at thermal equilibrium. We demonstrate that entanglement entropies with a R\'enyi index of less than or equal to one are positive at all temperatures above zero. Furthermore, for any positive R\'enyi index, we derive the asymptotic behavior of these entropies as the temperature and a scaling parameter approach large values, in two distinct regimes based on either a fixed chemical potential or a fixed particle density. This work completes the necessary proof for our previously established low and high-temperature results for $\gamma = 1$, which were initially presented without a complete mathematical justification.

The discrete Fourier transform, crucial for photonic quantum information, poses a significant challenge in terms of scaling it to high dimensions, particularly with regard to physical encoding methods in emerging platforms such as frequency bins. However, our research demonstrates that d-point frequency-bin DFTs can be efficiently implemented with a three-component quantum frequency processor by incorporating an additional radio-frequency harmonic for each increment in d. Numerical simulations confirm the high fidelity of our approach, yielding F > 0.9997 and P > 0.965 up to d = 10, and experimental results verify its feasibility for d = 3, enabling measurements of entanglement and complete tomography of multiple two-photon frequency-bin states. This breakthrough opens new possibilities for high-dimensional frequency-bin protocols in quantum communication and networking.

This study builds upon our prior research on spherical representations within operator algebras and introduces potential dimension group analogues in the current context by using operator systems. We then apply our findings to inductive limits of compact quantum groups and establish a quantum analogue of Olshanski's concept of spherical unitary representations for infinite-dimensional pairs of the form $G < G \times G$. This provides a theoretical justification for Ryosuke Sato's approach to quantum group asymptotic representation theory.

Detweiler's approximate solution of the Klein-Gordon equation for a scalar field in a Kerr black hole, initially employed in black hole stability analysis and axion-like particle research, was discovered by Pani to be incomplete, with a missing factor of one-half. This discrepancy has led to some unusual features that challenge traditional power-counting approaches. To rectify this issue, we introduce the next-to-leading order contribution to the equation, thereby reducing the percentage error of the initial solution by roughly half across all critical values of the parameter. This correction significantly improves accuracy, particularly for values below $0.35r_g\mu$, and presents a more manageable expression.

In the field of natural language understanding, natural language inference (NLI) has become a critical task that involves identifying the connection between a given sentence pair (premise and hypothesis). A significant number of recent studies have leveraged contrastive learning by utilizing NLI datasets to derive sentence representations based on their relationship. However, existing methods have primarily focused on sentence-level comparisons. This paper introduces a novel Pair-level Supervised Contrastive Learning (PairSCL) method, which incorporates a cross-attention module to learn joint representations for sentence pairs. A designed contrastive objective function enables PairSCL to differentiate between distinct classes of sentence pairs by attracting those in the same class and repelling those in different classes. Our evaluation of PairSCL on NLI datasets reveals that it outperforms other approaches by a margin of 2.1% on average. Additionally, PairSCL demonstrates superior performance compared to the previous state-of-the-art method on seven transfer tasks of text classification.

The experiment known as the "isobar run" at RHIC aimed to investigate the differences in various collision outcomes for $^{96}_{40}Zr$ and $^{96}_{44}Ru$, with a focus on how these differences depend on atomic number. However, recent STAR data have revealed more pronounced variations between the two nuclides than initially anticipated, with effects stemming from nuclear properties outweighing those of charge. Multiple studies have sought to quantify their shape differences in relation to various collision outcomes, attributing these differences to nuclear structure, particularly the properties of low-lying excited states. A clear connection between low-energy and high-energy nuclear physics remains elusive, which is why I propose a new approach that ties the two via the concept of thermal density matrices of "preheated" nuclei, leveraging an effective temperature to determine which excited states should be considered in calculations. Furthermore, I suggest employing a semiclassical "flucton" method at finite temperatures to calculate thermal density matrices.

A novel probabilistic model has been developed to identify approximate pattern repeats in sparse binary data with high precision, leveraging the "Noisy-OR model" to achieve accurate disease and topic modeling outcomes. By extracting meaningful patterns in retinal neuron recordings, this model demonstrates its versatility for discovering hidden structures in noisy binary data across various contexts. Specifically, in spiking neural data, the model aims to decipher the underlying causes of individual neuron spikes by associating them with groups of neurons known as "Cell Assemblies," which often fire simultaneously due to mutual interactions or other factors. Through the use of sparse binary latent variables, the model infers the activity levels of these cell assemblies, reducing the likelihood of neurons within an assembly being inactive when the assembly is active. By employing an expectation maximization scheme to refine its model parameters, the algorithm learns the conditional probability kernels governing the latent components from the data. Extensive validation of the model is conducted using synthesized spike trains mimicking recorded retinal responses to noise and visual stimuli, as well as its application to actual retinal ganglion cell data collected during movie stimulation, with notable insights into the discovered structures.

We examine a 3D ternary system obtained as a sharp interface limit of the Nakazawa-Ohta model for triblock copolymers, incorporating both an interfacial energy and a long-range interaction term. Although two-dimensional and three-dimensional binary systems, as well as two-dimensional ternary systems, have been extensively researched, the three-dimensional ternary system remains largely unexplored, particularly regarding whether its minimizers consist of a finite number of components. Our paper addresses this uncertainty by demonstrating that the number of components in a minimizer is capped by a quantity that depends solely on the system's total masses and interaction coefficients. The primary challenge in this 3D context lies in disentangling the long-range interaction from the perimeter term, resulting in the inability to accurately determine the shape of minimizers, even when the masses are relatively small, due to the lack of a quantitative isoperimetric inequality for a 3D system subject to two mass constraints.

A novel approach to image communication has been introduced, which prioritizes the transmission of semantic information for artificial intelligence tasks over image quality. In applications like autonomous driving, both image quality and AI task performance must be balanced simultaneously. To address this, a task-oriented communication method is proposed that aims to minimize both pixel-level and semantic-level distortions while meeting a given data rate. A new metric is developed to measure semantic distortion based on mutual information between reconstructed images and task labels. By solving the resulting rate-distortion optimization problem analytically, an optimal mapping between source images and semantic reconstructions can be determined. Building on this, an extended rate-distortion model is derived using variational approximation of mutual information, allowing it to be applied to multiple AI tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of this approach over traditional image communication methods and deep learning-based benchmarks in terms of image quality, AI task performance, and multi-task generalization ability.

When a polynomial $p$ undergoes the Chebyshev's method $C_p$, its degree is determined. For a specific case where $p$ is a cubic polynomial, possible degrees of $C_p$ are $4,6$, and $7$. The dynamics of $C_p$ in these scenarios are further investigated. A cubic polynomial $p$ being unicritical or non-generic results in a connected Julia set for $C_p$. A cubic polynomial $p$ being non-unicritical and generic yields a family of rational maps, with a parameterization based on the multiplier of an extraneous fixed point. Denoting this parameterization by $C_\lambda$, where the multiplier is $\lambda$, we've established that the Julia set of $C_\lambda$ remains connected for any $\lambda$ within the range $[-1,1]$.

Epilepsy is a widespread neurological condition affecting individuals across all age groups. As an alternative to medication or surgery, Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) has become a viable treatment option. To optimize DBS planning and standardize the process, developing a computational method to accurately identify the Anterior Nucleus of Thalamus (ANT) as the stimulation target is essential. This research conducts an in-depth analysis by comparing various localization techniques for ANT-DBS, including conventional registration methods and deep learning-based approaches such as heatmap matching and DSNT. Our experimental findings demonstrate that deep learning methods can achieve comparable results to human variability, while being significantly faster than traditional localization methods.

The behavior of 2D truncated Airy waves and three-component solitons within a coupled system of two fundamental-frequency and second-harmonic fields is examined, where the interactions are governed by quadratic terms. This system models optical media and Bose-Einstein condensates in atomic-molecular mixtures and also exhibits stable solitons alongside truncated-Airy-waves states in the fundamental-frequency components. These Airy waves, unlike their degenerate counterparts, are stable and can be imbued with vorticity in a 2D setting. Simulations reveal that the interaction between two 2D Airy waves, moving in opposite directions, through the second-harmonic field, results in the fusion of the input into a pair of narrow solitons. This outcome contrasts with the behavior observed in the 1D system, where Airy waves instead split into a multitude of solitons. When two truncated Airy waves carrying identical vorticities interact, an additional pair of solitons is formed, whereas waves with opposite vorticities produce a set of low-amplitude "debris." In addition, soliton interactions demonstrate unique properties, including the reflection, absorption, or elastic passage of solitons upon collision with each other or with heavy truncated Airy waves.

Amorphous solids subjected to mechanical stress exhibit a propensity for plastic behavior under deformation.
Previous studies have demonstrated in amorphous granular systems that plastic events with a typical quadrupolar nature can mask elastic responses.
When the density of quadrupoles is high, the gradients of the quadrupole field behave as emergent dipole sources, leading to notable changes in the mechanical behavior, as observed in the displacement field.
This paper investigates the phenomenon of screening in classical glass formers, comprising point particles interacting through binary forces.
Both inverse power law forces and Lennard-Jones interactions are analyzed, showing that in both cases, the elastic response can be significantly suppressed, consistent with a novel theoretical framework.
The extent to which classical elasticity theory deviates from actual behavior is quantified using a newly proposed measure, which is shown to correlate with the energy lost to plastic responses.

A particular type of branching program with read-once linear paths is being examined. This program uses $\mathbb{F}_2$ linear forms to query information, with each path containing linearly independent queries. Two specific variations of this model - weakly and strongly read-once models - are explored, both generalizing existing models like standard read-once branching programs and parity decision trees. Key results include: 

- Average-case complexity: Pseudo-random functions known as directional affine extractors are identified as being difficult for the strongly read-once model. A specific construction of these functions with favorable properties is presented. This builds upon the previous work by Cohen and Shinkar who demonstrated average-case hardness for parity decision trees. The significance of these new functions is underlined by their enhanced capabilities compared to traditional affine extractors. 

- Proof complexity: A specific proof system called $\text{Res}[\oplus]$ is analyzed, an extension of resolution that incorporates linear queries. A connection between this system and a linear branching program is established, showing that a weakly read-once linear branching program can be efficiently converted into a $\text{Res}[\oplus]$ refutation.

A proposed two-stage approach utilizes Lyapunov functions to systematically design and evaluate approximation algorithms. In the initial phase, Lyapunov functions are inputted to yield a provably effective continuous-time approximation algorithm. The second stage then translates this algorithm into a discrete-time version with comparable efficacy and established time complexities. The unique aspect of this framework lies in its ability to work with Lyapunov function specifications, where detailed information is not necessary initially. This method has several benefits: (i) it unifies existing algorithms, (ii) it provides a guide for developing and analyzing novel algorithms, and (iii) it offers new insights for potentially enhancing existing algorithms. Submodular maximization problems serve as demonstration cases for the approach.

A set of groups is said to be intersecting if any two individual groups within it share a common element.  A collection of groups is said to have the Helly property if every subset that shares at least one common element also shares another common element across all subsets.  A graph can be classified as /Helly/ based on whether the set of its largest completely connected subgroups possesses the Helly property.  We demonstrate that for a graph with k neighbors per vertex and n vertices, provided n exceeds 3k plus the square root of 2k squared minus k, then its complement will not have the Helly property.  Furthermore, we investigate whether Hellyness and stability under clique transformations are interchangeable characteristics for the complement of k-regular graphs, especially when k is at a small value.

We re-examine the issue where the Noether current linked to local scale symmetry, or equivalently, Weyl symmetry, always equals zero. Utilizing the second Noether theorem, we show that the Noether current associated with Weyl symmetry generally vanishes in any Weyl-invariant gravitational theories in four-dimensional Riemannian geometry. We also provide clarification: the Weyl transformation lacks a term involving the derivative of the transformation parameter, distinguishing it from conventional gauge transformations. We then extend this finding to a quantum theory of Weyl-invariant gravity, deriving currents associated with the chiral symmetry, specifically the $IOSp(10|10)$ supersymmetry.

Accurate 3D object detection is crucial for autonomous vehicles, and point cloud-based methods have gained popularity due to their reliable depth information. A large and diverse dataset like NuTonomy's nuScenes provides valuable information for training, but it has a severe imbalance of object classes. A proposed solution, the Class-balanced Grouping and Sampling method, aims to address this issue through augmentation and sampling strategies. Nevertheless, its performance can be compromised by the loss of spatial details in downscaled features. To address this limitation, we suggest a novel approach that integrates an auxiliary network into the model, effectively utilizing the structural properties of 3D point clouds to enhance localization accuracy. This auxiliary network is optimized using two key objectives - foreground segmentation and center estimation - and can be seamlessly detached during inference without adding extra computational overhead.

Our chosen command and control implementation is the Aegis Combat System. Key aspects of this system include missile guidance and target tracking functionalities. To investigate these components in detail, we will design a simplified model of the Aegis Combat System. In this model, a mini car will be made to autonomously track a small remote-controlled car. The system will consist of three primary components: a controller and two mini cars. This simplified model will enable the team to illustrate real-world command and control concepts, specifically command, communication, and data integration. The accompanying diagram illustrates the Aegis Combat System.

Research in decision-making, such as Fuzzy-Trace Theory, indicates that people often rely on a text's main point when making decisions. This study outlines the development of GisPy, a Python-based tool that calculates the Gist Inference Score in text. Testing GisPy on news and scientific articles from various benchmarks shows that the scores it produces clearly differentiate texts with low vs. high levels of gist. The tool is accessible for public use at: https://github.com/phosseini/GisPy.

Deep neural classifier-based text classification in a weakly supervised setting relies heavily on the quality of pseudo-labels generated through training. Although these pseudo-labels inevitably include errors due to their heuristic nature, selecting accurate ones can greatly enhance the model's overall performance. A simple approach to achieve this involves choosing samples based on their softmax probability scores from the neural classifier corresponding to their pseudo-labels. Nevertheless, research has demonstrated that this solution is inefficient and unreliable due to high-confidence predictions from poorly calibrated models. Recent studies have revealed that deep neural networks first learn patterns from well-labeled samples and then from those with incorrect labels, prompting the development of the novel pseudo-label selection method LOPS. This approach takes into account the learning order of samples, assuming it correlates with the likelihood of incorrect annotations. Thus, LOPS selects samples that were learned earliest, effectively serving as a high-performance add-on to existing weakly-supervised text classification methods, as supported by experiments on four real-world datasets.

There are various reasons why evaluating the faithfulness of explanations is crucial, such as fostering trust, enhancing interpretability, and pinpointing the sources of models' errors. This study focuses on the NLI task and introduces the Faithfulness-through-Counterfactuals approach, which works by generating counterfactual hypotheses from logical explanations and verifying if the resulting predictions align with the underlying logic. Unlike existing methods, this approach does not necessitate training a separate verification model, as it stands alone. Initially, we verify the efficacy of automatically generating counterfactual hypotheses using a few-shot priming technique. Subsequently, we demonstrate that our proposed metric can distinguish between human and model agreement or disagreement on novel counterfactual inputs. Moreover, we conduct a sensitivity analysis to ensure that our metric responds to unfaithful explanations.

Our research investigates how guided photons transmit angular momentum to a two-level atom with a specific electric quadrupole transition when positioned near an optical nanofiber. We've discovered that the generation of an axial orbital torque on the atom is controlled by its internal-state transition rules and the conservation of angular momentum. This torque is dependent on the photon's angular momentum, the change in the atom's internal state angular momentum, and the quadrupole-transition frequency. We've performed numerical calculations to determine the torques for specific transitions between energy levels of a rubidium atom, including those between the sublevel $M=2$ of the $5S_{1/2}F=2$ level and the sublevels $M'=0$, $1$, $2$, $3$, and $4$ of the $4D_{5/2}F'=4$ level. The results show that, except in a specific case, the absolute value of the torque for a higher-order mode is larger than that of the fundamental mode.

Our investigation is the first to examine the combination of the isoscalar pseudoscalar meson $\eta$ and the pseudoscalar glueball $G$ within the $N_f=2$ QCD framework at the pion mass $m_\pi\approx 350$ MeV. We have established the mass of $\eta$ to be $m_\eta=714.1(5.4)$ MeV, with the Witten-Veneziano relation allowing us to equate this value to a mass of $\sim 935$ MeV for its $SU(3)$ counterpart. Utilizing a large gauge ensemble, we have calculated the $\eta-G$ mixing energy and angle to be $|x|=107(14)$ MeV and $|\theta|=3.47(46)^\circ$ respectively from correlators computed using the distillation method. Notably, we have also found that $m_\eta$ can be accurately derived from correlators of $\eta$ with the pseudoscalar charmonium, $\eta_c$. Our results indicate that the $\eta-G$ mixing is negligible, with the QCD $U_A(1)$ anomaly being primarily responsible for the $\eta$ mass through topology-induced interactions.

The effectiveness of goal-oriented dialogue systems is largely dependent on how users perceive them to be helpful, yet this aspect and its associated fairness concerns have received insufficient attention in research. In this study, we investigate a quantitative approach to measuring helpfulness by defining and quantifying helpful dialogue responses. We then gather human evaluations of dialogue responses and develop a model to automatically assess their helpfulness. Furthermore, we propose a method for evaluating a dialogue system's fairness by analyzing its helpfulness in addressing queries from diverse user groups. Experimental results involving advanced dialogue systems under different scenarios show a bias in their helpfulness, favoring questions about developed countries over less-developed ones, highlighting underlying fairness issues in current goal-oriented dialogue systems.

Over the past few years, there has been a significant increase in learned representations that directly leverage point clouds. Although these representations are becoming increasingly complex, they still face challenges in generating ordered sets of points. To address this issue, we introduce Spotlights, a novel sampling model that represents 3D shapes as a compact, 1D array of depth values. By simulating a spherical configuration of cameras, Spotlights probes the intersections between virtual light rays and the surrounding object. This approach yields a structured point cloud, represented implicitly as a function of depth. A detailed geometric analysis confirms the effectiveness of Spotlights in point cloud completion, while experimental results on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate its accuracy, consistency, and efficiency. Moreover, Spotlights outperforms state-of-the-art completion methods in point cloud registration.

Research has highlighted potential privacy threats from large language models, specifically in the pre-training phase. However, relatively little has been studied about the risks during the fine-tuning phase, including how various fine-tuning techniques impact the memorization of training data. As the "pre-train and fine-tune" method becomes more widespread, it has become increasingly concerning that the vulnerability to attacks in this phase is not yet fully understood. This study aims to investigate the susceptibility of different fine-tuning methods, including fine-tuning the entire model, model head, and adapter, to membership inference and extraction attacks. Our analysis shows that fine-tuning the model head makes it most vulnerable to attacks, whereas fine-tuning smaller adapters appears to be less susceptible to certain extraction attacks.

Recent lightweight fine-tuning methods, which update a small set of parameters and keep the pre-trained model's parameters frozen, have proven to be effective in parameter-efficient transfer learning. However, existing studies do not examine the impact of knowledge about downstream fine-tuning methods on the pre-training stage. In our research, we demonstrate that considering the ultimate choice of fine-tuning approach during pre-training enhances parameter-efficient fine-tuning performance. By applying an optimization-based meta-learning approach using MAML with custom modifications, we adapt pre-trained models to parameter-efficient fine-tuning, achieving gains of up to 1.7 points in cross-lingual NER fine-tuning. Further analysis reveals the importance of introduced modifications to MAML in achieving these results.

The Paul Scherrer Institut's High Intensity Proton Accelerator cyclotron at PSI generates a continuous 590 MeV proton beam with a maximum power of 1.42 MW. After extraction, the beam is transported through a 120 m channel to target stations TgM and TgE for surface muon production before dissipating energy at the SINQ spallation target for neutron generation. To improve the surface muon production rate as part of the High Intensity Muon Beamline feasibility study, a new target will replace the current one. A critical issue for HIMB is minimizing proton beam losses along the beamline, which can be achieved by refining our comprehension of distributed losses by correlating measured temperature, beam profile, and beam current data with combined power deposition calculations and primary beam losses via Monte Carlo simulation.

In 1984, Gauduchon studied a functional associated with the square of the norm of the torsion 1-form of a compact Hermitian manifold, and identified its Euler-Lagrange equation. He found that in two-dimensional cases the metrics yielding the critical points of the functional have zero torsion 1-forms. This note extends his result to higher-dimensional manifolds, confirming that critical metrics are balanced in all dimensions. Furthermore, we explore the square of the norm of the Chern torsion and illustrate through examples that critical points of this functional can exist without being K\"ahler.

We examine how eccentricity influences the accuracy of gravitational wave parameter predictions for binary neutron star systems. Our research utilizes simulated signals with low eccentricity within the advanced LIGO's sensitivity range to determine the effects of using an incorrect waveform model on recovered parameters such as chirp mass, symmetric mass ratio, and tidal deformability. By comparing Bayesian and Fisher-Cutler-Vallisneri methods, we establish the conditions under which the latter approach is applicable. Applying the Fisher-Cutler-Vallisneri method to a diverse set of binary neutron star sources, we quantify the measurement errors and systematic biases associated with each parameter and derive their statistical distributions within the range of 0 to 0.025 eccentricity. Our findings reveal that biases for all three parameters grow more rapidly with increasing eccentricity. These biases primarily depend on eccentricity and weakly on component masses, resulting in a narrow range of systematic errors in the eccentricity-measurement error plane. This study includes examples of posterior distributions to demonstrate our results, including the phenomenon of bimodal posteriors. Furthermore, we provide a specific case study highlighting the importance of accounting for eccentricity in parameter estimation to ensure accurate predictions of neutron star properties.

This study focuses on the task of visually grounded dialog, where agents respond to a sequence of questions based on an image, taking into account the conversation history. Past approaches have used VisDial data for training, either through supervised learning or leveraging pre-trained models on related datasets. The proposed research presents a semi-supervised learning method called Generative Self-Training, which utilizes the internet to gather unlabeled images and generates synthetic dialogs about them using text generation based on the image and text. The generated data and original VisDial data are used to train the dialog agent, significantly increasing the training dataset size. Furthermore, a data selection method and a regularization technique are introduced to improve the robustness of the training process. The evaluation on VisDial v1.0 and v0.9 datasets demonstrates that the proposed approach achieves the highest performance to date, and it also exhibits significant performance gains in low-data scenarios.

To combat errors in inaccessible quantum bits, researchers utilize spectator qubits, highly sensitive to noise, which are frequently monitored and occasionally used to correct faulty data qubits. A novel, Bayesian approach utilizing complex linear transformations has been developed to optimize noise reduction for a key hardware-related issue - random telegraph noise-induced dephasing - resulting in a highly effective adaptive measurement strategy. Consequently, the method's success hinges on the sensitivity of the spectator qubits, demonstrating that it can be highly effective in the right circumstances.

Unfaithful text output is a prevalent issue for text generation models, particularly for real-world applications involving Data-to-Text (D2T) systems, where factual accuracy is paramount. To tackle this problem, we present R2D2, a training framework that addresses unfaithful D2T generation by simultaneously training a model as a text generator and a faithfulness evaluator with auxiliary tasks, including identifying replaced information and minimizing unlikely text. To support this training process, we develop two methods for creating unfaithful sentences. We also pinpoint poor entity recognition as a primary source of inaccuracy and propose novel metrics based on named entity recognition to measure the accuracy of D2T-generated text. Our results demonstrate that R2D2 systems effectively alleviate unfaithful text generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance on FeTaQA, LogicNLG, and ToTTo, with substantial improvements.

The primary objective of this thesis is to investigate potential attack pathways targeting the Iota network's 2.0 protocol and conduct a comprehensive analysis of their implications. In this study, we examine existing attack vectors in Distributed Ledger Technologies, assess their relevance to the Iota 2.0 protocol, and identify a specific attack that exploits honest nodes' ability to write to the ledger within a network running full-node software.

The development of effective massively multilingual image captioning systems has been hindered by a shortage of high-quality evaluation datasets that cater to multiple languages. To address this limitation, we introduce the Crossmodal-3600 dataset (XM3600), which comprises a diverse collection of 3600 images annotated with human-translated captions in 36 languages. These images were sourced globally, covering areas where the 36 languages are spoken, and accompanied by captions written in a consistent style across languages to prevent direct translation artifacts. Our evaluation demonstrates that using XM3600 as a reference standard significantly improves the correlation between automatic metrics and human assessments in the context of massively multilingual image captioning model selection.

We present FLEURS, a benchmark designed to evaluate the effectiveness of universal speech representations through few-shot learning in 102 languages. Constructed upon the machine translation FLoRes-101 benchmark, this n-way parallel speech dataset contains around 12 hours of speech data per language. FLEURS enables researchers to conduct various speech tasks such as Automatic Speech Recognition, Speech Language Identification, Translation and Retrieval. Our study provides initial baselines for these tasks using multilingual pre-trained models, with the ultimate goal of advancing speech technology in underserved languages and driving research in low-resource speech understanding.

We derive the existence, uniqueness, and regularity inequalities for the given Cauchy problem, specifically for the equation 
$\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \psi(t, \nabla)u + f$ with $u(0,x)=0$.
We obtain sufficient conditions for the symbol $\psi(t, \xi)$, which varies with respect to $t$, and is dependent on the smoothness of the symbol with respect to $\xi$ to ensure that the equation is well-defined in weighted $L_p$-spaces.
We demonstrate the existence of a constant $N$ such that 
$\int_0^T \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |(-\Delta)^{\gamma/2} u(t,x)|^p(t^2 + |x|^2)^{\alpha/2} dxdt \leq N\int_0^T \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |f(t,x)|^p(t^2 + |x|^2)^{\alpha/2} dxdt$
and
$\int_0^T \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |(-\Delta)^{\gamma/2} u(t,x)|^p|x|^{\alpha_2} dx \right)^{q/p} t^{\alpha_1}dt \leq N\int_0^T \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |f(t,x)|^p|x|^{\alpha_2} dx \right)^{q/p} t^{\alpha_1}dt$
under the conditions that $p,q\in(1,\infty)$, $-d-1<\alpha < (d+1)(p-1)$, $-1 < \alpha_1 < q-1$, $-d < \alpha_2 < d(p-1)$, and $\gamma$ is the order of the operator $\psi(t, \nabla)$.

The limitation of event extraction tasks has largely been attributed to a lack of data and unbalanced information sources. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel approach called self-training with gradient guidance (STGG). The framework consists of two primary components. First, a baseline event extraction model is trained on existing labeled data and applied to large datasets with no annotations to generate new event mentions. Secondly, a scoring model evaluates each predicted event, incorporating the relationships within its abstract meaning representation (AMR) graph to determine the likelihood of accuracy. The new predictions and associated probability scores are then used to refine the baseline model, leveraging the scores as pseudo-labels to guide the direction and magnitude of the model's gradient updates. Experimental results on ACE05-E, ACE05-E+, and ERE-EN datasets show that STGG enhances event extraction performance by up to 1.9 F-score over the baseline models. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that STGG is a versatile framework, capable of augmenting a wide range of event extraction models using abundant unlabeled data, even without access to high-quality AMR annotations.

The cartoon domain has recently seen a surge in popularity, with past research struggling to accurately transfer quality portrait stylization into this field. However, previous approaches failed to fully address critical constraints, including a high need for extensive training images and limited support for abstract cartoon faces. Recently, a new layer-swapping method has been developed, which achieves stylization with minimal training images, yet its practical applications remain restricted due to retained limitations. This paper introduces a novel approach called Cross-domain Style mixing, which successfully combines and integrates different latent codes from distinct domains. As a result, our proposed method enables the effective stylization of multiple cartoon faces at various levels of abstraction using a single generator, thereby overcoming the need for an extensive training dataset.

Multilingual question-answering systems that rely on document retrieval and answer extraction are susceptible to inconsistent information when dealing with documents written in different languages. This inconsistency arises from the varying information each document provides about a single topic. To investigate the influence of information availability and cultural factors, we examine the behavior of multilingual open-domain QA models, focusing on retrieval bias. We evaluate how different retriever models select passages in response to the same question across languages on TyDi QA and XOR-TyDi QA datasets, and hypothesize that document content disparities may indicate cultural differences and social biases.

A novel statistical method is introduced for constructing an asymptotically precise test for any group of hypotheses in high-dimensional linear regression analysis. This technique can be integrated into any multiple hypothesis testing procedure to make confident statements about relevant predictors. It generates permutation-based test statistics for each individual hypothesis by dividing the data and applying a variable selection technique, and aggregates these statistics to produce a subset-level test. The approach offers flexibility by accommodating various selection techniques and combining functions. We present two versions: a fully accurate and a computationally efficient approximation, which can handle larger datasets. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations and a case study using real gene expression data.

Despite advancements in Machine Translation, current models still face difficulties when dealing with challenging inputs such as noisy data and phrases that are not commonly used. Previous studies have tackled this robustness issue by identifying and adjusting for specific types of noise, but there is a lack of research on variations in subtle meaning shifts that maintain the original intended meaning. We define and explore this category, referred to as Natural Asemantic Variation, in the context of improving Machine Translation robustness. Our findings show that current models struggle with NAV, but demonstrate that fine-tuning them with human-generated variations can improve performance. Additionally, we observe that enhancing models to handle NAV can benefit languages beyond those used in the original data and also show that artificial NAV-like data can offer some benefits, although not all, as those from human-generated variations.

Standard mathematical approaches like discrete integration and gradient descent rely heavily on linear algebra, limiting their application to state vectors within traditional Euclidean spaces when implemented as initially described. However, certain state vectors, such as those representing rotational movements of rigid bodies, require adaptations to be effectively utilized in these mathematical frameworks. To address this need, this article provides a comprehensive analysis of SO(3) and SE(3) Lie groups, focusing on their distinct representations, tangent spaces, perturbation analysis, and the Jacobians necessary for applying calculus-based techniques, such as those mentioned earlier.

We examine the eigenbundle (localization bundle) associated with Hilbert modules over certain types of bounded symmetric domains, rank $r$, which results in complex-analytic fibre spaces that have a stratified structure of length $r+1.$ The fibers are characterized in terms of K\"ahler geometry as line bundle sections over flag manifolds, and we derive the metric embedding by considering derivatives of reproducing kernel functions. Key instances include the determinantal ideals specified by vanishing conditions on the distinct strata within the stratification.

We investigate controlled sampling from large pre-trained language models. These models can generate coherent text but are difficult to manipulate in order to produce text that adheres to specific requirements.
