We develop MuCoLa, a sampling strategy that integrates a language model's log-likelihood with diverse (differentiable) constraints within a unified scoring function. It generates text in a non-autoregressive manner by first initializing the entire sequence with random values, and then applying a Markov chain based on Langevin Dynamics, guided by the gradients of the energy function. We test MuCoLa's effectiveness in text generation under soft and rigid constraints, as well as their combinations, and achieve notable improvements over comparable baselines in tasks such as toxicity reduction, sentiment regulation, and content-directed text production.

Similar to other cybersecurity domains, machine learning has shown great potential in Android malware detection, with numerous studies employing various algorithms and feature sets achieving impressive results. However, a lack of standardization in evaluation methods and reproducibility hinders comparison between these proposals. This paper conducts a comprehensive analysis of 10 prominent studies on Android malware detection using a unified evaluation framework. Through thorough experimentation, we identify five critical factors that significantly impact trained machine learning models and their performance: duplicated samples, label attribution, class imbalance, evasion techniques, and app evolution. Our results indicate that existing ML-based detectors have been over-optimistically evaluated, leading to inflated published performance metrics. Therefore, it is essential to create realistic experimental scenarios, considering these factors, to facilitate the development of more effective ML-based Android malware detection solutions.

Modern natural language processing (NLP) systems primarily rely on Large Language Models, which deliver outstanding performance and resilience. However, their computational demands hinder efficient inference. Researchers have been working on techniques like structured and unstructured pruning, quantization, and distillation to mitigate these challenges and reduce costs. This study investigates Gradual Unstructured Magnitude Pruning's ability to facilitate model transfers across different domains and tasks. Experimental results indicate that models pruned early during general-domain training can adapt to new domains and tasks with minimal hyperparameter tuning. Notably, our general sparse model, Sparse*BERT, can be transformed into domain-specific models, such as SparseBioBERT, by fine-tuning on specialized data. Moreover, our results demonstrate that SparseBioBERT achieves comparable quality to BioBERT while utilizing a fraction of its parameters, just 10%.

Cellular extensions at the forefront of a cell are crucial for detecting external signals, during cell movement and expansion. Recent research indicates that these protrusions envelop (curl around) the extracellular fibers. The specifics of this curling process and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study integrates theoretical analysis and experimental investigation to examine the curling of cellular protrusions on fibers with different shapes and geometries. A proposed model describes the generation of membrane protrusions by curved membrane proteins, which in turn recruit the propulsive forces of actin polymerization, and identifies the influence of bending and adhesion energies on the orientation of protrusions in the curling direction. The model predicts that cells' leading edges coil around circular fibers, whereas the curling process halts on fibers with flat cross-sections. These predictions are supported by high-resolution 3D imaging of curling on suspended fibers, using a specialized microscopy technique called Dual-View light-sheet microscopy (diSPIM). This study provides a comprehensive theoretical framework backed by high-spatiotemporal resolution experiments that enable the observation of curling of cellular protrusions around extracellular fibers with diverse diameters.

Deep learning models on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging face challenges due to the limited amount of expert-annotated data and data complexity. Recently, self-supervised contrastive learning has shown promising results in several medical imaging tasks. Nevertheless, the level of representation learning in pre-trained models for the primary organ of interest versus surrounding tissues remains uncertain. This work explores the best approach to incorporating anatomical prior knowledge into self-supervised learning, focusing on using segmentation networks to pinpoint the heart in CMR images and pretraining in multiple tasks. Our results show that integrating anatomical knowledge can significantly enhance diagnostic performance downstream, with pretraining using in-domain data generally leading to better performance and more human-like visual salience. Surprisingly, incorporating anatomical knowledge into pretraining does not yield significant improvements.

This research investigated the influence of repulsive nucleon-nucleon forces resulting from the Pauli exclusion principle on the half-lives of heavy, even-even nuclei, focusing on those with atomic numbers ranging from 84 to 92. The Pauli exclusion principle was applied in our analysis by readjusting nucleon-nucleon interactions based on the Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization rule and incorporating its effect as a modification term into the double-folding method by examining how variations in kinetic energy affect overlapping densities of the alpha and daughter nuclei. When incorporating the kinetic energy variation into the double-folding method, our calculations showed that the standard deviation of the calculated half-lives compared to their corresponding experimental data was 0.309. This value decreased to 0.340 when using the standard double-folding method. Our analysis suggests that accounting for kinetic energy within the double-folding method leads to more accurate calculations of alpha decay half-lives compared to experimental data.

Investigations into the neutron-rich isotopes of Ca, Ni, Zr, and Sn using a continuum Skyrme Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov theory reveal the presence of exotic nuclear properties. These properties are well-supported by experimental data for two-neutron separation energies and one-neutron separation energies. However, significant discrepancies arise between the predicted and actual drip lines. Theoretical studies of neutron pairing energies confirm that odd-numbered nuclei exhibit significantly smaller pairing energies compared to even-even nuclei due to the absence of pairing contributions from unpaired neutrons. Analysis of single-particle structures, radii, and density distributions in the neutron-rich isotopes of Ca, Ni, and Sn reveals the presence of predicted halo structures, characterized by unusually large radii and diffuse density distributions. These properties deviate from traditional models and are found to be primarily attributed to the presence of orbitals with low angular momenta located near the Fermi surface. Additionally, studies of the number of neutrons in the continuum show consistent behaviors with those of pairing energies, further supporting the crucial role of pairing correlations in the development of halo phenomena.

The traditional DeGroot-style opinion formation model assumes ongoing interactions within a social network, but this limits its ability to accommodate external entities that interact temporarily with its permanent members. Many real-world organizations and individuals fit into this temporary influencer category, such as a company trying to convince as many people as possible to buy their products, but can only exert influence for a limited time due to constraints. We have developed an adapted DeGroot model that permits external agents to interact with the permanent network for a predetermined period. Through analysis and simulation, we gain several insights into how external agents can maximise their influence in shaping opinions within the social network.

As networked control systems expand in scale and complexity of interactions, the need to assess their resilience becomes increasingly crucial. The integration of graph theory into system and control theory is emerging as a vital research area, prompting the need to redefine traditional notions using graph-based language. This paper reviews graph-based approaches for evaluating the resilience of networked control systems, examining distributed algorithms and their ability to withstand malicious actions by analyzing underlying network structures. It presents methods to quantify attack effects and reinterpret system robustness concepts from a graph-theoretic perspective to minimize the impact of attacks. The paper also explores miscellaneous security issues in networked control systems, utilizing graph theory as a key analytical tool. Finally, it suggests directions for future research in this field.

This presentation, using advanced visualization tools, delves into the microscopic composition of the non-trivial vacuum fields in QCD, the fundamental building blocks of matter. It specifically focuses on centre vortices within these fields, as discovered through lattice QCD. Our current research aims to elucidate the effect of dynamical fermions in the QCD vacuum on centre-vortex configurations. Notably, the influence of dynamical fermions is substantial and offers new perspectives on the part centre vortices play in QCD's mechanism for both confinement and chiral symmetry breaking.

When ions are densely packed, their physical size significantly impacts their interactions.  To account for this steric effect, we modified the conventional Poisson-Boltzmann equation by incorporating it into the steady-state Poisson-Nernst-Planck equations. This led us to a Poisson-Boltzmann equation with steric effects, characterized by the parameter $\Lambda$ and positive constants $\lambda_i$. As $\Lambda$ approaches zero, the equation simplifies to the conventional Poisson-Boltzmann equation, while a larger $\Lambda$ strengthens the repulsive forces between ions and solvent molecules. We found that by taking the limit as $\Lambda$ tends to infinity under certain boundary conditions, the Poisson-Boltzmann equation with steric effects converges to a modified Poisson-Boltzmann equation, similar to previously established models. This reveals that the modified equation can be seen as a generalization of these existing models.

Recent advances in multi-agent reinforcement learning often rely on deep neural networks, but interpreting these models can be a significant challenge. Existing work on interpretable reinforcement learning has been successful in creating more understandable decision tree-based policies from single-agent neural networks, but this work needs to be adapted for multi-agent settings. To address this, we introduce a new set of algorithms that can extract interpretable decision tree policies from neural networks trained with multi-agent reinforcement learning. Our first algorithm, IVIPER, extends a recent method for single-agent interpretable learning to the multi-agent setting, and demonstrates that it can produce high-quality policies for each agent. To further improve coordination between agents, we propose a centralized training algorithm, MAVIPER, which jointly trains decision trees for multiple agents by predicting their behaviors and focusing on critical interactions. Our results show that both algorithms outperform baseline methods, and MAVIPER-trained agents achieve better-coordinated performance than IVIPER-trained agents in three different multi-agent environments.

The internal workings of neural language models are notoriously difficult to decipher, but recent progress has been made in automatically generating machine rationales that explain their behavior. Nevertheless, there has been limited advancement in leveraging these rationales to enhance neural language model performance, particularly in out-of-distribution generalization. This is where explanation regularization (ER) comes into play, with the goal of boosting neural language model generalization by aligning machine rationales with human rationales. Previous research has primarily evaluated ER models through in-distribution generalization, but their performance in out-of-distribution settings has been largely unexplored. Additionally, it remains unclear how ER model performance is influenced by the choice of ER criteria or the number and selection of training instances with human rationales. In response, we introduce ER-TEST, a comprehensive framework for assessing ER models' out-of-distribution generalization across three dimensions: unseen datasets, contrast sets, and functional tests. Through ER-TEST, we investigate three pivotal questions: (A) Which ER criteria are most effective for a given out-of-distribution scenario? (B) How does ER respond to variations in the number and selection of training instances with human rationales? (C) Can ER be effective even with distantly supervised human rationales? By employing ER-TEST across a diverse range of tasks and datasets, we reveal that ER has minimal impact on in-distribution performance, but can yield substantial gains in out-of-distribution performance, particularly in unseen datasets, contrast sets, and functional tests. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the most effective ER criterion varies across tasks, and ER can still enhance out-of-distribution performance even with limited or distantly-supervised human rationales.

A significant difficulty in reinforcement learning is defining tasks that can be both easily understood and confirmed as correct. To overcome this challenge, a typical approach involves describing tasks through reward machines - simple systems that outline the task to be accomplished. We introduce skill machines, a framework that can be learned directly from these reward machines, capturing the solution to such tasks. Our framework involves an agent first learning a set of fundamental skills without a reward, and then using these skills along with the learned skill machine to create more complex behaviors that can be defined by any logical language, such as temporal logics. This enables the agent to map from intricate logical task descriptions to near-optimal behaviors without requiring any additional learning. We evaluate our method in both simple and complex video game environments, where the agent is faced with numerous complex, long-duration tasks. Our results show that the agent is able to satisfy very complex task specifications, achieving near-optimal performance with no further learning required. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the performance of skill machines can be improved using offline reinforcement learning algorithms when optimal behaviors are the primary objective.

Our investigation focuses on the concentration phenomenon in discrete-time random systems that operate within an infinite-dimensional space. By employing a novel functional analytical approach, we establish exponential concentration inequalities for these systems without making any boundedness assumptions about their states. Moreover, we demonstrate that the presence of an exponential-type Lyapunov function not only confers stability in these systems but also leads to exponential concentration inequalities when sampling from their stationary distributions, leveraging a transport-entropy inequality. These findings have far-reaching implications for reinforcement learning and control applications, enabling exponential concentration inequalities for unbounded observables without requiring either reversibility or precise knowledge of the underlying random systems – two key assumptions typically made in concentration inequalities for Markov diffusion processes and statistical mechanics.

Those familiar with circuitry are likely aware of the fundamental circuit elements, namely capacitors, resistors, and inductors, which are defined by relationships between variables such as current, voltage, charge, and flux. In 1971, Professor Leon Chua proposed the concept of a fourth fundamental element, known as the memristor, which relates flux to charge due to symmetry. A physical realization model for the memristor was later introduced in 2008 by HP Labs, highlighting its potential benefits, including variable resistance, flexibility, and no leakage current, as well as compatibility with CMOS technology. The memristor's characteristics can be tailored for specific applications, resulting in various models. With its potential applications in memory, logic, and neuromorphic systems, a computer model of the memristor would be a valuable tool for simulating circuit behavior and developing this passive circuit element. In this paper, several VerilogA memristor models were simulated using sinusoidal inputs, with various window functions employed to verify the circuit analysis of these models.

Federated learning's concern with user privacy is exacerbated by the susceptibility of Vision Transformers to gradient-based inversion attacks. It's discovered that the low-dimensional spatial priors embedded in ViT's position information speed up the model's training, but this advantage makes ViTs position-dependent and vulnerable to data leakage. To counter this risk, enhancing a ViT's position-insensitivity seems a viable way to protect against these attacks. Nonetheless, simply removing the position information hinders model convergence, accuracy, and increases the risk of privacy breach. To resolve this dilemma, a novel Masked Jigsaw Puzzle (MJP) approach is proposed, which can seamlessly integrate with existing ViT architectures and variants. Experimental results reveal that the MJP method not only improves model performance on large datasets like ImageNet-1K but also significantly enhances its resilience against typical gradient attacks.

Research on Entity Linking typically assumes a comprehensive reference database, allowing for effortless linking of all mentions. However, in reality, knowledge bases are often incomplete and subject to constant changes due to novel concepts emerging. To address this, this paper introduces the EDIN benchmark, which integrates unknown entities lacking descriptions in the database and annotated mentions into an existing entity linking system, highlighting the additional complexities it presents when compared to zero-shot entity linking. Building on a dense-retrieval based approach, the EDIN pipeline is developed as a complete system to identify, group, and index mentions of unknown entities within their context. Our experiments indicate that indexing entities with a single unified embedding, encompassing the information from multiple mentions, performs better than indexing mentions individually.

Significant advancements in natural language processing tasks have been made using neural attention models. Nevertheless, the quadratic memory complexity of the self-attention module in these models poses a challenge when applied to long text summarization tasks. Instead of optimizing the attention modules, we investigate whether localized models that focus on restricted context can achieve comparable performance to global context models that treat the input as a single sequence. Our approach divides input into individual pages or sections that share a common principle or characteristic, both during encoding and decoding stages. We tested our locality-aware model on various levels of text granularity, from sentences to documents, and the results demonstrate its superior performance over strong baselines that employ efficient attention modules, also providing deeper insights into our modeling strategy.

Advanced Language Models have set benchmarks in many Natural Language Processing tasks. To tackle the growing number of benchmarks, researchers have resorted to developing even more complex models. However, this approach poses significant challenges in terms of time, cost, and environmental impact. To address these limitations, a team explored an innovative method: they examined whether it's feasible to rephrase questions in line with the model's capabilities, thereby rendering them more answerable. The researchers investigated if humans could dissect a complex query into a series of simpler ones, which are more easily resolved by models. A comprehensive analysis across various reasoning tasks confirmed that this approach yields substantial performance enhancements for GPT3 and RoBERTa-SQuAD, even when paired with a symbolic calculator, at 24% and 29%, respectively. This finding opens up a promising avenue for human involvement in NLP research and suggests that the Human-in-the-loop Question Decomposition technique may serve as a viable alternative to developing massive Language Models. The project's code and data are available on GitHub at https://github.com/Pruthvi98/QuestionDecomposition.

Surveys serve as vital evidence in policymaking, decision-making, and societal understanding, yet collecting sufficient data for detailed subpopulation analysis can be resource-intensive and time-consuming. A novel approach called Multilevel Regression and Poststratification (MRP) can provide reliable subpopulation estimates using existing surveys. Despite its potential, there has been limited research on how to effectively visualize MRP data. This study conducts a systematic literature review to assess the current visualization practices in MRP and applies the method to the 2016 US presidential election, highlighting the importance of uncertainty representation. It also explores alternative visualizations to convey point estimates and bias-variance trade-offs, ultimately proposing a comprehensive strategy for evaluating MRP models.

As technology miniaturization and the increasing reliance on parallel processing in hazardous environments like space continue, runtime errors caused by radiation have become a significant issue affecting both performance and architectural design. This study introduces an architectural approach to runtime-configurable soft-error resilience at the core level, incorporating a novel On-Demand Redundancy Grouping (ODRG) scheme into an open-source six-core RISC-V cluster. The ODRG scheme enables the cluster to function either as two fault-resistant cores or six individual cores optimized for high-performance, with minimal overhead for runtime mode switching. The ODRG unit requires less than 11% of a core's area for a three-core grouping, representing just 1% of the cluster's area, and incurs negligible timing penalties, outperforming a commercial state-of-the-art counterpart and achieving 2.5 times faster fault recovery resynchronization. Furthermore, unlike other approaches, the ODRG method allows redundant cores to be utilized for independent computations, leading to a performance boost of up to 2.96 times for targeted applications when redundancy is unnecessary.

Calculating the similarity between terms, words, or text data is crucial in various text-based applications, including knowledge acquisition, recommendation systems, and natural language processing. In recent years, ontologies have been developed to represent knowledge bases for information systems in a structured format. Ontology-based semantic similarity calculations have advanced, and in specific contexts, they're often supplemented by other similarity measurement techniques. This paper introduces a method for calculating semantic similarity based on ontologies in the context of a recommendation system.

A new method for learning set generation from sequences of tokens is presented, which effectively addresses the challenges of several NLP tasks, including entity typing and dialogue emotion tagging. The method enhances Seq2Seq models by incorporating the key properties of sets, namely order-invariance and cardinality, without requiring any additional annotations. It does this by proposing a novel data augmentation approach, SETAUG, which samples informative orders from the combinatorial space of label orders. The SETAUG method is model-independent, allowing it to be applied to various Seq2Seq models, including BART, T5, and GPT-3. Experimental results show a significant improvement of 20% on average across four benchmark datasets, making SETAUG a useful tool for improving the performance of Seq2Seq models on set generation tasks.

Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) excel in generation tasks but lack in efficiency. As these models iteratively denoise a Gaussian noise to obtain a sample, they often require an impractically large number of steps. To mitigate this issue, we introduce Early-Stopped DDPM (ES-DDPM), an acceleration strategy for DDPMs that terminates the diffusion process early. By beginning the reverse denoising process from a non-Gaussian distribution, ES-DDPM leverages the power of pre-trained generative models, like GANs and VAEs, to efficiently sample from complex distributions. As a result, the number of required denoising steps decreases significantly, and the sample quality of ES-DDPM substantially outperforms both vanilla DDPM and the pre-trained generative model. Through experiments on diverse datasets, ES-DDPM achieves notable acceleration and improved performance over baseline methods. Furthermore, ES-DDPM boasts several desirable properties, including independence from existing acceleration techniques and the ability to control image generation at both the global and pixel-level.

Deep Neural Networks have been successfully applied in hyperspectral image classification. Despite their success, previous studies have mainly employed general architectures, neglecting the inherent properties of hyperspectral images, such as noise generation. This oversight prevents deep models from extracting effective features, ultimately limiting their classification capabilities. To address this, a novel deep learning approach is introduced, which incorporates a noise-sensitive module and denoising framework to enhance hyperspectral image classification. Initially, a physical noise model is developed to describe the spectral signatures of hyperspectral images, accounting for the high intra-class variance and class overlap inherent in the data. A noise-sensitive module is then designed to capture the physical noise inherent within objects, followed by a denoising framework to remove this noise. The proposed method utilizes a CNN with the noise-sensitive module and denoising framework to produce discriminative features, ultimately leading to improved classification performance. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through experiments on two real-world datasets, with the implementation details available at https://github.com/shendu-sw/noise-physical-framework.

In situations where data-storage qubits are isolated and minimally interacted with, effective noise reduction can still be achieved by employing additional probes that only intervene when necessary. Focusing on the context of solid-state qubits, we explore the application of noise mitigation via a two-state fluctuator model and a spectator qubit. Assuming projective measurements of the spectator qubit, we establish a theoretical framework and evaluate the performance of various measurement strategies. Initially, we investigate the Greedy algorithm, which prioritizes maximizing the data qubit's coherence at any given moment, and find it to be highly effective. Through numerical analysis, we simplify its adaptive strategy into a more manageable algorithm with a limited number of parameters. Using this foundation and Bayesian maps, we develop a one-parameter family of algorithms that can be optimized. In scenarios where the noise sensitivity of the spectator qubit is extremely high, our analytical framework reveals that this algorithmic family reduces the data qubit's decoherence rate in accordance with the square of its noise sensitivity. By adjusting the parameter to its optimal value, we obtain the Map-based Optimized Adaptive Algorithm for Asymptotic Regime (MOAAAR). Our analytical and numerical results confirm that MOAAAR outperforms the Greedy algorithm, particularly in cases of high noise sensitivity of the spectator qubit.

The idea that "nobody is safe until everybody is safe" has been brought to the forefront by the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. To address this concern, a model of virus spread in interconnected communities was created, considering different vaccination levels and scenarios. The model starts with susceptible populations, categorized as "Bronze," "Silver," and "Gold" based on vaccination rates, and connected through various types of networks. It was found that interactions between non-vaccinated and vaccinated communities result in a detrimental effect, where the non-vaccinated communities drive an increase in infections. Network density and the strength of interactions play a crucial role in determining the spread of the virus. When comparing different types of networks, such as Barabasi-Albert and Erdos-Renyi, the results indicate that densely connected networks can prevent the spread of the virus more effectively. However, even a small number of non-vaccinated communities can trigger a surge in infections in vaccinated communities.

In a theoretical study, we examined the $D\bar{D}K$ three-body system using a fixed center approximation to the Faddeev equations, incorporating the chiral unitary approach for $DK$ and $D\bar{D}$ interactions. We analyzed the $K$ meson scattering off a $D\bar{D}$ system that potentially forms a scalar $X(3720)$ meson. A resonance emerged due to the strong $DK$ interaction, which dynamically generates the scalar $D^*_{s0}(2317)$ meson. This led to the appearance of a three-body $K$-$(D\bar{D})_{X(3720)}$ scattering amplitude with a resonance structure, supporting the possibility of a $D\bar{D}K$ bound state. This result aligns with prior theoretical work suggesting the existence of a new hidden charm $K$ meson, $K_{c\bar{c}}(4180)$ with quantum numbers $I(J^P) = \frac{1}{2}(0^-)$ and a mass of about $4180$ MeV. Future experimental measurements are likely to be motivated by these findings.

We investigate a dynamic resource allocation problem in which $T$ divisible resources are sequentially assigned to a set of $n$ fixed agents, who have additive utility functions drawn randomly from a known distribution. In this context, decisions are made immediately and are non-reversible. Unlike traditional dynamic resource allocation methods, which prioritize overall efficiency over fairness, our work aims to achieve an equitable allocation that balances efficiency and fairness by optimizing for egalitarian welfare rather than utilitarian welfare. We begin by analyzing a fluid-based policy derived from a deterministic approximation of the problem and show that it yields a regret of order $\Theta(\sqrt{T})$ compared to the optimal egalitarian allocation that could be achieved with complete prior knowledge. Subsequently, we introduce the $\mathsf{BIRT}$ policy, which involves at most $O(\log\log T)$ re-solving of the fluid problem. We prove that the $\mathsf{BIRT}$ policy achieves an $O(1)$ regret against the hindsight optimum, unaffected by the length of the time horizon $T$ and the initial welfare level. Additionally, numerical experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains of our approach over various baseline policies.

As autonomous systems continue to advance, safety issues emerge when navigating unpredictable environments. This research develops an additional safeguard to mechanical systems that identifies and addresses instability triggered by external disruptions. The safety feature integrates seamlessly with existing primary controllers, such as pose or force tracking, and intervenes by limiting power supply when potential instability looms. This method hinges on calculating the Largest Lyapunov Exponent (LLE), a gauge of dynamic divergence or convergence rates, which enables swift detection of potentially hazardous system behaviors. By leveraging this metric in tandem with Control Barrier Functions, power constraints can be imposed on a system controlled by jerks. The proposed safety architecture has been rigorously tested on an Omnidirectional Micro Aerial Vehicle (OMAV), both in free flight and interactive scenarios.

The problem of dividing a divisible and heterogeneous resource among a group of people, often represented as a cake, has been studied extensively. However, when agents are placed on a graph, where each agent's evaluation of their share is limited to their neighbors, finding an efficient and fair allocation becomes more challenging. Currently, the best-known algorithm for this problem has a very high complexity. This work identifies a specific type of graph, trees with a depth of two, where a more efficient protocol can be used to find a fair allocation with minimal cake cutting. For a more restrictive type of tree, where each non-root agent is connected to only two others, the number of queries needed to find a fair allocation is significantly reduced. Interestingly, a lower bound on the number of queries needed to find a fair allocation on a different type of graph, where each agent is connected to only one other, shows that the new protocol is quite efficient.

Current cybersecurity risk analysis approaches primarily automate the analysis procedure, leaving critical decisions to expert judgment, which is often subjective and influenced by personal biases. In practice, teams of experts rely on manual, group-based analysis, such as brainstorming workshops, to identify security risks, but this approach can lead to uneven expertise contribution due to underrepresented diversity dimensions like gender in security teams. The impact of diversity on risk analysis of technical artefacts has not been empirically studied beyond non-technical threats. To address this gap, this study aims to develop an experimental framework to identify key factors contributing to diversity in cybersecurity risk analysis.

This study addresses a significant issue in 5G mobile networks resulting from mobility, which leads to substantial performance degradation. A new channel prediction approach, called the multi-dimensional matrix pencil (MDMP), is introduced. It uses angular and frequency structures of wideband channels to estimate path parameters. MDMP also includes an innovative path pairing technique, which leverages the high-resolution property of angle estimation. Our proposed method handles the realistic constraint of changing path delays due to user movement. We demonstrate theoretically that when the number of base station antennas increases, the prediction error decreases to zero with just two initial channel samples. Moreover, a lower-bound of base station antennas for satisfactory performance is established. Simulation results using the 3GPP industrial channel model show that our MDMP approach approaches optimal performance even at 120 km/h and with a latency of 16 ms.

Personalizing interactions between humans and virtual agents involves capturing their behavior style. To achieve this, we developed an efficient machine learning method that generates gestures by combining prosodic features, text, and unseen speaker styles. Our model applies zero-shot multimodal style transfer to data from the PATS database, which includes videos of various speakers. We view style as a pervasive aspect of communication that influences expressivity and speech content. By separating content from style, our model can infer style embeddings for unseen speakers without retraining. The model's primary objectives are: generating source speaker gestures from audio and text inputs; conditioning these gestures on target speaker style embeddings; and transferring style variability from unseen speakers without retraining. Our system comprises two key components: a style encoder network that generates fixed-dimensional speaker style embeddings and a sequence-to-sequence synthesis network that synthesizes gestures based on input modalities and speaker style. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model by evaluating gesture synthesis and zero-shot style transfer, as well as converting 2D gestures to 3D poses and animations. We conduct objective and subjective evaluations to validate our approach and compare it to a baseline model.

Consider a finite group G with identity element e and a non-trivial subgroup H of G. We define a specific type of graph, denoted as the generalized non-coprime graph GAmma_{G,H}, whose vertices are the non-identity elements of G. Two vertices are connected by an edge if and only if the greatest common divisor of their orders is not 1, and at least one of them belongs to subgroup H. In this study, we investigate various graph properties of these generalized non-coprime graphs, focusing on cyclic groups, and determine the necessary and sufficient conditions for the graphs to belong to different categories, including stars, paths, cycles, and others. We also examine how the class of groups is extended to include finite nilpotent groups, and provide a contrasting example using EPPO groups, before concluding with a connection to the Gruenberg--Kegel graph.

A compartmental model based on nonlinear partial differential equations simulates COVID-19 spread over a continuous timeframe and geographic area. Increasing model resolution, compartments, and clinical stratification results in an extremely large number of unknown variables, often exceeding millions. To efficiently solve these complex high-fidelity models, a scalable parallel solver is employed, combining techniques like domain decomposition and multigrid preconditioning at various levels to ensure scalability and performance. A specific numerical example uses a five-compartment SEIRD model for COVID-19 to demonstrate the proposed solver's effectiveness, particularly when modeling large areas like Southern Ontario. The solver significantly reduces computation time, allowing for accurate three-month infection predictions for 92 million people within just 7 hours using 1780 processes, thereby saving substantial time and effort compared to traditional solvers.

Dorigoni, Green, and Wen recently proposed a precise equation for the combined correlator of four superconformal operators within $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. This work focuses on the large N limit of their equation and reveals how it can be reinterpreted as a sum of the influences from (p,q) strings. Due to SL(2,Z) duality, a single function dictates all these influences, one that typically corresponds to the fundamental string contribution. Analyzing the large-order behavior in the genus expansion of this function exposes the large N non-perturbative corrections. These corrections are identified as D3-brane instantons within the holographically dual type IIB string theory. Similarly, a Laplace-difference equation for the combined correlator provides a more systematic derivation of the same result.

Determining the physical properties of massive star-forming clouds from observations is a difficult task, particularly due to their high sensitivity and resolution requirements. Our goal is to assess how accurately we can infer the conditions within these clouds from observations, with a focus on the capabilities of the Next Generation VLA interferometer. Utilizing magnetohydrodynamic simulation data, we simulated observations of spectral lines for a filamentary cloud structure, producing synthetic ngVLA data and analyzing the column density, gas temperature, and kinematics. The results were then compared to both ideal observations and the actual 3D model, with notable improvements in resolution and accuracy achieved by the ngVLA. At a distance of 4 kpc, the ngVLA provides an unprecedented level of detail, allowing for the mapping of cloud kinematics and structure at sub-arcsecond scales, and the recovery of kinetic temperatures to within 1 K precision for certain molecules.

To achieve highly reliable low-latency communication systems with high efficiency and security, a multi-objective optimization problem is developed to address downlink communication scenarios with multiple users and potential eavesdroppers, under finite blocklength constraints. This problem involves maximizing a collective secrecy rate by designing a secure precoder while minimizing a maximum error probability and an information leakage rate. Due to the complexities of this multi-objective problem, the non-trivial back-off factors resulting from finite blocklength assumptions, and the non-linear nature of secrecy rates, a novel optimization approach is proposed to address these challenges. This approach involves an alternating optimization strategy, comprising two phases: designing secure precoders, and minimizing maximum error probabilities and information leakage rates. In the first phase, a lower bound on the secrecy rate is established, and a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker condition is derived to identify optimal solutions with respect to precoder variables. This condition is then interpreted as a generalized eigenvalue problem, and a power iteration-based method is employed to find the optimal solutions. In the second phase, a weighted-sum approach is adopted to derive KKT conditions in terms of error probabilities and leakage rates for given precoders, and simulation results validate the proposed algorithm.

To quantify the entanglement between two separated spacetime regions surrounding a static black hole, calculations are performed for various black hole types, including Schwarzschild, charged Reissner-Nordstrom, and Schwarzschild-de Sitter black holes with multiple horizons, as well as the static solutions to F(R) gravity. Using the replica trick, the entanglement entropy is determined by deriving the specific metric of the replica spacetime for each black hole type. Notably, the entanglement entropy for spherically-symmetric and static black holes adheres to the Bekenstein-Hawking area law for entropy.

Deep learning models have achieved impressive results across various applications, but they are susceptible to a significant vulnerability - adversarial attacks. These attacks subtly alter an input image, rendering it almost imperceptible to the human eye, yet significantly affecting the model's classification outcome. This study investigates the impact of projected gradient descent (PGD) and adaptive mask segmentation attack (ASMA) on DeepLabV3, employing MobileNetV3 and ResNet50 architectures, and discovers that PGD consistently achieves the desired classification outcome, whereas ASMA's effectiveness in multi-class targets is limited. The existence of such attacks poses a threat to all deep learning models in image classification tasks.

This research introduces a highly scalable and efficient framework for dynamic supply landscape analysis in real-time auctions, leveraging predictive model uncertainty to inform exploration decisions within a high-performance, low-latency infrastructure. Our experiments validate the effectiveness of uncertainty-driven exploration in enhancing both model accuracy and key business metrics.

A significant issue in computational biology is to reconcile the need for precise and detailed models with the limitations of available data. Although tools such as identifiability analysis and information criteria have been created to bridge this gap, they often fall short in resolving the disparity between data quality and model complexity. Simple, phenomenological models such as the logistic and Gompertz growth models are usually identifiable with standard experimental measurements. However, to derive insights from complex, non-identifiable models that incorporate crucial biological mechanisms, we study the geometric relationship between these complex models and simpler, identifiable surrogate models. By exploring the quantitative connection between non-identifiable and identifiable parameters, we establish an intermediate layer of interpretation between non-identifiable parameters and goodness-of-fit metrics. Our approach is illustrated through the analysis of a series of mathematical models describing multicellular tumour spheroid growth. Characterized by limited and noisy data, these models are often excessively complicated. Our geometric method is capable of anticipating non-identifiabilities, partitioning non-identifiable parameter spaces into identifiable combinations related to individual data characteristics, and ultimately providing additional biological insights from complex non-identifiable models.

Calculations for the nucleosynthesis of heavy elements rely heavily on the accuracy of photon strength functions, which can be experimentally constrained through investigations into the photo-response of atomic nuclei. To contribute to this understanding, the photo-response of $^{66}$Zn was analyzed within the energy range of 5.6 MeV to 9.9 MeV, focusing specifically on the "elastic" decay channel that leads back to the nucleus's ground state. Furthermore, the contributions of electric and magnetic dipole transitions in the elastic channel were separated and evaluated. Using nuclear resonance fluorescence experiments, the photo-response of $^{66}$Zn was studied using a linearly-polarized quasi-monoenergetic photon beam from the High Intensity $\gamma$-ray Source, with two High Purity Germanium detectors employed for gamma-ray spectroscopy. Full photoabsorption cross sections were determined from the collected data and the average contribution of electric and magnetic dipole strengths to the ground-state decay channel was isolated. Moreover, the average branching ratio back to the ground state was calculated, yielding results that contrast with those obtained in a previous experiment using bremsstrahlung on $^{66}$Zn. Statistical-model calculations performed for the earlier study significantly underestimated the branching ratio, suggesting that the discrepancy in cross section values may be partly attributed to the differing estimates of this ratio.

Localizing objects from coarse annotations such as image categories is a complex task that has long plagued deep network approaches. Current class activation map-based methods excel at highlighting local object features but struggle to account for the entire object. Conversely, recent transformer-based techniques frequently prioritize the background over the target object, hindering complete object identification. To address these limitations, a re-attention mechanism called token refinement transformer (TRT) is proposed, leveraging object-level semantics to guide localization effectively. The TRT model incorporates a novel token priority scoring module (TPSM) to mitigate background interference and focuses on the target object. Furthermore, the class activation map is used as semantically informed input to confine the attention map to the target object. Extensive experiments on two benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of the proposed TRT approach over existing methods, particularly those using image category annotations. The source code for TRT is available on GitHub at https://github.com/su-hui-zz/ReAttentionTransformer.

Recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown impressive results across multiple domains, but GNNs are susceptible to noise and adversarial attacks in their input data. Developing robust GNNs that can withstand such threats is a significant challenge. Current defense strategies for GNNs are resource-intensive and not scalable. This paper presents a general framework for strengthening GNNs, referred to as the Weighted Laplacian GNN (RWL-GNN). The method incorporates Weighted Graph Laplacian learning into GNN architecture, leveraging the positive semi-definiteness property of the Laplacian matrix to ensure smooth feature representation and discard noisy or adversarial edges. A unified optimization framework enables appropriate connection weighting in the graph. We demonstrate the efficacy of RWL-GNN using the Graph Convolutional Neural Network (GCNN) architecture, but the framework can be easily adapted to any existing GNN architecture. Simulation results on benchmark datasets validate the proposed method's accuracy and computational efficiency, with code available at https://github.com/Bharat-Runwal/RWL-GNN.

Predicting the motion of other vehicles surrounding an autonomous car is essential for effective and efficient decision-making. Deep neural networks, although powerful, pose challenges due to their black-box nature in high-stakes applications like autonomous driving. To address this issue, we introduce a structured framework for forecasting opposing vehicles' movements using deep neural networks, ensuring that the output trajectories are constrained. This constraint allows for reliable quality guarantees on the predictions. We compare the performance of this model with an LSTM-based encoder-decoder architecture using data from realistic simulations. The results show that our approach surpasses the baseline in accuracy while maintaining the required quality standards. This achievement proves the model's potential for a reliable real-world application. The model was successfully implemented on a car from the Technical University of Munich for the Indy Autonomous Challenge 2021. The research code is freely available on GitHub at www.github.com/TUMFTM/MixNet.

Research on galaxy population has traditionally divided galaxies into two categories based on star formation and structure: star-forming disk galaxies and passive, bulge-dominated or spherical galaxies. This study uses data from the MaNGA galaxy survey to examine the kinematic characteristics of 4574 galaxies in the local universe, finding that galaxies at a similar mass have a more complex distribution than previously assumed. By analyzing the relationship between a galaxy's rotation velocity and velocity dispersion, researchers identified at least two sub-populations among fast-rotating galaxies, with disk galaxies making up the majority. Furthermore, the study reveals that passive galaxies, characterized by low star formation rates, contain a mix of different galaxy types, including disk galaxies, while disk galaxies represent approximately 30% of passive galaxies, a significantly higher proportion than slow rotators. These findings indicate that a majority of galaxies in the local universe are disk galaxies, with most transforming into less rotationally supported systems following a period of reduced star formation, while spherical galaxies, though present, are not the typical endpoint for galaxy evolution.

Tractable density models called normalizing flows can approximate intricate distributions, such as those of complex physical systems. Yet existing methods for training flows either exhibit mode-seeking behavior, rely on expensive simulations, or suffer from highly variable losses. To address these issues, flows are augmented with annealed importance sampling (AIS), which minimizes variance in importance weights when using the mass-covering $\alpha$-divergence with $\alpha=2$. The resulting Flow AIS Bootstrap (FAB) method uses AIS to generate samples in areas where the flow inaccurately approximates the target, thereby enabling the discovery of new modes. FAB is applied to complex multimodal targets, yielding highly accurate results where other methods fail. Furthermore, FAB achieves the first successful approximation of the alanine dipeptide molecule's Boltzmann distribution using solely the unnormalized target density, outperforming training via maximum likelihood on simulated samples while requiring a significantly lower number of target evaluations. Following reweighting with importance weights, FAB yields unbiased histograms of dihedral angles nearly indistinguishable from their true values.

Capturing users' diverse behaviors is a crucial component of modern e-commerce, frequently utilized in conjunction with optimizing click-through and conversion rate predictions. Many current techniques overlook the significant impact of two key user behavior characteristics: contextual dependence, where a user's interactions with one item are influenced by their previous actions on other items, and multiple time scales, indicating that users tend to click frequently but purchase less frequently over time. To address this, we introduce a novel multi-scale user behavior network named HEROES, which incorporates contextual information to predict users' behaviors at various scales. By implementing a hierarchical framework with two interconnected layers, HEROES can automatically learn suitable time scales to capture dynamic behavioral patterns. Furthermore, we propose using a novel recurrent unit based on the Hawkes process, which can integrate items' features with users' past behaviors to simulate excitement or discouragement. Additionally, HEROES can be integrated with survival analysis to create unbiased ranking systems. Through experiments on three large-scale datasets, HEROES demonstrates superior performance compared to existing methods.

The Lightning Network (LN) has witnessed accelerated growth in recent times, and it has become the most widely used solution to scale the Bitcoin blockchain. The LN's reliability relies on nodes being able to settle balances by closing channels, a process that requires verifying transactions on the Bitcoin blockchain within a predetermined timeframe. The inherent time constraints of the LN render it vulnerable to malicious attacks that aim to overload the Bitcoin blockchain, disrupting protocol execution. We investigate the LN's susceptibility to \emph{mass exit} attacks carried out by a small group of adversarial nodes. Specifically, we analyze two types of attacks: (i) The \emph{zombie} attack, where a subset of nodes deliberately become non-responsive, causing multiple channels to be locked for an extended period, exceeding the LN's protocol constraints. (ii) The \emph{mass double-spend} attack, where a group of nodes submit numerous closing transactions that utilize outdated channel states, prompting honest nodes to quickly respond with invalidating transactions. Simulation results indicate that, under historically realistic congestion conditions and mild statistical assumptions about channel balances, both attacks can be executed by a very small coalition. We formulated the problem of identifying the worst-case coalition of adversarial nodes as a graph cut problem to support our experimental findings, which are theoretically justified by the LN's scale-free network topology.

Our research aims to discover new cataclysmic variable stars (CVs), specifically AR~Scorpii-type binary systems. We utilize GAIA data and light curves from the Zwicky Transient Facility, Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, and Lulin One-meter Telescope to identify potential candidates. From our analysis, eight sources emerged as CV prospects, with six being newly identified. Two previously recognized CVs were re-examined, and two systems exhibiting eclipses and associated with X-ray sources, and a single polar candidate were discovered. Two polar candidates are potentially located within the period gap of CVs, and six others possess shorter orbital periods. Although we didn't find a suitable candidate for AR~Scorpii-type binaries, our study implies that CV systems emitting X-rays but lacking frequent outbursts may have been overlooked in previous surveys.

Most theoretical studies of shear instability in layered fluids assume that shear and density gradients coincide. However, we investigate how asymmetry affects shear instability, using a combination of linear stability analysis and direct numerical simulations. Our results show that asymmetry leads to a mix of characteristics from both Holmboe and Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities, and provide a method to determine whether the instabilities resemble Holmboe or Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities more closely. Furthermore, the asymmetric instabilities generate asymmetrical mixing patterns that combine features of overturning and scouring flows, and often realign the shear and density gradients. We also observe a convergence in the distribution of the Richardson number in simulations with asymmetry, indicating that asymmetry reduces the influence of specific parameters on Kelvin-Helmholtz-driven mixing events. These findings have significant implications for the interpretation of data from oceanographic research, particularly with regards to the influence of small-scale details on turbulent behavior.

In recent years, significant advancements have been made in unpaired image denoising. However, the effectiveness of current methods heavily relies on knowing the underlying noise patterns or making assumptions that don't always apply in real-world scenarios. By shifting the focus from noise statistics to structural aspects, a more robust approach to image denoising can be developed. With this goal in mind, we present a self-supervised, unpaired denoising technique based on spatial degradation and regularized refinement. This method outperforms existing methods and demonstrates consistent performance across various datasets.

The integrin transmembrane receptor protein plays a vital role in cell membrane dynamics by reorganizing the actin network and connecting the cell membrane to the extracellular matrix through complex mechanical processes. Integrin facilitates the formation of specific lipid and protein clusters that are crucial for certain endocytosis mechanisms at active membrane regions. To understand this process, we have developed a simplified model that accounts for the interaction between integrin's on and off states and the intrinsic dynamics of the cell membrane. This model provides a mathematical equation for the membrane's deformation, local velocity, and clustering of lipids, which are influenced by the stochastic movement of integrin and the membrane's properties.

Researchers develop numerical solutions to the Einstein constraint equations on a range of compact, orientable three-dimensional spaces with complex topological features. They compute a simple, constant mean curvature solution and a more complex, non-constant mean curvature solution on manifolds classified under three different geometrization categories. Notably, the constant mean curvature solutions derived also solve the Yamabe problem, which involves transforming a geometry into one with uniform scalar curvature.

Homophily, a principle that suggests "birds of a feather flock together," can be quantified in networks.  A network is considered homophilic if the connections between similar vertices are significantly denser than random chance would suggest.  We define this phenomenon using a random coloring model, where a vector representing the sizes of subgraphs within classes is seen as the outcome of a random vector.  A network is deemed homophilic at a certain significance level if the probability of observing such an extreme outcome is lower than that level.  Since calculating this probability is difficult, we use a multidimensional extension of Cantelli's inequality to find an upper bound, known as the homophily index, which can be used to measure network homophily.  We also derive a formula for the covariance matrix of subgraph sizes under the random coloring model, which can be used to compute the homophily index more accurately.

The Fabbri-Russo model, representing a two-dimensional dilaton gravity theory, encompasses multiple parameters denoted as "$n$" that characterize specific types of gravity. The Russo-Susskind-Thorlacius model, which matches the $n=1$ condition, serves as a specific application of the generalized model. Within this model, researchers have analyzed the dynamics of Page curves and the entanglement island in the context of eternal and evaporating black holes. The emergence of islands leads to decelerated growth of the entanglement entropy of radiation beyond the Page time, thereby adhering to unitarity principles. In the context of eternal black holes, the fine-grained entropy reaches a saturation value twice that of the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, while in evaporating black holes, this entropy eventually drops to zero. The parameter "$n$" significantly influences the early behavior of the Page curve, although at late times and large distance limits, its effects become exponentially suppressed, rendering the shape of the Page curve largely independent of "$n$" in leading order. Furthermore, researchers have explored the relationship between entanglement islands and firewalls, concluding that islands offer a more suitable solution to the quantum entanglement-monogamy problem. The gravity/ensemble duality has also been proposed as a potential resolution to the state conundrum posed by the island formula.

A common technique called temporal point process (TPP) is used to analyze sequences of events with timestamps and understand their probability of occurrence based on historical influences. Despite previous studies focusing on the accuracy of TPP models by maximizing their likelihood, they often fail to accurately predict future event times, resulting in a significant gap between generated and observed timestamps. Generative models have achieved remarkable success in image generation by producing high-quality samples, but their potential in modeling event occurrences for TPP has yet to be explored comprehensively. In this work, we bridge this gap by developing a unified generative framework called GNTPP to investigate its feasibility and effectiveness in enhancing TPP model predictive performance. Furthermore, we improve the attentive models by incorporating an adaptive weighting term that takes into account the relationships between historical events and their time intervals. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior predictive capabilities of GNTPP with various generative decoders and the benefits of the revised attention mechanism. To the best of our knowledge, this work presents the first comprehensive study of generative models in a unified framework for TPP and provides an open codebase to facilitate future research in Neural TPPs.

For vehicular networks, Federated edge learning technology is a promising solution to mitigate computation overhead while preserving user privacy. The system enables vehicles to upload data to edge servers, which update local models and return results, all without sharing original data. However, the limited cache capacity and time-varying wireless channels in vehicular networks pose significant challenges in determining the optimal number of vehicles to upload data to maintain a stable cache queue while maximizing accuracy. Moreover, selectively choosing vehicles with varying resource capabilities affects data volume, impacting overall model accuracy. To address this, we introduce a vehicle selection strategy that balances accuracy and cache stability, accounting for the diverse statuses of all vehicles within the edge server's coverage. Our proposed approach demonstrates superior performance in simulation studies compared to established benchmarks.
